knowledge_point.title: Identifying the Local Area Scale Factor of a Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(2,1)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}\log{\left(u - v \right)}\\- u^{2} + v\end{bmatrix}?
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))\approx\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\cdot\underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\& =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{u - v}&- \frac{1}{u - v}\\- 2 u&1\end{vmatrix}\\& =\left(\frac{1}{u - v}\right)\cdot (1)-\left(- \frac{1}{u - v}\right)\cdot (- 2 u)\\& =\frac{1-2u}{u-v}\\\left.\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(2,1)} & =\left(- \frac{2 u - 1}{u - v}\right)\big|_{u=2,v=1}\\& =- \frac{2 (2) - 1}{- (1) + (2)}\\& =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & \approx|-3|\cdot\delta A\\ & =3\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Identifying the Local Area Scale Factor of a Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(2,-1)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}2 \left(u + v\right)^{2}\\2 \left(u - v\right)^{3}\end{bmatrix}?
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))\approx\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\cdot\underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\& =\begin{vmatrix}4 \left(u + v\right)&4 \left(u + v\right)\\6 \left(u - v\right)^{2}&- 6 \left(u - v\right)^{2}\end{vmatrix}\\& =(4 \left(u + v\right))\cdot (- 6 \left(u - v\right)^{2})-(4 \left(u + v\right))\cdot (6 \left(u - v\right)^{2})\\& =- 48 u^{3} + 48 u^{2} v + 48 u v^{2} - 48 v^{3}\\& =- 48 \left(u - v\right)^{2} \left(u + v\right)\\\left.\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(2,-1)} & =\left(- 48 \left(u - v\right)^{2} \left(u + v\right)\right)\big|_{u=2,v=-1}\\& =- 48 \left(- (-1) + (2)\right)^{2} \left((-1) + (2)\right)\\& =-432\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & \approx|-432|\cdot\delta A\\ & =432\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Identifying the Local Area Scale Factor of a Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(2,-3)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}3 u v^{3}\\2 u^{2} + 3 v^{2}\end{bmatrix}?
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))\approx\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\cdot\underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\& =\begin{vmatrix}3 v^{3}&9 u v^{2}\\4 u&6 v\end{vmatrix}\\& =(3 v^{3})\cdot (6 v)-(9 u v^{2})\cdot (4 u)\\& =- 36 u^{2} v^{2} + 18 v^{4}\\& =- 18 v^{2} \left(2 u^{2} - v^{2}\right)\\\left.\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(2,-3)} & =\left(- 18 v^{2} \left(2 u^{2} - v^{2}\right)\right)\big|_{u=2,v=-3}\\& =- 18 (-3)^{2} \left(- (-3)^{2} + 2 (2)^{2}\right)\\& =162\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & \approx|162|\cdot\delta A\\ & =162\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\left(u - 4\right)^{2} \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=\left(u - 4\right)^{2},\,y(u,v,w)=v,\,z(u,v,w)=w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2 u - 8 & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2 u - 8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(2 u - 8)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(2 u - 8)(1\cdot(1)-(0)\cdot(0)) \\  & =2 \left(u - 4\right).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 2 \left(u - 4\right) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The critical points lie on the plane $u - 4=0.$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: The critical points lie on the plane $v - 4=0.$
The critical points lie on the plane $u + 4=0.$
The critical points lie on the plane $u=0.$
The critical points lie on the plane $u - 4=0.$
The critical points lie on the plane $w - 4=0.$

question.:question/problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u - v + 2 w \\ - 4 u^{2} + v \\ - 4 u^{2} + 3 u + w\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u - v + 2 w,\,y(u,v,w)=- 4 u^{2} + v,\,z(u,v,w)=- 4 u^{2} + 3 u + w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-1 & \frac{∂x}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =- 8 u & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =3 - 8 u & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ - 8 u & 1 & 0 \\ 3 - 8 u & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}+(1)\begin{vmatrix}- 8 u & 0 \\ 3 - 8 u & 1\end{vmatrix}+(2)\begin{vmatrix}- 8 u & 1 \\ 3 - 8 u & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)(1\cdot(1)-(0)\cdot(0))+(1)(- 8 u\cdot(1)-(0)\cdot(3 - 8 u))+(2)(- 8 u\cdot(0)-(1)\cdot(3 - 8 u)) \\  & =8 u - 5.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 8 u - 5 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The critical points lie on the plane $8 u - 5=0.$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u v,\,y(u,v,w)=5 u + 7 v,\,z(u,v,w)=w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u & \frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =5 & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & =7 & \frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}v & u & 0 \\ 5 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(v)\begin{vmatrix}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}+(- u)\begin{vmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(v)(7\cdot(1)-(0)\cdot(0))+(- u)(5\cdot(1)-(0)\cdot(0)) \\  & =- 5 u + 7 v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ - 5 u + 7 v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The critical points lie on the plane $- 5 u + 7 v=0.$

question.:question/problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}(u-1)(v+2) \\ (u-1)+(v+2) \\ (w+1)\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=(u-1)(v+2),\,y(u,v,w)=(u-1)+(v+2),\,z(u,v,w)=(w+1).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =(v+2) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =(u-1) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}(v+2) & (u-1) & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}(v+2) & (u-1) \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(v+2)-(u-1).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ (v+2)-(u-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $(v+2)-(u-1)=0$ defines the plane $(v+2)=(u-1)..$

question.:question/problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{(u-1)}^{2}-(v+2) \\ {(u-1)}^{2}+(v+2) \\ {e}^{(w+1)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={(u-1)}^{2}-(v+2),\,y(u,v,w)={(u-1)}^{2}+(v+2),\,z(u,v,w)={e}^{(w+1)}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2(u-1) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2(u-1) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{(w+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2(u-1) & -1 & 0 \\ 2(u-1) & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{(w+1)}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{(w+1)}\begin{vmatrix}2(u-1) & -1 \\ 2(u-1) & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{(w+1)}(2(u-1)+2(u-1)) \\  & =4(u-1){e}^{(w+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 4(u-1){e}^{(w+1)} & =0 \\ (u-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $(u-1)=0$ defines the plane $(u-1)=0,$ i.e., plane $u=1$.

The critical points are exactly the domain points satisfying $v + 2=0.$

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

$$
\iint_D x + y\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y
$$

where $D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 4,\quad 0\le x + y\le 2\}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le x\le 4,\quad 0\le x + y\le 2,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x + y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):0\le u\le 4,\,0\le v\le 2\}.
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left|\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\right|\\&=1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=1=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\ne0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Solving the transformation equations gives $x=u,\ y=- u + v$, so the transformation is one-to-one on this domain.

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D x + y\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y & =\iint_\Delta v\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\iint_\Delta \left(v\right)\cdot \left(1\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =1\int_{0}^{2} [\int_{0}^{4} v\,\mathrm{d}u]\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =1\int_{0}^{2} v[\int_{0}^{4} 1\,\mathrm{d}u]\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =1\int_{0}^{2} v\left[u\right]_{0}^{4}\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =1\int_{0}^{2} v\left(\left(4\right)-(\left(0\right))\right)\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(4\right)\int_{0}^{2} v\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(4\right)\left[\frac{v^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{2} \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(4\right)\left(\left(2\right)-(\left(0\right))\right) \\ & =\left(1\right)\cdot \left(4\right)\cdot \left(2\right) \\ & =8\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

$$
\iint_D e^{x^{2} + x + 4 y}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y
$$

where $D=\{(x,y):1\le x\le 4,\quad 1\le x^{2} + 4 y\le 3\}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
1\le x\le 4,\quad 1\le x^{2} + 4 y\le 3,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x^{2} + 4 y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):1\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le 3\}.
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left|\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\2 x & 4\end{bmatrix}\right|\\&=4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Note that $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\ne0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Solving the transformation equations gives $x=u,\ y=- \frac{u^{2}}{4} + \frac{v}{4}$, so the transformation is one-to-one on this domain.

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D e^{x^{2} + x + 4 y}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y & =\iint_D e^{x+(x^{2} + 4 y)}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y \\ & =\iint_\Delta e^{u + v}\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\iint_\Delta \left(e^{u + v}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\int_{1}^{4} [\int_{1}^{3} e^{u} e^{v}\,\mathrm{d}v]\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\int_{1}^{4} \left(e^{u}\right)[\int_{1}^{3} e^{v}\,\mathrm{d}v]\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\int_{1}^{4} \left(e^{u}\right)\left[e^{v}\right]_{1}^{3}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\int_{1}^{4} \left(e^{u}\right)\left(\left(e^{3}\right)-(\left(e\right))\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot \left(e^{3} - e\right)\int_{1}^{4} e^{u}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot \left(e^{3} - e\right)\left[e^{u}\right]_{1}^{4} \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot \left(e^{3} - e\right)\left(\left(e^{4}\right)-(\left(e\right))\right) \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot \left(e^{4} - e\right)\cdot \left(e^{3} - e\right) \\ & =\frac{e^{2}}{4} - \frac{e^{4}}{4} - \frac{e^{5}}{4} + \frac{e^{7}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}T^{-1}(-1,1)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(-1\right)+\left(2\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(-1\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(1,1) \\ T^{-1}(2,1)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(2\right)+\left(2\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(2\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(4,1) \\ T^{-1}(-4,4)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(-4\right)+\left(2\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(-4\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(4,4) \\ T^{-1}(-7,4)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(-7\right)+\left(2\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(0\right),\left(0\right)\cdot \left(-7\right)+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(1,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\partial u/\partial x&\partial u/\partial y\\\partial v/\partial x&\partial v/\partial y\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=1
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
\iint_D \left(3 x - y\right) e^{\left(3 x - y\right)^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(3,8)$, $(4,11)$, $(4,8)$ and $(3,5)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=\left(3 x - y\right) e^{\left(3 x - y\right)^{2}}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x,\qquad v=3 x - y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y)\mapsto (u(x,y),v(x,y)).
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T^{-1}(3,8)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(3\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot \left(8\right)+\left(0\right),\left(3\right)\cdot \left(3\right)+\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(8\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(3,1) \\ T^{-1}(4,11)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot \left(11\right)+\left(0\right),\left(3\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(11\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(4,1) \\ T^{-1}(4,8)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot \left(8\right)+\left(0\right),\left(3\right)\cdot \left(4\right)+\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(8\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(4,4) \\ T^{-1}(3,5)&=(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(3\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot \left(5\right)+\left(0\right),\left(3\right)\cdot \left(3\right)+\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(5\right)+\left(0\right)) \\ &=(3,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):3\le u\le 4,\ 1\le v\le 4\}
$$

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186198374/4e01b7b25bf48dabef3d.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\partial u/\partial x&\partial u/\partial y\\\partial v/\partial x&\partial v/\partial y\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1&0\\3&-1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=-1
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Solving these affine equations also gives

$$
x=u,\qquad y=3 u - v.
$$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D \left(3 x - y\right) e^{\left(3 x - y\right)^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y&=\iint_\Delta v e^{v^{2}}\,\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ &=\iint_\Delta v e^{v^{2}}\,\left|-1\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ &=1\cdot \int_{1}^{4}\int_{3}^{4}v e^{v^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ &=1\cdot \int_{1}^{4}v e^{v^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}v\cdot \int_{3}^{4}1\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=1\cdot \left[\frac{e^{v^{2}}}{2}\right]_{1}^{4}\cdot \left[u\right]_{3}^{4} \\ &=1\cdot \left(e^{\left(4\right)^{2}}/2-\left(e^{\left(1\right)^{2}}/2\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(4\right)-\left(\left(3\right)\right)\right) \\ &=1\cdot \left(\left(\frac{e^{16}}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{e}{2}\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(4\right)-\left(3\right)\right) \\ &=1\cdot \left(- \frac{e \left(1 - e^{15}\right)}{2}\right)\cdot \left(1\right) \\ &=- \frac{e \left(1 - e^{15}\right)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\iint_D f(x,y)\,dx\,dy=\iint_Δ f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\left|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\right|\,du\,dv.
$$

The supplied change of variables gives us the inverse function $T^{-1}$.

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $T^{-1}$.

$$
Δ=\{(u,v):4\le u\le 6,\ 1\le v\le 2\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T^{-1}$.

$$
\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix}1&1\\-1&1\end{vmatrix}=2.
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$.

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that the Jacobian determinant is nonzero everywhere inside $Δ$.

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables.

In this case, we first need to solve the transformation equations for $x$ and $y$, which gives

$$
x=\frac{u}{2} - \frac{v}{2},\qquad y=\frac{u}{2} + \frac{v}{2}.
$$

$$

$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

$$
u=2x+5y,\,v=x+3y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 5 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

In this case, we first need to solve the transformation equations

$$
u=2x+5y,\,v=x+3y
$$

 
for $x$ and $y$, which gives

$$
x=3u-5v,\,y=2v-u.
$$

 

Now, performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$

T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 16,\,2\le v\le 5\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\left(-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}\right)}=-\frac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(xy)^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}\cdot |\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{\int }_{1}^{16}\frac{{v}^{2}}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{v}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{16}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{v}^{2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{1}^{16}]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{v}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡16-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}{v}^{2}\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}\,{|}_{2}^{5} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{9}\cdot (125-8) \\  & =26\operatorname{ln}⁡4.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating a Triple Integral Using a Change of Variables

question.:question/problem:
Use the change of variables 

$$
u=2 x + 2 y,\quad v=y - 2 z,\quad w=4 z
$$

to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\iiint_R \left(\left(2 x + 2 y\right) \left(y - 2 z\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}V,
$$

 
where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z):0\le 2 x + 2 y\le 3,\quad 0\le y - 2 z\le 2,\quad 0\le z\le 3\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=2 x + 2 y,\quad v=y - 2 z,\quad w=4 z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v,w):0\le u\le 3,\quad 0\le v\le 2,\quad 0\le w\le 12\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(4\right)(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(4\right)\left(\left(2\right)\cdot \left(1\right)-\left(2\right)\cdot \left(0\right)\right) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{8}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R \left(\left(2 x + 2 y\right) \left(y - 2 z\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}V & =\iiint_\Delta \left(u v\right)\cdot \left|\frac{1}{8}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\iiint_\Delta \left(\frac{u v}{8}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{12}\left(\frac{u v}{8}\right)\,\mathrm{d}w\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{2}\left(\left[\frac{u v w}{8}\right]_{w=0}^{w=12}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{2}\left(\left(\frac{u v \left(12\right)}{8}\right)-\left(\frac{u v \left(0\right)}{8}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{2}\left(\left(\frac{3 u v}{2}\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{2}\left(\frac{3 u v}{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left[\frac{3 u v^{2}}{4}\right]_{v=0}^{v=2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(\frac{3 u \left(2\right)^{2}}{4}\right)-\left(\frac{3 u \left(0\right)^{2}}{4}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(3 u\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{3}\left(3 u\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{3 u^{2}}{2}\right]_{u=0}^{u=3} \\  & =\left(\frac{3 \left(3\right)^{2}}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{3 \left(0\right)^{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =\left(\frac{27}{2}\right)-\left(0\right) \\  & =\frac{27}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\iiint_R \left(\left(y + z\right) e^{x + y^{2}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}V,

where the region $R$ is given by

$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$

$$

$$

$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x + y^{2},\quad v=y + z,\quad w=4 z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v,w):1\le u\le 3,\quad 1\le v\le 3,\quad 4\le w\le 12\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 y & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(4\right)(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 y \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(4\right)\left(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(1\right)-\left(2 y\right)\cdot \left(0\right)\right) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R \left(\left(y + z\right) e^{x + y^{2}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}V & =\iiint_\Delta \left(v e^{u}\right)\cdot \left|\frac{1}{4}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\iiint_\Delta \left(\frac{v e^{u}}{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\int_{4}^{12}\left(\frac{v e^{u}}{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}w\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left[\frac{v w e^{u}}{4}\right]_{w=4}^{w=12}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(\frac{v \left(12\right) e^{u}}{4}\right)-\left(\frac{v \left(4\right) e^{u}}{4}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(3 v e^{u}\right)-\left(v e^{u}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(2 v e^{u}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left[v^{2} e^{u}\right]_{v=1}^{v=3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(\left(3\right)^{2} e^{u}\right)-\left(\left(1\right)^{2} e^{u}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(9 e^{u}\right)-\left(e^{u}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(8 e^{u}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\left[8 e^{u}\right]_{u=1}^{u=3} \\  & =\left(8 e^{\left(3\right)}\right)-\left(8 e^{\left(1\right)}\right) \\  & =\left(8 e^{3}\right)-\left(8 e\right) \\  & =- 8 e \left(- e^{2} + 1\right)\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}4xy\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u,\,y=v,\,z=6-3u-2v
$$

for $0\le u\le \frac{5}{2}$ and $0\le v\le \frac{1}{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,6-3u-2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(6-3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(6-3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 0 & -2\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,2,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨3,\,2,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =4xy\,{|}_{x=u\,y=v\,z=6-3u-2v} \\  & =4uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le \frac{5}{2},\,0\le v\le \frac{1}{2}\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}4xy\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4uv\sqrt{14}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{5}{2}}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{\frac{5}{2}}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{14}[\left(\frac{25}{4}\right)-(0)]\cdot [\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)-(0)] \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot \frac{25}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{25\sqrt{14}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u+v,\,y=u,\,z=v
$$

for $-\frac{3}{2}\le u\le \frac{3}{2}$ and $-\frac{1}{2}\le v\le 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,u,\,v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & ={x}^{2}-2yz\,{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u\,z=v} \\  & =(u+v)^{2}-2uv \\  & ={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-\frac{3}{2}\le u\le \frac{3}{2\},\,-\frac{1}{2}\le v\le 0},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}+{v}^{2})\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}({\int }_{-\frac{3}{2}}^{\frac{3}{2}}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}{[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u{v}^{2}]}_{u=-\frac{3}{2}}^{u=\frac{3}{2}}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}[(\frac{3v^{2}}{2}+\frac{9}{8})-(\left(-\frac{3v^{2}}{2}\right)+\left(-\frac{9}{8}\right))]\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}\frac{9}{4}+3{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[\frac{9}{4}v+{v}^{3}]}_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0} \\  & =\sqrt{3}[(0+0)-(\left(-\frac{9}{8}\right)+\left(-\frac{1}{8}\right))] \\  & =\sqrt{3}(0+0)-\sqrt{3}(-\frac{9}{8}-\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

{∬}_{S}(xy+z)\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u+v,\,y=u-v,\,z=0
$$

for $1\le u\le 2$ and $-\frac{1}{2}\le v\le 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,u-v,\,0⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,0,\,-2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+0+4} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =xy+z\,{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u-v\,z=0} \\  & =(u+v)(u-v) \\  & ={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,-\frac{1}{2}\le v\le 0\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(xy+z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\cdot 2\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}({\int }_{1}^{2}({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =2{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}{[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}-{v}^{2}u]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}v \\  & =2{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}[((-2v^{2})+\frac{8}{3})-((-v^{2})+\frac{1}{3})]\text{d}v \\  & =2{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}(\frac{7}{3}-{v}^{2})\text{d}v \\  & =2{[\frac{7v}{3}-\frac{{v}^{3}}{3}]}_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0} \\  & =2[(0+0)-(\left(-\frac{7}{6}\right)+\frac{1}{24})] \\  & =2[0+0-(-\frac{7}{6}+\frac{1}{24})] \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}2xz\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u,\,y=u+v,\,z=2v
$$

for $0\le u\le \frac{5}{2}$ and $0\le v\le \frac{1}{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,u+v,\,2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =2xz\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=2v} \\  & =2u(2v) \\  & =4uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le \frac{5}{2\},\,0\le v\le \frac{1}{2}},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}2xz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4uv\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\frac{5}{2}}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =3\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{\frac{5}{2}}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =3[\left(\frac{25}{4}\right)-(0)]\cdot [\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)-(0)] \\  & =3\cdot \frac{25}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{75}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

{∬}_{S}x(y+z)\,\text{d}S,

$$
x=2u,\,y=-3v,\,z=4v
$$

for $0\le u\le \frac{5}{2}$ and $0\le v\le \frac{1}{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u,\,-3v,\,4v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-3v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-3v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-3,\,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ -3 & 4\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-8,\,-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-8,\,-6⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(-8)^{2}+(-6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+64+36} \\  & =\sqrt{100} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =x(y+z)\,{|}_{x=2u\,y=-3v\,z=4v} \\  & =2u(-3v+4v) \\  & =2uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le \frac{5}{2\},\,0\le v\le \frac{1}{2}},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}x(y+z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2uv\cdot 10\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{\frac{5}{2}}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =5\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{\frac{5}{2}}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =5[\left(\frac{25}{4}\right)-(0)]\cdot [\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)-(0)] \\  & =5\cdot \frac{25}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{125}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}({x}^{2}-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=2u+v,\,y=2u-2v,\,z=u+2v
$$

for $-\frac{3}{2}\le u\le \frac{3}{2}$ and $-\frac{1}{2}\le v\le 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u+v,\,2u-2v,\,u+2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨6,\,-3,\,-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨6,\,-3,\,-6⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(-6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36+9+36} \\  & =\sqrt{81} \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & ={x}^{2}-{z}^{2}\,{|}_{x=2u+v\,y=2u-2v\,z=u+2v} \\  & =(2u+v)^{2}-(u+2v)^{2} \\  & =3{u}^{2}-3{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-\frac{3}{2}\le u\le \frac{3}{2\},\,-\frac{1}{2}\le v\le 0},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(3{u}^{2}-3{v}^{2})\cdot 9\,\text{d}A \\  & =9{∬}_{D}\,(3{u}^{2}-3{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =9{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}({\int }_{-\frac{3}{2}}^{\frac{3}{2}}(3{u}^{2}-3{v}^{2})\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =9{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}{[{u}^{3}-3{v}^{2}u]}_{-\frac{3}{2}}^{\frac{3}{2}}\,\text{d}v \\  & =9{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}[(\left(-\frac{9v^{2}}{2}\right)+\frac{27}{8})-(\frac{9v^{2}}{2}+\left(-\frac{27}{8}\right))]\text{d}v \\  & =9{\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}(\frac{27}{4}-9{v}^{2})\text{d}v \\  & =9\cdot [\frac{27v}{4}-3{v}^{3}]_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0} \\  & =9[(0+0)-(\left(-\frac{27}{8}\right)+\frac{3}{8})] \\  & =9\cdot (3) \\  & =27.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}(2x+y+z)\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u-v,\,3u+2,\,u+2v⟩
$$

 
over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,-\frac{1}{2}\le v\le 0\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{70}.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{70}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(2x+y+z)\,{|}_{x=2u-v\,y=3u+2\,z=u+2v} \\  & =2(2u-v)+(3u+2)+(u+2v) \\  & =8u+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(8u+2)\sqrt{70}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{70}{∬}_{D}\,(8u+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{70}{\int }_{1}^{2}(8u+2)\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{70}\cdot [4{u}^{2}+2u]_{1}^{2}\cdot [v]_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{0} \\  & =\sqrt{70}[(4+16)-(2+4)]\cdot [(0)-(\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right))] \\  & =\sqrt{70}\cdot 14\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =7\sqrt{70}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$

$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by 

$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\langle - \cos{\left(t \right)}, - 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}, 1\rangle$ for $t\in [0,2 \pi).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=\langle 3 y, - 3 x, 0\rangle,$ evaluate the integral

$$
\iint_S\operatorname{curl}F\cdot\mathrm{d}S.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=- \cos{\left(t \right)},\quad y=- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)},\quad z=1
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\langle 3 y, - 3 x, 0\rangle \\ & =\langle 3 \left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right), - 3 \left(- \cos{\left(t \right)}\right), 0\rangle \\ & =\langle - 9 \sin{\left(t \right)}, 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}, 0\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r\prime(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\langle \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(- \cos{\left(t \right)}\right), \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right), \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(1\right)\rangle \\ & =\langle \sin{\left(t \right)}, - 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}, 0\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r\prime(t) & =\langle - 9 \sin{\left(t \right)}, 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}, 0\rangle\cdot \langle \sin{\left(t \right)}, - 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}, 0\rangle \\ & =\left(- 9 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\cdot \left(\sin{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\cdot \left(- 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot \left(0\right) \\ & =\left(- 9 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(- 9 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =- 9 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} - 9 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)} \\ & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S\operatorname{curl}F\cdot\mathrm dS & =\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr \\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi} F(r(t))\cdot r\prime(t)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left(-9\right)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\left[\left(- 9 t\right)\right]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ & =\left(\left(- 18 \pi\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right)\right) \\ & =- 18 \pi\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=- 2 \cos{\left(t \right)},\quad y=- \sin{\left(t \right)},\quad z=3 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 3
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\langle 2 y - 2 z, - 2 x + 2 z, 2 x - 2 y\rangle \\ & =\langle 2 \left(- \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) - 2 \left(3 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 3\right), - 2 \left(- 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) + 2 \left(3 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 3\right), 2 \left(- 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) - 2 \left(- \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\rangle \\ & =\langle 6 - 8 \sin{\left(t \right)}, 6 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 4 \cos{\left(t \right)} - 6, 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 4 \cos{\left(t \right)}\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r\prime(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\langle \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(- 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right), \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(- \sin{\left(t \right)}\right), \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(3 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 3\right)\rangle \\ & =\langle 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}, - \cos{\left(t \right)}, 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r\prime(t) & =\langle 6 - 8 \sin{\left(t \right)}, 6 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 4 \cos{\left(t \right)} - 6, 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 4 \cos{\left(t \right)}\rangle\cdot \langle 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}, - \cos{\left(t \right)}, 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\rangle \\ & =\left(6 - 8 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\cdot \left(2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(6 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 4 \cos{\left(t \right)} - 6\right)\cdot \left(- \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 4 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\cdot \left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ & =\left(- 16 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 12 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(- 6 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)} - 4 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(6 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)} - 12 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ & =- 16 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 12 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 16 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)} \\ & =12 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)} - 16\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the volume bounded by the region $R,$ given by

$$
R=\big\{(x,y,z)\, :\, 0\le 3 x\le 6,\quad 0\le 2 x + y\le 3,\quad 0\le 3 z\le 5\big\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$
V={∭}_{R}\text{d}V.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required volume, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$
0\le 3 x\le 6,\quad 0\le 2 x + y\le 3,\quad 0\le 3 z\le 5,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=3 x,\quad v=2 x + y,\quad w=3 z.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y,z)\longmapsto(u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z)).
$$

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\Delta=\big\{(u,v,w):0\le u\le 6,\quad 0\le v\le 3,\quad 0\le w\le 5\big\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(3\right)(-1)^{1+1}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix}+\left(0\right)(-1)^{1+2}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix}+\left(0\right)(-1)^{1+3}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

The map to $R$ is

$$
T(u,v,w)=\left(\frac{u}{3},- \frac{2 u}{3} + v,\frac{w}{3}\right).
$$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R\mathrm{d}V & =\iiint_\Delta 1\cdot |\frac{1}{9}|\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\int_{0}^{6}\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{9}\,\mathrm{d}w\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot \int_{0}^{6}1\,\mathrm{d}u\cdot \int_{0}^{3}1\,\mathrm{d}v\cdot \int_{0}^{5}1\,\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot [u]_{0}^{6}\cdot [v]_{0}^{3}\cdot [w]_{0}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot \left(\left(\left(6\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right)\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(\left(3\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right)\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(\left(5\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right)\right)\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot \left(\left(6\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(3\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(5\right)-\left(0\right)\right) \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing the Volume of a Region Using a Change of Variables

question.:question/problem:
Find the volume bounded by the region $R,$ given by

$$
R=\big\{(x,y,z)\, :\, 2\le x\le 8,\quad 1\le - 3 x^{2} - y - 2 z\le 4,\quad 1\le \sqrt{z}\le 4\big\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$
V={∭}_{R}\text{d}V.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required volume, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$
2\le x\le 8,\quad 1\le - 3 x^{2} - y - 2 z\le 4,\quad 1\le \sqrt{z}\le 4,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=x,\quad v=- 3 x^{2} - y - 2 z,\quad w=\sqrt{z}.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y,z)\longmapsto(u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z)).
$$

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\Delta=\big\{(u,v,w):2\le u\le 8,\quad 1\le v\le 4,\quad 1\le w\le 4\big\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ - 6 x & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{z}}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(1\right)(-1)^{1+1}\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{z}}\end{vmatrix}+\left(0\right)(-1)^{1+2}\begin{vmatrix}- 6 x & -2 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{z}}\end{vmatrix}+\left(0\right)(-1)^{1+3}\begin{vmatrix}- 6 x & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =- \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{z}} \\  & =- \frac{1}{2 w}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=- 2 w.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

The map to $R$ is

$$
T(u,v,w)=\left(u,- 3 u^{2} - v - 2 w^{2},w^{2}\right).
$$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R\mathrm{d}V & =\iiint_\Delta 1\cdot |- 2 w|\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\int_{2}^{8}\int_{1}^{4}\int_{1}^{4}2 w\,\mathrm{d}w\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =1\cdot \int_{2}^{8}1\,\mathrm{d}u\cdot \int_{1}^{4}1\,\mathrm{d}v\cdot \int_{1}^{4}2 w\,\mathrm{d}w \\  & =1\cdot [u]_{2}^{8}\cdot [v]_{1}^{4}\cdot [w^{2}]_{1}^{4} \\  & =1\cdot \left(\left(\left(8\right)\right)-\left(\left(2\right)\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(\left(4\right)\right)-\left(\left(1\right)\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(\left(4\right)^{2}\right)-\left(\left(1\right)^{2}\right)\right) \\  & =1\cdot \left(\left(8\right)-\left(2\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(4\right)-\left(1\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(16\right)-\left(1\right)\right) \\  & =270\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$

$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$

$$

$$

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\Delta=\big\{(u,v,w):2\le u\le 8,\quad 1\le v\le 4,\quad 2\le w\le 7\big\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(-3\right)(-1)^{1+1}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{vmatrix}+\left(0\right)(-1)^{1+2}\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}+\left(2\right)(-1)^{1+3}\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-6\end{aligned}

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))$, given that

$$
u=8 x\qquad v=y\qquad w=z.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation

$$
T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T$ is $\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}$.

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}$, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$.

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=8 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=1 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=8\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=8\left(1\cdot 1-0\right) \\ &=8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: x,y,z real; nonzero constant inverse determinant

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}2\left(y{z}^{2}\right) \\ 4\left(z{x}^{2}\right) \\ 4\left(x{y}^{2}\right)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z>0.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=2\left(y{z}^{2}\right),\,v(x,y,z)=4\left(z{x}^{2}\right),\,w(x,y,z)=4\left(x{y}^{2}\right).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =2\left({z}^{2}\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2\left(2yz\right) \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =4\left(2xz\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =4\left({x}^{2}\right) \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =4\left({y}^{2}\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =4\left(2xy\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $2, 4, 4$ multiplies the determinant by $32$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2\left({z}^{2}\right) & 2\left(2yz\right) \\ 4\left(2xz\right) & 0 & 4\left({x}^{2}\right) \\ 4\left({y}^{2}\right) & 4\left(2xy\right) & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =32\left(-{z}^{2}\begin{vmatrix}2xz & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 0\end{vmatrix}+2yz\begin{vmatrix}2xz & 0 \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =32\left(-{z}^{2}(0-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})+2yz(4{x}^{2}yz-0)\right)\\  & =32\left({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\right)\\  & =288 x^{2} y^{2} z^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}32\left(9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\right) & =32\left(9{({x}^{3}{y}^{3}{z}^{3})}^{2/3}\right) \\  & =32\left(9{(y{z}^{2}\cdot z{x}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2})}^{2/3}\right) \\  & =32\left(9(\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)\left(\frac{v}{4}\right)\left(\frac{w}{4}\right))^{2/3}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[3]{2}}{36 \left(u v w\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=2\left(3x+yz\right),\,v=4\left(z\right),\,w=4\left(-y\right).
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2\left(3\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =2\left(z\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2\left(y\right) \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =4\left(1\right) \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =4\left(-1\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $2, 4, 4$ multiplies the determinant by $32$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2\left(3\right) & 2\left(z\right) & 2\left(y\right) \\ 0 & 0 & 4\left(1\right) \\ 0 & 4\left(-1\right) & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =32\left(3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =32\left(3(0+1)\right)\\  & =96\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{96}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Circulation Over Space Curves

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=\left(- y\right)\,i+\left(x\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\left(3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\left(1 - t^{2}\right)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)},\quad y=4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)},\quad z=1 - t^{2}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\left(- y\right)\,i+\left(x\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k \\ & =\left(- 4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(1 - t^{2}\right)\,k \\ & =\left(- 3 \pi \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(4 \pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\left(- 2 t\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(\left(- 4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k\right)\cdot\left(\left(- 3 \pi \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(4 \pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\left(- 2 t\right)\,k\right) \\ & =\left(- 4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\cdot\left(- 3 \pi \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)+\left(3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\cdot\left(4 \pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot\left(- 2 t\right) \\ & =\left(12 \pi \sin^{2}{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)+\left(12 \pi \cos^{2}{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =12 \pi\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\left(u + 1\right)^{2} \\ 4 v + 12\end{bmatrix},
$$

is (locally) orientation-reversing?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\left(u + 1\right)^{2} \\ 4 v + 12\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} &=\begin{vmatrix}2 u + 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\ &=(2 u + 2)\cdot (4)-(0)\cdot (0) \\ &=8 u + 8.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}8 u + 8 &<0 \\ u < -1\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the equation

$$
u = -1
$$

defines a vertical line.

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:
