knowledge_point.title: Finding Regions Where a Transformation is Orientation-Preserving or Reversing

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}2 v + \left(u + 1\right)^{2} + 6 \\ - 3 u - \left(v + 3\right)^{2} - 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

is (locally) orientation-reversing?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}2 v + \left(u + 1\right)^{2} + 6 \\ - 3 u - \left(v + 3\right)^{2} - 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} &=\begin{vmatrix}2 u + 2 & 2 \\ -3 & - 2 v - 6\end{vmatrix} \\ &=(2 u + 2)\cdot (- 2 v - 6)-(2)\cdot (-3) \\ &=- 4 u v - 12 u - 4 v - 6.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}- 4 u v - 12 u - 4 v - 6 &<0 \\ \left(u + 1\right) \left(v + 3\right) > \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solution $v > -3 + \frac{3}{2 \left(u + 1\right)}$ for $u>-1$ and $v < -3 + \frac{3}{2 \left(u + 1\right)}$ for $u<-1.$ At $u=-1,$ the Jacobian is positive, so this line is excluded from the required region.

Notice that the equation

$$
v = -3 + \frac{3}{2 \left(u + 1\right)}
$$

defines a hyperbola.

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186129283/plot-4ffed708e8033c8201bf.png)

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by

$$

is (locally) orientation-preserving?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving at the points where the Jacobian determinant is positive:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}>0.
$$

We have

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{(u + 1)}^{2}-v \\ (u + 1)v+1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2(u + 1) & -1 \\ v & (u + 1)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(u + 1)\cdot (u + 1)-v\cdot (-1) \\  & =2{(u + 1)}^{2}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(u + 1)}^{2}+v & >0 \\ v & >-2{(u + 1)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=-2{(u + 1)}^{2}
$$

defines a parabola, and the coordinates of, say, $(0,1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving must be the following:

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating a Line Integral Using Stokes' Theorem

question.:question/problem: Let $C$ be the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ and the plane $z=1$. The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above. Given that $\text{curl}\,F=\langle - 3 x z,\,- 3 y z,\,3 x + 3 z^{2}\rangle$, use Stokes' theorem to evaluate $\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C.$ One such surface is our graph $S$ with the equation

$$
z=g(x,y)=1.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(1\right)=0\\
\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(1\right)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F|_{z=g(x,y)}&=\langle - 3 x z,\,- 3 y z,\,3 x + 3 z^{2}\rangle|_{z=1}\\
&=\langle - 3 x,\,- 3 y,\,3 x + 3\rangle\\
&=\langle - 3 x,\,- 3 y,\,3 x + 3\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S\text{curl}\,F\cdot\mathrm{d}S&=\iint_D(-P g_x-Q g_y+R)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(-\left(- 3 x\right)\left(0\right)-\left(- 3 y\right)\left(0\right)+\left(3 x + 3\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left((0)+(0)+(3 x + 3)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(3 x + 3\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.
Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=1.$ Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\cos\theta,\quad y=r\sin\theta,\quad \mathrm{d}A=r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta,
$$

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D\left(3 x + 3\right)\,\mathrm{d}A
&=\int_0^{1}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(3 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 3\right)r\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{1}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(3 r^{2} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 3 r\right)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{1}\left[3 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 3 r \theta\right]_0^{2\pi}\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{1}\left[\left(6 \pi r\right)-\left(0\right)\right]\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{1}\left(6 \pi r\right)\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\left[3 \pi r^{2}\right]_0^{1}\\
&=\left[\left(3 \pi\right)\right]-\left[\left(0\right)\right]\\
&=3 \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $C$ be the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=4$ and the surface $z=\left(x - 1\right)^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2}$. The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above. Given that $\text{curl}\,F=\langle 2 x + 2 y,\,- 2 x + 2 y,\,- 4 z\rangle$, use Stokes' theorem to evaluate $\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C.$ One such surface is our graph $S$ with the equation

$$
z=g(x,y)=\left(x - 1\right)^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\left(x - 1\right)^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2}\right)=2 x - 2\\
\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\left(x - 1\right)^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2}\right)=2 y + 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F|_{z=g(x,y)}&=\langle 2 x + 2 y,\,- 2 x + 2 y,\,- 4 z\rangle|_{z=\left(x - 1\right)^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2}}\\
&=\langle 2 x + 2 y,\,- 2 x + 2 y,\,- 4 \left(x - 1\right)^{2} - 4 \left(y + 1\right)^{2}\rangle\\
&=\langle 2 x + 2 y,\,- 2 x + 2 y,\,- 4 x^{2} + 8 x - 4 y^{2} - 8 y - 8\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S\text{curl}\,F\cdot\mathrm{d}S&=\iint_D(-P g_x-Q g_y+R)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(-\left(2 x + 2 y\right)\left(2 x - 2\right)-\left(- 2 x + 2 y\right)\left(2 y + 2\right)+\left(- 4 x^{2} + 8 x - 4 y^{2} - 8 y - 8\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left((\left(- 2 x - 2 y\right) \left(2 x - 2\right))+(\left(2 x - 2 y\right) \left(2 y + 2\right))+(- 4 x^{2} + 8 x - 4 y^{2} - 8 y - 8)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(- 8 x^{2} + 16 x - 8 y^{2} - 8 y - 8\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.
Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=4.$ Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\cos\theta,\quad y=r\sin\theta,\quad \mathrm{d}A=r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta,
$$

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D\left(- 8 x^{2} + 16 x - 8 y^{2} - 8 y - 8\right)\,\mathrm{d}A
&=\int_0^{2}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(- 8 r^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 8 r^{2} \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 8 r \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 16 r \cos{\left(\theta \right)} - 8\right)r\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{2}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(- 8 r^{3} \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 8 r^{3} \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)} - 8 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 16 r^{2} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} - 8 r\right)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{2}\left[- 8 r^{3} \left(\frac{\theta}{2} - \frac{\sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{2}\right) - 8 r^{3} \left(\frac{\theta}{2} + \frac{\sin{\left(\theta \right)} \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{2}\right) + 16 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 8 r^{2} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} - 8 r \theta\right]_0^{2\pi}\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{2}\left[\left(- 16 \pi r^{3} + 8 r^{2} - 16 \pi r\right)-\left(8 r^{2}\right)\right]\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{2}\left(16 \pi r \left(- r^{2} - 1\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\left[- 4 \pi r^{4} - 8 \pi r^{2}\right]_0^{2}\\
&=\left[\left(- 32 \pi\right)+\left(- 64 \pi\right)\right]-\left[\left(0\right)+\left(0\right)\right]\\
&=- 96 \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $C$ be the intersection of the surface $z=x^{2} + 2 y^{2} + 1$ and the vertical column over $D$, where $0\leq x\leq 1$ and $x - 1\leq y\leq 0$. The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above. Given that $\text{curl}\,F=\langle 3 y,\,- 3 x,\,3\rangle$, use Stokes' theorem to write down the integral that gives the circulation along $C.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C.$ One such surface is our graph $S$ with the equation

$$
z=g(x,y)=x^{2} + 2 y^{2} + 1.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(x^{2} + 2 y^{2} + 1\right)=2 x\\
\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(x^{2} + 2 y^{2} + 1\right)=4 y.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F|_{z=g(x,y)}&=\langle 3 y,\,- 3 x,\,3\rangle|_{z=x^{2} + 2 y^{2} + 1}\\
&=\langle 3 y,\,- 3 x,\,3\rangle\\
&=\langle 3 y,\,- 3 x,\,3\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S\text{curl}\,F\cdot\mathrm{d}S&=\iint_D(-P g_x-Q g_y+R)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(-\left(3 y\right)\left(2 x\right)-\left(- 3 x\right)\left(4 y\right)+\left(3\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left((- 6 x y)+(12 x y)+(3)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(6 x y + 3\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

question.:question/problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=3 x z + y$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,- v,\,- v^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression? Choose an integrand equal to the required expression as a function on $D$.

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{4 v^{2} + 1}.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{4 v^{2} + 1}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(3 x z + y)\,{|}_{x=u\,y=- v\,z=- v^{2}} \\  & =3\cdot (u)\cdot (-v^{2})+(-v) \\  & =- 3 u v^{2} - v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{4 v^{2} + 1} \left(- 3 u v^{2} - v\right)\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=3 x - 2 y^{2} z$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2 u v,\,- u,\,3 u - v^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression? Choose an integrand equal to the required expression as a function on $D$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2 u v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(- u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3 u - v^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2 v,\,-1,\,3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2 u v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(- u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3 u - v^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2 u,\,0,\,- 2 v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 v & -1 & 3 \\ 2 u & 0 & - 2 v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 0 & - 2 v\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}2 v & 3 \\ 2 u & - 2 v\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}2 v & -1 \\ 2 u & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨2 v,\,6 u + 4 v^{2},\,2 u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2 v,\,6 u + 4 v^{2},\,2 u⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(2 v)^{2}+(6 u + 4 v^{2})^{2}+(2 u)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{40 u^{2} + 48 u v^{2} + 16 v^{4} + 4 v^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(3 x - 2 y^{2} z)\,{|}_{x=2 u v\,y=- u\,z=3 u - v^{2}} \\  & =6 u v-2\cdot (- u)^{2}\cdot (3 u - v^{2}) \\  & =- 6 u^{3} + 2 u^{2} v^{2} + 6 u v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\left(- 6 u^{3} + 2 u^{2} v^{2} + 6 u v\right) \sqrt{40 u^{2} + 48 u v^{2} + 16 v^{4} + 4 v^{2}}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+0} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(3 x^{2} + y^{2})\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u\,z=v} \\  & =3\cdot (u)^{2}+u^{2} \\  & =4 u^{2}\end{aligned}

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{2} \cdot 4 u^{2}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $p=⟨1,1,3⟩$ and $q=⟨-1,x,4⟩.$ Given that the scalar projection of $p$ onto $q$ is zero, find the value of $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $p$ is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector $q$ equals zero only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
p⊥q\,⟹\,p\cdot q=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & ={p}_{x}\cdot {q}_{x}+{p}_{y}\cdot {q}_{y}+{p}_{z}\cdot {q}_{z} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)+1\cdot x+3\cdot 4 \\  & =x+11.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & =0 \\ x+11 & =0 \\ x & =-11.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z): 0\le x + 3 y\le \frac{\pi}{2},\quad 0\le - 3 y + z\le \frac{\pi}{2},\quad 0\le z\le 2\}.
$$

Given the change of variables

$$
u=x + 3 y,\quad v=- 3 y + z,\quad w=z,
$$

Which of the following could be the missing part of the expression below?

$$
\iiint_R 3 \cos^{2}{\left(x + z \right)} \cos{\left(3 y - z \right)}\,dV=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{2}\left(\boxed{?}\right)\,dw\,dv\,du
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:(u,v,w)\longmapsto (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint_R f(x,y,z)\,dV=\iiint_Δ f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\left|\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x + 3 y,\quad v=- 3 y + z,\quad w=z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1}$.

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y,z)\longmapsto (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z)).
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
Δ=\{(u,v,w): 0\le u\le \frac{\pi}{2},\quad 0\le v\le \frac{\pi}{2},\quad 0\le w\le 2\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} &=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\\\frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix}\\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 0\\0 & -3 & 1\\0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\\ &=(1)\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1\\0 & 1\end{vmatrix}-(3)\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1\\0 & 1\end{vmatrix}+(0)\begin{vmatrix}0 & -3\\0 & 0\end{vmatrix}\\ &=-3\\ &=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=- \frac{1}{3}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R 3 \cos^{2}{\left(x + z \right)} \cos{\left(3 y - z \right)}\,dV &=\iiint_Δ \left(3 \cos{\left(v \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(u + v \right)}\right)\left|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw\\ &=\iiint_Δ \left(3 \cos{\left(v \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(u + v \right)}\right)\left|- \frac{1}{3}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw\\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{2}\left(\cos{\left(v \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(u + v \right)}\right)\,dw\,dv\,du.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\iiint_R 3 \sin{\left(3 x + y \right)} \cos{\left(y + z \right)}\,dV &=\iiint_Δ \left(3 \sin{\left(u \right)} \cos{\left(v \right)}\right)\left|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw\\ &=\iiint_Δ \left(3 \sin{\left(u \right)} \cos{\left(v \right)}\right)\left|\frac{1}{3}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw\\ &=\int_{\frac{3 \pi}{4}}^{\pi}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{-1}^{2}\left(\sin{\left(u \right)} \cos{\left(v \right)}\right)\,dw\,dv\,du.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Performing a Change of Variables in a Triple Integral

question.:question/problem:
Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z): 1\le x y\le 2,\quad -2\le y\le -1,\quad 0\le z\le 3\}.
$$

Given the change of variables

$$
u=x y,\quad v=y,\quad w=4 z,
$$

Write the triple integral

$$
\iiint_R 2 x y^{2} + 3 y z\,dV
$$

as a repeated integral in terms of $u$, $v$, and $w$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:(u,v,w)\longmapsto (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint_R f(x,y,z)\,dV=\iiint_Δ f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\left|\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x y,\quad v=y,\quad w=4 z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1}$.

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y,z)\longmapsto (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z)).
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
Δ=\{(u,v,w): 1\le u\le 2,\quad -2\le v\le -1,\quad 0\le w\le 12\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} &=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\\\frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix}\\ &=\begin{vmatrix}y & x & 0\\0 & 1 & 0\\0 & 0 & 4\end{vmatrix}\\ &=(y)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & 4\end{vmatrix}-(x)\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0\\0 & 4\end{vmatrix}+(0)\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1\\0 & 0\end{vmatrix}\\ &=4 y\\ &=4 v.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4 v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$ The sign of $v$ is fixed throughout $Δ$.

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R 2 x y^{2} + 3 y z\,dV &=\iiint_Δ \left(\frac{v \left(8 u + 3 w\right)}{4}\right)\left|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw\\ &=\iiint_Δ \left(\frac{v \left(8 u + 3 w\right)}{4}\right)\left|\frac{1}{4 v}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw\\ &=\int_{1}^{2}\int_{-2}^{-1}\int_{0}^{12}\left(- \frac{u}{2} - \frac{3 w}{16}\right)\,dw\,dv\,du.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Performing a Change of Variables in a Triple Integral

question.:question/problem:
Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z): 1\le x + 3 y\le 3,\quad 1\le x - 3 y\le 3,\quad 1\le z\le \left(x - 3 y\right) \left(x + 3 y\right)\}.
$$

Given the change of variables

$$
u=x + 3 y,\quad v=x - 3 y,\quad w=\sqrt{z},
$$

Write the triple integral

$$
\iiint_R 2 \sqrt{z}\,dV
$$

as a repeated integral in terms of $u$, $v$, and $w$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:(u,v,w)\longmapsto (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint_R f(x,y,z)\,dV=\iiint_Δ f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\left|\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x + 3 y,\quad v=x - 3 y,\quad w=\sqrt{z}
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1}$.

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y,z)\longmapsto (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z)).
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
Δ=\{(u,v,w): 1\le u\le 3,\quad 1\le v\le 3,\quad 1\le w\le \sqrt{u v}\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} &=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\\\frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix}\\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 0\\1 & -3 & 0\\0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{z}}\end{vmatrix}\\ &=(1)\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 0\\0 & \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{z}}\end{vmatrix}-(3)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{z}}\end{vmatrix}+(0)\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3\\0 & 0\end{vmatrix}\\ &=- \frac{3}{\sqrt{z}}\\ &=- \frac{3}{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=- \frac{w}{3}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$ Since $z\ge1$ and $w=\sqrt z$, the branch is $w>0$.

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R 2 \sqrt{z}\,dV &=\iiint_Δ \left(2 w\right)\left|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw\\ &=\iiint_Δ \left(2 w\right)\left|- \frac{w}{3}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw\\ &=\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{\sqrt{u v}}\left(\frac{2 w^{2}}{3}\right)\,dw\,dv\,du.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

Consider the picture shown above. Find a unit vector that is parallel to $a$. Choose the unit vector in the same direction.
question.:question/worked-solution:

In $\bigtriangleup AHB$ we have $\angle AHB=90^\circ$, $AH=3$ and $BH=5$. So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
AB &= \sqrt{AH^2+BH^2} \\
&= \sqrt{(3)^2+(5)^2} \\
&= \sqrt{9+25} \\
&= \sqrt{34}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the magnitude of $a$ is $\sqrt{34}$. Consequently, the unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= \frac{1}{|a|}\cdot a \\
&= \frac{\sqrt{34}}{34}a
\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Solving for an Unknown Given Two Perpendicular Vectors

question.:question/problem: What is the value of $x$ given that $a=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4 \\ -3x\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ 4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}$ and $a⊥b$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
We know that $a⊥b$ ($a$ and $b$ are perpendicular) if and only if $a\cdot b=0.$

Computing the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b &={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  &=3\cdot x+4\cdot 4+(-3x)\cdot 3 \\  &=3x+16-9x \\  &=-6x+16.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b &=0 \\ -6x+16 &=0 \\ x &=\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Solving for an Unknown Given Two Perpendicular Vectors

question.:question/problem: Let $g=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3{r}^{2} \\ 3\end{bmatrix}$ and $h=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ 3{r}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$ Given that $g⊥h$ and $r>0$, find the value of $r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We know that $g⊥h$ ($g$ and $h$ are perpendicular) if and only if $g\cdot h=0.$

Computing the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}g\cdot h &={g}_{x}\cdot {h}_{x}+{g}_{y}\cdot {h}_{y}+{g}_{z}\cdot {h}_{z} \\  &=(-2)\cdot 2+3{r}^{2}\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 3{r}^{2} \\  &=-4-6r^{2}+9r^{2} \\  &=3{r}^{2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}g\cdot h &=0 \\ 3{r}^{2}-4 &=0 \\ 3{r}^{2} &=4 \\ {r}^{2} &=\frac{4}{3} \\ r &=\pm \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution since we are told that $r>0.$ Therefore, $r=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}.$

question.:question/problem: Let $u=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -3 \\ a\end{bmatrix}$ and $v=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ a\end{bmatrix}.$ Given that $u⊥v$ and $a<0$, find the value of $a.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We know that $u⊥v$ ($u$ and $v$ are perpendicular) if and only if $u\cdot v=0.$

Computing the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot v &={u}_{x}\cdot {v}_{x}+{u}_{y}\cdot {v}_{y}+{u}_{z}\cdot {v}_{z} \\  &=(-4)\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot 3+a\cdot a \\  &={a}^{2}-17.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot v &=0 \\ {a}^{2}-17 &=0 \\ {a}^{2} &=17 \\ a &=\pm \sqrt{17}\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the positive solution since we are told that $a<0.$ Therefore, $a=-\sqrt{17}.$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating Flux Across a Rectangle Using Two Symmetry Properties

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179647/images/flux-1.0.2-8c7428d2b40a578c2791-field.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F=-x\,\mathbf i+3y\,\mathbf j$ and a square $C$ with side length $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds,
$$

where $\mathbf n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds+\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds\\
&\quad+\int_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_3\,\mathrm ds+\int_{C_4}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_4\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179647/images/flux-1.0.2-8c7428d2b40a578c2791-normals.png)

We compute this integral in two stages.

- First, consider the side $C_1.$ We have that $\mathbf n_1=\mathbf i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_1}(-x\,\mathbf i+3y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf i\,\mathrm ds\\
&=-\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=1\mathbf i+t\,\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf j,\quad t\in[-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds
&=-\int_{-1}^{1}1\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(-1)\int_{-1}^{1}\mathrm dt\\
&=(-1)\cdot 2\\
&=-2.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_3$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_3\,\mathrm ds=-2.
$$

- Next, consider the side $C_2.$ We have that $\mathbf n_2=\mathbf j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_2}(-x\,\mathbf i+3y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf j\,\mathrm ds\\
&=3\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_2,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+1\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf i,\quad t\in[-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
3\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds
&=3\int_{-1}^{1}1\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(3)\int_{-1}^{1}\mathrm dt\\
&=(3)\cdot 2\\
&=6.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_4}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_4\,\mathrm ds=6.
$$

Finally, then

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds=2\cdot(-2)+2\cdot(6)=8.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding a Unit Vector Parallel to a Vector Sum

question.:question/problem: The vector $a$ is directed due south-west and $|a|=8$, while the vector $b$ is directed due north-west and $|b|=4.$ Which of the following is a unit vector that is parallel to $a+b?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we have to find $a+b.$ According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant $a+b$ goes from the tail of $a$ to the head of $b:$

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186096815/sum-b0790380872b09bfb3c8da3f.png)

To find the unit vector corresponding to $a+b,$ we have to divide by the magnitude:

$$
u=\frac{a+b}{|a+b|}
$$

The given directions are perpendicular, so we obtain a right triangle. We can use the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}|a+b|^2&=|a|^2+|b|^2\\
&=(8)^2+(4)^2\\
&=64+16\\
&=80\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the magnitude is

$$
|a+b|=\sqrt{80}=4 \sqrt{5}
$$

and the corresponding unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}u&=\frac{a+b}{|a+b|}\\
&=\frac{1}{4 \sqrt{5}}(a+b).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: The vector $a$ is directed horizontally to the left and has magnitude $24$, while the vector $b$ is directed vertically up and has magnitude $27.$ Which of the following is a unit vector that is parallel to $a+b?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we have to find $a+b.$ According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant $a+b$ goes from the tail of $a$ to the head of $b:$

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186096815/sum-098099c238c10c841257eba8.png)

To find the unit vector corresponding to $a+b,$ we have to divide by the magnitude:

$$
u=\frac{a+b}{|a+b|}
$$

The given directions are perpendicular, so we obtain a right triangle. We can use the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}|a+b|^2&=|a|^2+|b|^2\\
&=(24)^2+(27)^2\\
&=576+729\\
&=1305\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the magnitude is

$$
|a+b|=\sqrt{1305}=3 \sqrt{145}
$$

and the corresponding unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}u&=\frac{a+b}{|a+b|}\\
&=\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{145}}(a+b).\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Determining the Lengths of the Major and Minor Axes Given the Equation of an Ellipse

question.:question/problem:
What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{49}=1?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=9$ and ${b}^{2}=49.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=9,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{9}=3.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=49,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{49}=7.$

So the semi-major axis has length $b=7,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=3.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 7=14,$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot 3=6.$

knowledge_point.title: Finding an Area by Transforming to a Type I Region

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x - 6 y,\,v=y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x - 6 y)^{2}-(y)=0$ and the line $y=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x - 6 y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $x - 6 y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
(x - 6 y)^{2}-(y)=0\,⟹\,u^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v=u^{2}.
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
v=1.
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &=u^{2} \\ v &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,u=\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 1,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,u^{2}\le v\le 1\}.
$$

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186129197/plots/285e4a212301c46ce0123cc4.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1&-6\\0&1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |1|\,dudv \\ &=1\int_{-1}^{1}[\int_{u^{2}}^{1}dv]du \\ &=1\int_{-1}^{1}[v]_{u^{2}}^{1}du \\ &=1\int_{-1}^{1}(1)-(u^{2})du \\ &=1\int_{-1}^{1}(1 - u^{2})du \\ &=1[- \frac{u^{3}}{3} + u]_{-1}^{1} \\ &=1(((1)+\left(- \frac{1}{3}\right))-((-1)+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right))) \\ &=1\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \\ &=\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

while substituting $x=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$

$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$

$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt{6},1).$

Arrow lengths use a common display scale; no numerical magnitude is specified.

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}5 u + 2 v \\ 3 u + v\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix}\to\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}$, is given by

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=5 u + 2 v$ and $y(u,v)=3 u + v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&=5&\quad \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}&=2\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&=3&\quad \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}&=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\begin{vmatrix}5&2\\3&1\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left(5\right)\cdot\left(1\right)-\left(2\right)\cdot\left(3\right)\\&=5-6\\&=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix}\to\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&=5 \cos{\left(v \right)}&\quad \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}&=- 5 u \sin{\left(v \right)}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&=2 \sin{\left(v \right)}&\quad \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}&=2 u \cos{\left(v \right)}\end{aligned}

T:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix}\to\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},

question.:question/problem: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T(\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix})=\begin{bmatrix}5 \sin{\left(u + v \right)} \\ 2 \cos{\left(u - v \right)}\end{bmatrix}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix}\to\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}$, is given by

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Here, we have $x=5 \sin{\left(u + v \right)}$ and $y=2 \cos{\left(u - v \right)}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&=5 \cos{\left(u + v \right)}\\\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}&=5 \cos{\left(u + v \right)}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&=- 2 \sin{\left(u - v \right)}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}&=2 \sin{\left(u - v \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\begin{vmatrix}5 \cos{\left(u + v \right)}&5 \cos{\left(u + v \right)}\\- 2 \sin{\left(u - v \right)}&2 \sin{\left(u - v \right)}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left(5 \cos{\left(u + v \right)}\right)\cdot\left(2 \sin{\left(u - v \right)}\right)\\&\quad{}-\left(5 \cos{\left(u + v \right)}\right)\cdot\left(- 2 \sin{\left(u - v \right)}\right)\\&=20 \sin{\left(u - v \right)} \cos{\left(u + v \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression

question.:question/problem:
Calculate $$
\int x\operatorname{cos}(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $I=\int x\operatorname{cos}(x)\,\text{d}x$. Use integration by parts.

$$
\int uv^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}x=uv-\int vu^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

Choose the linear factor as $u$:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =x \\ u^{\prime} & =1 \\ v^{\prime} & =\operatorname{cos}(x) \\ v & =\operatorname{sin}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}uv & =x\left(\operatorname{sin}(x)\right) \\ \int vu^{\prime}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(\operatorname{sin}(x)\right)1\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the remaining integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =x\operatorname{sin}(x)-\int \operatorname{sin}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}(x)-(-\operatorname{cos}(x))+C \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}(x)+\operatorname{cos}(x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate $$
\int 3 x\operatorname{csc}^{2}(x + 3)\,\text{d}x.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $I=\int 3 x\operatorname{csc}^{2}(x + 3)\,\text{d}x$. Use integration by parts.

$$
\int uv^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}x=uv-\int vu^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

Choose the linear factor as $u$:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =3 x \\ u^{\prime} & =3 \\ v^{\prime} & =\operatorname{csc}^{2}(x + 3) \\ v & =-\operatorname{cot}(x + 3)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}uv & =3 x\left(-\operatorname{cot}(x + 3)\right) \\ \int vu^{\prime}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(-\operatorname{cot}(x + 3)\right)3\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Use $t=\operatorname{sin}(x + 3)$ and $\mathrm{d}t=\operatorname{cos}(x + 3)\,\mathrm{d}x$. Evaluate the remaining integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-3 x\operatorname{cot}(x + 3)+3\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}(x + 3)}{\operatorname{sin}(x + 3)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3 x\operatorname{cot}(x + 3)+3\int \frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3 x\operatorname{cot}(x + 3)+3\ln|t|+C \\  & =-3 x\operatorname{cot}(x + 3)+3\ln|\operatorname{sin}(x + 3)|+C\end{aligned}
$$

This holds on each interval where $\operatorname{sin}(x + 3)\ne0$.

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Chain Rule

question.:question/problem: Find $f_x(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=\tan{\left(\ln{\left(3 x + 2 y + 2 \right)} \right)}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=3 x + 2 y + 2\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=3\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\tan(\ln u)&=\sec^2(\ln u)\cdot\frac{1}{u}\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(\frac{\sec^{2}{\left(\ln{\left(u \right)} \right)}}{u}\right)\cdot\left(3\right)\\
&=\frac{3 \sec^{2}{\left(\ln{\left(3 x + 2 y + 2 \right)} \right)}}{3 x + 2 y + 2}
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for $3 x + 2 y + 2>0$ and $\cos(\ln(3 x + 2 y + 2))\ne0$.

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Chain Rule

question.:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y)=2 x^{2} y + \ln{\left(e^{- 2 x^{2} + y} + 1 \right)},
$$

evaluate both partial derivatives at $(-1,-2)$.

$f_x(-1,-2)=$

{{field-1}}

$f_y(-1,-2)=$

{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=- 2 x^{2} + y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=- 4 x\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\ln(1+e^u)&=\frac{1}{1+e^u}\cdot e^u\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(2 x^{2} y\right)&=4 x y\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(\frac{e^{u}}{e^{u} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(- 4 x\right)+\left(4 x y\right)\\
&=4 x y - \frac{4 x e^{- 2 x^{2} + y}}{e^{- 2 x^{2} + y} + 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=-1$ and $y=-2$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=- 2 \left(-1\right)^{2} + \left(-2\right)=-4.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(-1,-2)&=\left(\frac{e^{u_0}}{e^{u_0} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(4\right)+\left(8\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{1}{\left(e^{-4} + 1\right) e^{4}}\right)\cdot\left(4\right)+\left(8\right)\\
&=\frac{4 \left(3 + 2 e^{4}\right)}{1 + e^{4}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Treat $x$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $y$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=- 2 x^{2} + y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=1\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\ln(1+e^u)&=\frac{1}{1+e^u}\cdot e^u\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(2 x^{2} y\right)&=2 x^{2}\\
f_y(x,y)&=\left(\frac{e^{u}}{e^{u} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)+\left(2 x^{2}\right)\\
&=2 x^{2} + \frac{e^{- 2 x^{2} + y}}{e^{- 2 x^{2} + y} + 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=-1$ and $y=-2$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=- 2 \left(-1\right)^{2} + \left(-2\right)=-4.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(-1,-2)&=\left(\frac{e^{u_0}}{e^{u_0} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)+\left(2\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{1}{\left(e^{-4} + 1\right) e^{4}}\right)\cdot\left(1\right)+\left(2\right)\\
&=\frac{3 + 2 e^{4}}{1 + e^{4}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for all real $x,y$.

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\arctan{\left(2 x^{2} y \right)}$, evaluate $f_x(2,1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as constant and differentiate with respect to $x$. Apply the chain rule, and the sum and constant multiple rules where needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=2 x^{2} y\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=4 x y\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\arctan{\left(u \right)}\right)&=\left(\frac{1}{u^{2} + 1}\right)\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(\frac{1}{u^{2} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(4 x y\right)\\
&=\frac{4 x y}{4 x^{4} y^{2} + 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=2$ and $y=1$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=2 \left(2\right)^{2} \left(1\right)=8.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(2,1)&=\left(\frac{1}{u_0^{2} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(8\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{1}{65}\right)\cdot\left(8\right)\\
&=\frac{8}{65}.
\end{aligned}
$$

These derivatives apply for all real $x,y$.

knowledge_point.title: Computing a Definite Integral Using Integration by Parts

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int_{0}^{1} x e^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $I$ denote the given integral. Choose the factors so that differentiating the linear factor simplifies the remaining integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=x, & u^\prime&=1,\\
v^\prime&=e^{2 x}, & v&=\frac{e^{2 x}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Apply the definite integration-by-parts formula:

$$
\int_a^b uv^\prime\,\mathrm{d}x=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b vu^\prime\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\left[\frac{x e^{2 x}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}\\
&\quad-\int_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{e^{2 x}}{2}\right)\left(1\right)\,\mathrm{d}x,\\
&=\left[\frac{x e^{2 x}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}e^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate the remaining function and combine the two primitive terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\left[\frac{x e^{2 x}}{2} - \frac{e^{2 x}}{4}\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $F(x)$ denote the primitive inside the brackets. Evaluate each endpoint, then subtract the entire lower value:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F\left(1\right)&=\frac{e^{2}}{4}=\frac{e^{2}}{4},\\
F\left(0\right)&=- \frac{1}{4}=- \frac{1}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\left(\frac{e^{2}}{4}\right)-\left(- \frac{1}{4}\right)\\
&=\frac{1}{4} + \frac{e^{2}}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

v^\prime&=e^{- 2 x}, & v&=- \frac{e^{- 2 x}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\int_a^b uv^\prime\,\mathrm{d}x=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b vu^\prime\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

&\quad-\int_{0}^{1}\left(- \frac{e^{- 2 x}}{2}\right)\left(-2\right)\,\mathrm{d}x,\\
&=\left[x e^{- 2 x}\right]_{0}^{1}-\int_{0}^{1}e^{- 2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate the remaining function and combine the two primitive terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\left[x e^{- 2 x} + \frac{e^{- 2 x}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}

knowledge_point.title: Identifying Singular Matrices

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $B$?

Select all that apply.

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix is singular if and only if its determinant is zero.

Expand along the top row, with signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\det(B) &= 0\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 8 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-4)\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\
&= 0\left(8-(-8)\right) \\
&\quad +(-4)\left(4-(0)\right) \\
&\quad +2\left(8-(0)\right) \\
&= 0\cdot 16 \\
&\quad +(-4)\cdot 4 \\
&\quad +2\cdot 8 \\
&= 0-16+16 \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(B)=0$, $B$ is singular.

Do not select “$\det(B)=16$.”

Do not select “$\det(B)=-32$.”

Select “$B$ is a singular matrix.”

question.:question/problem:
The matrices $F$ and $A$ differ in just one entry. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

$$
F=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix is singular if and only if its determinant is zero. A singular matrix has no multiplicative inverse; a nonsingular square matrix has one. Compare both determinants rather than assuming that one changed entry changes singularity.

Expand along the top row, with signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\det(F) &= 1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-2)\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-1)\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\
&= 1\left(1-(-2)\right) \\
&\quad +(-2)\left(1-(-1)\right) \\
&\quad +(-1)\left(-2-(-1)\right) \\
&= 1\cdot 3 \\
&\quad +(-2)\cdot 2 \\
&\quad +(-1)\cdot (-1) \\
&= 3-4+1 \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\det(A) &= 1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-2)\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-1)\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\
&= 1\left(1-(0)\right) \\
&\quad +(-2)\left(1-(-1)\right) \\
&\quad +(-1)\left(0-(-1)\right) \\
&= 1\cdot 1 \\
&\quad +(-2)\cdot 2 \\
&\quad +(-1)\cdot 1 \\
&= 1-4-1 \\
&= -4
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(F)=0$, $F$ is singular.

Since $\det(A)=-4\ne0$, $A$ is **not** singular.

Do not select “$F$ is **not** a singular matrix.”

Do not select “$\det(A)=2$.”

Do not select “$F$ has a multiplicative inverse, but $A$ does not.”

Select “$A$ is **not** a singular matrix.”

Expand along the first row, using the signs $+,-,+$. Compute the three signed contributions separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1} & =(5)\begin{vmatrix}0 & 5 \\ 1 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(5)((0)(x)-(5)(1)) \\  & =(5)(-5) \\  & =-25\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{3} & =(5)\begin{vmatrix}-8 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(5)((-8)(1)-(0)(3)) \\  & =(5)(-8) \\  & =-40\end{aligned}
$$

Add the signed contributions to obtain the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =T_1+T_2+T_3 \\  & =- 40 x - 140\end{aligned}
$$

Set the determinant equal to the given value.

$$
\begin{aligned}- 40 x - 140 & =-42 \\ - 40 x & =98 \\ x & =- \frac{49}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=- \frac{49}{20}$.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{2} & =-(-5)\begin{vmatrix}5 & 0 \\ p - 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(-5)((5)(-1)-(0)(p - 3)) \\  & =-(-5)(-5) \\  & =-25\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{3} & =(2)\begin{vmatrix}5 & p \\ p - 3 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(2)((5)(0)-(p)(p - 3)) \\  & =(2)(- p^{2} + 3 p) \\  & =- 2 p^{2} + 6 p\end{aligned}
$$

Add the signed contributions to obtain the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =T_1+T_2+T_3 \\  & =- 2 p^{2} + 6 p - 25\end{aligned}
$$

Set the determinant equal to the given value.

$$
\begin{aligned}- 2 p^{2} + 6 p - 25 & =-33 \\ - 2 p^{2} + 6 p + 8 & =0 \\ p & =\frac{-(6)\pm\sqrt{(6)^2-4(-2)(8)}}{2(-2)} \\  & =\frac{-6\pm 10}{-4} \\ p & =-1,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $p=-1$ and $p=4$.

Expand along the first row, using the signs $+,-,+$. Compute the three signed contributions separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1} & =(x - 5)\begin{vmatrix}x & x + 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(x - 5)((x)(3)-(x + 1)(0)) \\  & =(x - 5)(3 x) \\  & =3 x^{2} - 15 x\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{3} & =(4)\begin{vmatrix}5 & x \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4)((5)(0)-(x)(1)) \\  & =(4)(- x) \\  & =- 4 x\end{aligned}
$$

Add the signed contributions to obtain the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =T_1+T_2+T_3 \\  & =5 x^{2} - 47 x\end{aligned}
$$

A singular matrix has determinant $0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}5 x^{2} - 47 x & =0 \\ x (5 x - 47) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,\frac{47}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in **ascending order**, the solutions are $x=0$ and $x=\frac{47}{5}$.

$$

$$

Add the signed contributions to obtain the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =T_1+T_2+T_3 \\  & =- 10 k^{2} + 10 k\end{aligned}
$$

A singular matrix has determinant $0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}- 10 k^{2} + 10 k & =0 \\ - 10 k (k - 1) & =0 \\ k & =0,\,1\end{aligned}

Expand along the first row, using the signs $+,-,+$. Compute the three signed contributions separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1} & =(x^{2} - 5)\begin{vmatrix}5 & -1 \\ 4 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(x^{2} - 5)((5)(0)-(-1)(4)) \\  & =(x^{2} - 5)(4) \\  & =4 x^{2} - 20\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{2} & =-(3)\begin{vmatrix}x & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(3)((x)(0)-(-1)(1)) \\  & =-(3)(1) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{3} & =(0)\begin{vmatrix}x & 5 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(0)((x)(4)-(5)(1)) \\  & =(0)(4 x - 5) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Add the signed contributions to obtain the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =T_1+T_2+T_3 \\  & =4 x^{2} - 23\end{aligned}
$$

Set the determinant equal to the given value.

$$
\begin{aligned}4 x^{2} - 23 & =39 \\ 4 x^{2} & =62 \\ x^2 & =\frac{31}{2} \\ x & =\pm\sqrt{\frac{31}{2}} \\ x & =- \frac{\sqrt{62}}{2},\,\frac{\sqrt{62}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in **ascending order**, the solutions are $x=- \frac{\sqrt{62}}{2}$ and $x=\frac{\sqrt{62}}{2}$.

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\nabla f(x,y,z)$ at $(-1,1,\frac{3 \pi}{4})$ given $f(x,y,z)=e^{x y} \cos{\left(x z \right)}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold the other two coordinates constant in each partial derivative. Apply the power, chain, or product rule to the factors that depend on the active coordinate.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}(x,y,z)&=y e^{y x} \cos{\left(x z \right)} - z e^{y x} \sin{\left(x z \right)} \\ &=y e^{x y} \cos{\left(x z \right)} - z e^{x y} \sin{\left(x z \right)} \\ f_{y}(x,y,z)&=x e^{y x} \cos{\left(x z \right)} \\ &=x e^{x y} \cos{\left(x z \right)} \\ f_{z}(x,y,z)&=- x e^{y x} \sin{\left(x z \right)} \\ &=- x e^{x y} \sin{\left(x z \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the partials in $x,y,z$ order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y,z)&=\begin{pmatrix}y e^{x y} \cos{\left(x z \right)} - z e^{x y} \sin{\left(x z \right)} \\ x e^{x y} \cos{\left(x z \right)} \\ - x e^{x y} \sin{\left(x z \right)}\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=-1$, $y=1$, $z=\frac{3 \pi}{4}$ into these partial derivatives. Here $\cos\left(- \frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)=- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ and $\sin\left(- \frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)=- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}(-1,1,\frac{3 \pi}{4})&=- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2 e} + \frac{3 \sqrt{2} \pi}{8 e} \\ f_{y}(-1,1,\frac{3 \pi}{4})&=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2 e} \\ f_{z}(-1,1,\frac{3 \pi}{4})&=- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2 e}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(-1,1,\frac{3 \pi}{4})&=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2 e} + \frac{3 \sqrt{2} \pi}{8 e} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2 e} \\ - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2 e}\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\nabla f(x,y,z)$ at $(-2,1,2)$ given $f(x,y,z)=\frac{2 x y z}{- x + y + z}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the quotient rule in each coordinate, holding the other coordinates constant. The denominator is nonzero at the requested point.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}(x,y,z)&=\frac{2 y x z + 2 y z \left(y - x + z\right)}{\left(y - x + z\right)^{2}} \\ &=\frac{2 x y z + 2 y z \left(- x + y + z\right)}{\left(- x + y + z\right)^{2}} \\ f_{y}(x,y,z)&=\frac{- 2 y x z + 2 x z \left(y - x + z\right)}{\left(y - x + z\right)^{2}} \\ &=\frac{- 2 x y z + 2 x z \left(- x + y + z\right)}{\left(- x + y + z\right)^{2}} \\ f_{z}(x,y,z)&=\frac{- 2 y x z + 2 y x \left(y - x + z\right)}{\left(y - x + z\right)^{2}} \\ &=\frac{- 2 x y z + 2 x y \left(- x + y + z\right)}{\left(- x + y + z\right)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the partials in $x,y,z$ order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y,z)&=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{2 x y z + 2 y z \left(- x + y + z\right)}{\left(- x + y + z\right)^{2}} \\ \frac{- 2 x y z + 2 x z \left(- x + y + z\right)}{\left(- x + y + z\right)^{2}} \\ \frac{- 2 x y z + 2 x y \left(- x + y + z\right)}{\left(- x + y + z\right)^{2}}\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=-2$, $y=1$, $z=2$ into these partial derivatives.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}(-2,1,2)&=\frac{12}{25} \\ f_{y}(-2,1,2)&=- \frac{32}{25} \\ f_{z}(-2,1,2)&=- \frac{12}{25}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(-2,1,2)&=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{12}{25} \\ - \frac{32}{25} \\ - \frac{12}{25}\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\nabla f(x,y,z)$ at $(-2,\pi,-1)$ given $f(x,y,z)=e^{x z} \cos{\left(y z \right)}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold the other two coordinates constant in each partial derivative. Apply the power, chain, or product rule to the factors that depend on the active coordinate.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}(x,y,z)&=z e^{x z} \cos{\left(z y \right)} \\ &=z e^{x z} \cos{\left(y z \right)} \\ f_{y}(x,y,z)&=- z e^{x z} \sin{\left(z y \right)} \\ &=- z e^{x z} \sin{\left(y z \right)} \\ f_{z}(x,y,z)&=x e^{x z} \cos{\left(z y \right)} - y e^{x z} \sin{\left(z y \right)} \\ &=x e^{x z} \cos{\left(y z \right)} - y e^{x z} \sin{\left(y z \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the partials in $x,y,z$ order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y,z)&=\begin{pmatrix}z e^{x z} \cos{\left(y z \right)} \\ - z e^{x z} \sin{\left(y z \right)} \\ x e^{x z} \cos{\left(y z \right)} - y e^{x z} \sin{\left(y z \right)}\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=-2$, $y=\pi$, $z=-1$ into these partial derivatives. Here $\cos(- \pi)=-1$ and $\sin(- \pi)=0$.

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(-2,\pi,-1)&=\begin{pmatrix}e^{2} \\ 0 \\ 2 e^{2}\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\nabla f(x,y,z)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi}{4},-2)$ given $f(x,y,z)=\sin{\left(x y z \right)}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold the other two coordinates constant in each partial derivative. Apply the power, chain, or product rule to the factors that depend on the active coordinate.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}(x,y,z)&=z y \cos{\left(x z y \right)} \\ &=y z \cos{\left(x y z \right)} \\ f_{y}(x,y,z)&=x z \cos{\left(x z y \right)} \\ &=x z \cos{\left(x y z \right)} \\ f_{z}(x,y,z)&=x y \cos{\left(x z y \right)} \\ &=x y \cos{\left(x y z \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the partials in $x,y,z$ order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y,z)&=\begin{pmatrix}y z \cos{\left(x y z \right)} \\ x z \cos{\left(x y z \right)} \\ x y \cos{\left(x y z \right)}\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=1$, $y=\frac{\pi}{4}$, $z=-2$ into these partial derivatives. Here $\cos\left(- \frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$ and $\sin\left(- \frac{\pi}{2}\right)=-1$.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}(1,\frac{\pi}{4},-2)&=0 \\ f_{y}(1,\frac{\pi}{4},-2)&=0 \\ f_{z}(1,\frac{\pi}{4},-2)&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(1,\frac{\pi}{4},-2)&=\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\nabla f(x,y)$ at $(1,2)$ if $f(x,y)=e^{- x y - y^{2} + 7}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to one coordinate at a time, holding the other constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=- ye^{- y^{2} - y x + 7} \\ &=- y e^{- x y - y^{2} + 7} \\ f_y(x,y)&=(- 2 y - x)e^{- y^{2} - y x + 7} \\ &=\left(- x - 2 y\right) e^{- x y - y^{2} + 7}\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the partial derivatives in order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y)&=(- y e^{- x y - y^{2} + 7})\,\mathbf i \\ &\quad+(\left(- x - 2 y\right) e^{- x y - y^{2} + 7})\,\mathbf j\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(1,2)&=- \left(2\right) e^{- \left(1\right) \left(2\right) - \left(2\right)^{2} + 7} \\ &=- 2 e \\ f_y(1,2)&=\left(- \left(1\right) - 2 \left(2\right)\right) e^{- \left(1\right) \left(2\right) - \left(2\right)^{2} + 7} \\ &=- 5 e\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(1,2)=\langle - 2 e,\,- 5 e\rangle$.

question.:question/problem: Find $\nabla f(x,y)$ if $f(x,y)=\frac{2 x - 3 y}{- x + y}$. Work on the domain $y - x\ne0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Apply the quotient rule to each partial. The denominator-derivative contribution is subtracted in both components.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=\frac{(2)(y - x)-(- 3 y + 2 x)(-1)}{(y - x)^2} \\ &=- \frac{y}{\left(- x + y\right)^{2}} \\ f_y(x,y)&=\frac{(-3)(y - x)-(- 3 y + 2 x)\cdot1}{(y - x)^2} \\ &=\frac{x}{\left(- x + y\right)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the partial derivatives in order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y)&=\left(- \frac{y}{\left(- x + y\right)^{2}}\right)\,\mathbf i \\ &\quad+\left(\frac{x}{\left(- x + y\right)^{2}}\right)\,\mathbf j.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to one coordinate at a time, holding the other constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=0+2 y- 6 x+2 \\ &=- 6 x + 2 y + 2 \\ f_y(x,y)&=- 6 y+2 x+0+0 \\ &=2 x - 6 y\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(2,1)=\langle -8,\,-2\rangle$.

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\nabla f(x,y)$ at $(-1,2)$ if $f(x,y)=- 4 y \arctan{\left(x \right)}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to one coordinate at a time, holding the other constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=- 4 y\cdot\frac{1}{1+x^2} \\ &=- \frac{4 y}{x^{2} + 1} \\ f_y(x,y)&=-4\arctan(x) \\ &=- 4 \arctan{\left(x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the partial derivatives in order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y)&=\left(- \frac{4 y}{x^{2} + 1}\right)\,\mathbf i \\ &\quad+(- 4 \arctan{\left(x \right)})\,\mathbf j\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(-1,2)&=- \frac{4 \left(2\right)}{\left(-1\right)^{2} + 1} \\ &=-4 \\ f_y(-1,2)&=- 4 \arctan{\left(\left(-1\right) \right)} \\ &=\pi\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(-1,2)=\langle -4,\,\pi\rangle$.

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\nabla f(x,y)$ at $(2,2)$ if $f(x,y)=y \ln{\left(- x + y + 2 \right)}$. Work on the domain $y - x + 2>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For the second partial use the product and chain rules. For the first, the second factor is constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=y\cdot\frac{1}{y - x + 2}\cdot -1 \\ &=- \frac{y}{- x + y + 2} \\ f_y(x,y)&=1\cdot\ln(y - x + 2)+y\cdot\frac{1}{y - x + 2}\cdot 1 \\ &=\frac{y}{- x + y + 2} + \ln{\left(- x + y + 2 \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the partial derivatives in order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y)&=\left(- \frac{y}{- x + y + 2}\right)\,\mathbf i \\ &\quad+(\frac{y}{- x + y + 2} + \ln{\left(- x + y + 2 \right)})\,\mathbf j\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(2,2)&=- \frac{\left(2\right)}{- \left(2\right) + \left(2\right) + 2} \\ &=-1 \\ f_y(2,2)&=\frac{\left(2\right)}{- \left(2\right) + \left(2\right) + 2} + \ln{\left(- \left(2\right) + \left(2\right) + 2 \right)} \\ &=\ln{\left(2 \right)} + 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(2,2)=\langle -1,\,\ln{\left(2 \right)} + 1\rangle$.

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\nabla f(x,y)$ at $(1,e^{2})$ if $f(x,y)=\left(- x + y\right) \left(x^{2} + \ln{\left(y \right)}\right)$. Work on the domain $y>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Both factors depend on each coordinate. Apply the product rule separately, holding the other coordinate constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=-1(x^{2} + \ln{\left(y \right)})+(y - x)(2 x) \\ &=- x^{2} + 2 x \left(- x + y\right) - \ln{\left(y \right)} \\ f_y(x,y)&=x^{2} + \ln{\left(y \right)}+(y - x)\cdot\frac{1}{y} \\ &=x^{2} + \ln{\left(y \right)} + \frac{- x + y}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the partial derivatives in order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y)&=(- x^{2} + 2 x \left(- x + y\right) - \ln{\left(y \right)})\,\mathbf i \\ &\quad+(x^{2} + \ln{\left(y \right)} + \frac{- x + y}{y})\,\mathbf j\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(1,e^{2})&=- \left(1\right)^{2} + 2 \left(1\right) \left(- \left(1\right) + \left(e^{2}\right)\right) - \ln{\left(\left(e^{2}\right) \right)} \\ &=-5 + 2 e^{2} \\ f_y(1,e^{2})&=\left(1\right)^{2} + \ln{\left(\left(e^{2}\right) \right)} + \frac{- \left(1\right) + \left(e^{2}\right)}{\left(e^{2}\right)} \\ &=4 - e^{-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(1,e^{2})=\langle -5 + 2 e^{2},\,4 - e^{-2}\rangle$.

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\nabla f(x,y)$ at $(0,2)$ if $f(x,y)=- \ln{\left(x^{2} + y^{2} \right)}$. Work on the domain $y^2+x^2>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to one coordinate at a time, holding the other constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=\frac{-1}{y^2+x^2}\cdot 2x \\ &=- \frac{2 x}{x^{2} + y^{2}} \\ f_y(x,y)&=\frac{-1}{y^2+x^2}\cdot 2y \\ &=- \frac{2 y}{x^{2} + y^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the partial derivatives in order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y)&=\left(- \frac{2 x}{x^{2} + y^{2}}\right)\,\mathbf i \\ &\quad+\left(- \frac{2 y}{x^{2} + y^{2}}\right)\,\mathbf j\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\nabla f(x,y)$ at $(2,e)$ if $f(x,y)=y^{- 2 x}$. Work on the domain $y>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
In the second partial, the exponent is constant. In the first, the positive base is constant, so use exponential differentiation and the chain rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=y^{- 2 x}\ln(y)\cdot -2 \\ &=- 2 y^{- 2 x} \ln{\left(y \right)} \\ f_y(x,y)&=- 2 x\cdot y^{- 2 x - 1} \\ &=- 2 x y^{- 2 x - 1}\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the partial derivatives in order:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(x,y)&=(- 2 y^{- 2 x} \ln{\left(y \right)})\,\mathbf i \\ &\quad+(- 2 x y^{- 2 x - 1})\,\mathbf j\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(2,e)&=- 2 \left(e\right)^{- 2 \left(2\right)} \ln{\left(\left(e\right) \right)} \\ &=- \frac{2}{e^{4}} \\ f_y(2,e)&=- 2 \left(2\right) \left(e\right)^{- 2 \left(2\right) - 1} \\ &=- \frac{4}{e^{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
&\left(2 - z\right)^{2}\\
&{}-\left(y + 2\right)\\
&{}+2 x^{2}\\
&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

at $P(-1,1,1)$. Use $t\in\mathbb R$, with $t=0$ at $P$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Bring the variable terms together and set

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F(x,y,z)&=\left(2 - z\right)^{2}\\
&{}-\left(y + 2\right)\\
&{}+2 x^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The surface is the level surface $F=0$. Differentiate with respect to each coordinate, holding the others fixed. Use the product and chain rules, including signs from inner linear functions:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(x,y,z)&=4 x
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(x,y,z)&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(x,y,z)&=-2 \left(2 - z\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

At $P$, the linear expressions in these formulas have the values

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
\left(2 - z\right)&=1\\
x&=-1\\
\left(y + 2\right)&=3
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute these values into the partial derivatives:

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{x}(P)&=4 \left(-1\right)\\
&=-4
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{y}(P)&=-1\\
&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\small\begin{aligned}
F_{z}(P)&=-2 \left(1\right)\\
&=-2
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\nabla F(-1,1,1)=\langle -4,-1,-2\rangle\ne\mathbf 0$. A normal line passes through $P$ and has this direction.

Multiply every component by the same nonzero scalar $2$ to obtain the equivalent direction

$$
\mathbf n=2\langle -4,-1,-2\rangle=\langle -8,-2,-4\rangle.
$$

The point supplies the constant vector, and the normal supplies the direction:

$$
\mathbf r=\langle -1,1,1\rangle+t\,\langle -8,-2,-4\rangle,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the plane curve $2 x^{2} + 3 y^{2}=5.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at $(1,-1).$

Use $f(x,y)=2 x^{2} + 3 y^{2}.$ The nonzero gradient gives the direction of the normal line. A line through $(x_0,y_0)$ parallel to $\left\langle a,b\right\rangle$ satisfies $b(x-x_0)=a(y-y_0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=2 x^{2} + 3 y^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the curve gives the level set $f(x,y)=5.$ Compute the partial derivatives, holding the other coordinate fixed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=4 x \\
f_y(x,y)&=6 y \\
\nabla f(1,-1)&=\left\langle 4,-6\right\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero, so it gives a direction for the normal line. A line through the given point parallel to $\left\langle 4,-6\right\rangle$ satisfies

$$
\begin{aligned}
b(x-x_0)&=a(y-y_0) \\
\left(-6\right)\left(x - 1\right)&=\left(4\right)\left(y + 1\right) \\
- 6 x - 4 y + 2&=0 \\
3 x + 2 y - 1&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying the whole equation gives the normal line $3 x + 2 y - 1=0.$ Its direction is parallel to the gradient; using the gradient as the coefficient vector would give the tangent line instead.

\nabla f(0,2)&=\left\langle -20,13\right\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero, so it gives a direction for the normal line. A line through the given point parallel to $\left\langle -20,13\right\rangle$ satisfies

$$
\begin{aligned}
b(x-x_0)&=a(y-y_0) \\
\left(13\right)\left(x\right)&=\left(-20\right)\left(y - 2\right) \\
13 x + 20 y - 40&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying the whole equation gives the normal line $13 x + 20 y - 40=0.$ Its direction is parallel to the gradient; using the gradient as the coefficient vector would give the tangent line instead.

knowledge_point.title: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface

question.:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=- y z + \ln{\left(- x z + y^{2} \right)}
$$

find a nonzero vector perpendicular to the level surface through $P=(2,2,-1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A nonzero gradient is perpendicular to its level surface. Treat the other variables as constants when taking each partial derivative.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x&=- \frac{z}{- x z + y^{2}}\\f_y&=\frac{2 y}{- x z + y^{2}} - z\\f_z&=- \frac{x}{- x z + y^{2}} - y
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate at $P=(2,2,-1)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(P)&=- \frac{\left(-1\right)}{- \left(2\right) \left(-1\right) + \left(2\right)^{2}}=\frac{1}{6}\\f_y(P)&=\frac{2 \left(2\right)}{- \left(2\right) \left(-1\right) + \left(2\right)^{2}} - \left(-1\right)=\frac{5}{3}\\f_z(P)&=- \frac{\left(2\right)}{- \left(2\right) \left(-1\right) + \left(2\right)^{2}} - \left(2\right)=- \frac{7}{3}\\\nabla f(P)&=\frac{1}{6}\,\mathbf i+\frac{5}{3}\,\mathbf j-\frac{7}{3}\,\mathbf k
\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero.

Every nonzero scalar multiple of this gradient is normal. In particular,

$$
-1\nabla f(P)=-\frac{1}{6}\,\mathbf i-\frac{5}{3}\,\mathbf j+\frac{7}{3}\,\mathbf k.
$$

So the listed vector $-\frac{1}{6}\,\mathbf i-\frac{5}{3}\,\mathbf j+\frac{7}{3}\,\mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the surface at $P$.

knowledge_point.title: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface

question.:question/problem:
For the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=\left(x^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2} + 2 \left(z + 1\right)^{2} - 1\right)^{3}
$$

find a nonzero vector perpendicular to the level surface through $P=(0,-2,-1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
At the supplied point, $f(P)=0$. Thus the level surface is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(x^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2} + 2 \left(z + 1\right)^{2} - 1\right)^{3}&=0\\x^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2} + 2 \left(z + 1\right)^{2} - 1&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

A real number has cube zero exactly when it is zero, so these equations describe the same surface. By the chain rule,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla f&=3\left(x^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2} + 2 \left(z + 1\right)^{2} - 1\right)^{2}\nabla g\\\nabla f(P)&=\mathbf 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The zero vector has no direction. It does not establish that the surface lacks a normal. Use the equivalent defining function

$$
g(x,y,z)=x^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2} + 2 \left(z + 1\right)^{2} - 1
$$

A nonzero gradient is perpendicular to its level surface. Treat the other variables as constants when taking each partial derivative.

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_x&=2 x\\g_y&=2 y + 2\\g_z&=4 z + 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate at $P=(0,-2,-1)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_x(P)&=2 \left(0\right)=0\\g_y(P)&=2 \left(-2\right) + 2=-2\\g_z(P)&=4 \left(-1\right) + 4=0\\\nabla g(P)&=-2\,\mathbf j
\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero.

Every nonzero scalar multiple of this gradient is normal. In particular,

$$
-2\nabla g(P)=4\,\mathbf j.
$$

So the listed vector $4\,\mathbf j$ is perpendicular to the surface at $P$.

knowledge_point.title: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface

question.:question/problem:
Find a nonzero normal vector to the surface

$$
- 2 x^{2} + 2 y^{2} + y z + z^{2}=2 z + 6
$$

at $P=(-1,0,-2)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Move all terms to one side and define

$$
F(x,y,z)=- 2 x^{2} + 2 y^{2} + y z + z^{2} - 2 z - 6
$$

The point satisfies $F(P)=0$. Include derivatives of the terms moved from the right side.

A nonzero gradient is perpendicular to its level surface. Treat the other variables as constants when taking each partial derivative.

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_x&=- 4 x\\F_y&=4 y + z\\F_z&=y + 2 z - 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate at $P=(-1,0,-2)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_x(P)&=- 4 \left(-1\right)=4\\F_y(P)&=4 \left(0\right) + \left(-2\right)=-2\\F_z(P)&=\left(0\right) + 2 \left(-2\right) - 2=-6\\\nabla F(P)&=4\,\mathbf i-2\,\mathbf j-6\,\mathbf k
\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero.

Every nonzero scalar multiple of this gradient is normal. In particular,

$$
1\nabla F(P)=4\,\mathbf i-2\,\mathbf j-6\,\mathbf k.
$$

So the listed vector $4\,\mathbf i-2\,\mathbf j-6\,\mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the surface at $P$.

$$

question.:question/problem:
![Directed segments: C_1: C to B; C_2: A to D; C_3: A to B; C_4: A to C; C_5: D to C](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179672/3d8cc3de5b7bdd3438b1db00e68f8753d458b66834f0f086b0e732266e211ac5.png)

The arrows show the orientations of the segments. The same continuous vector field $\mathbf F$ is used throughout. Let $L_1$ follow $A\to B\to C\to A$ and $L_2$ follow $A\to D\to C\to A$. You are given

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{L_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r&=-2\\\int_{L_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r&=-3\end{aligned}
$$

The closed path $C$ follows $A\to B\to C\to D\to A$ **counterclockwise**. This path is the **outer boundary**. Evaluate its line integral.

$\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=$ {{answer}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $I_j=\int_{C_j}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r$ for each segment in its arrow direction. Trace both named loops in their given directions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{L_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r&=-I_1+I_3-I_4\\\int_{L_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r&=I_2-I_4+I_5\end{aligned}
$$

The requested outer traversal has signed sum

$$
\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=-I_1-I_2+I_3-I_5
$$

Choose the loop orientations so that their shared diagonal cancels and the outer segments have those signs:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r&=(-I_1+I_3-I_4)-(I_2-I_4+I_5)\\&=\int_{L_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r-\int_{L_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r\\&=(-2)-(-3)\\&=1\end{aligned}
$$

This uses orientation reversal and additivity; a closed path alone does not imply a zero integral.

question.:question/problem:

Write $I_j=\int_{C_j}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r$ for each segment in its arrow direction. Compare each arrow with the requested traversal. Reversed segments contribute negative integrals. By additivity,

$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following could be the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)=-y^2+\left(x+1\right)$? Use the relationship between level curves and gradient directions. Arrows show directions only.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First set $f(x,y)=c$.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)&=c\\-y^2+\left(x+1\right)&=c\\x&=-1+c+y^2\end{aligned}
$$

These level curves are right-opening parabolas. With $y$ fixed, moving right increases the function. With $x$ fixed, moving toward $y=0$ increases it.

![Derived labeled level curves](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179712/plot-90b281f3aab3c51ae71060bb4850317326e48fcbf7ddd86279bbf9b3e84b30ea.png)

A derivative check gives $\nabla f=\left\langle 1,-2y\right\rangle$. These directions are normal to the level curves and point toward increasing values. Other curve shapes have a different normal direction somewhere; a reversed field, if offered, points downhill.

![Matching contours and gradient directions](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179712/plot-b496284915b289f22169cf7e265ee540d8b653a322b56e64b917c6156f61a191.png)
