The field must be perpendicular to every regular level curve. One compatible function, used here to check the geometric match, is $f(x,y)=x$.

knowledge_point.title: Establishing the Connection With Line Integrals of Scalar Fields

question.:question/problem:
Let

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=\left(5 x z\right)\,\mathbf{i}+\left(3 x y\right)\,\mathbf{j}+\left(4 y z\right)\,\mathbf{k}
$$

and let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth path in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. Which coordinate-integral expression is equivalent to $\int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a piecewise-smooth path and a field defined on it,

$$
\int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}=\int_C \left(P\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(Q\right)\,\mathrm{d}y+\left(R\right)\,\mathrm{d}z
$$

Here the whole coefficients, including their signs, are

$$
P=5 x z,\quad Q=3 x y,\quad R=4 y z
$$

Substituting into the identity gives

$$
\int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}=\int_C \left(5 x z\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(3 x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y+\left(4 y z\right)\,\mathrm{d}z
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: \int_C \left(- 4 y z\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(- 5 x z\right)\,\mathrm{d}y+\left(3 x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}z
\int_C \left(5 x z\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(3 x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y+\left(4 y z\right)\,\mathrm{d}z
\int_C \left(3 x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(- 4 y z\right)\,\mathrm{d}y+\left(- 5 x z\right)\,\mathrm{d}z
\int_C \left(5 x z\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(4 y z\right)\,\mathrm{d}y+\left(- 3 x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}z
\int_C \left(- 4 y z\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(- 3 x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y+\left(- 5 x z\right)\,\mathrm{d}z

question.:question/problem:

$$
\int_C \left(- 5 y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(5 y - 4 z\right)\,\mathrm{d}y+\left(4 z^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}z
$$

with the components of a vector field. Which field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)$ gives this coordinate representation of $\int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a piecewise-smooth path and a field defined on it,

$$
\int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}=\int_C \left(P\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(Q\right)\,\mathrm{d}y+\left(R\right)\,\mathrm{d}z
$$

Here the whole coefficients, including their signs, are

$$
P=- 5 y,\quad Q=5 y - 4 z,\quad R=4 z^{2}
$$

Place those coefficients on the corresponding basis vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)&=\left(- 5 y\right)\,\mathbf{i}+\left(5 y - 4 z\right)\,\mathbf{j}+\left(4 z^{2}\right)\,\mathbf{k}\\ \int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}&=\int_C \left(- 5 y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(5 y - 4 z\right)\,\mathrm{d}y+\left(4 z^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves

question.:question/problem:
![](images/c0/c0a4f042748ddadd824bed4ee71bca9724d7ca7dcc376a0ccf7c1353d59ec4fc.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(-2,2)$ to the point $B(-1,2),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(-1,2)$ to the point $D(-1,0).$

Traverse $C=C_1\cup C_2$ in the stated order. Let

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=(2 x + y)\mathbf i+(2 x)\mathbf j.
$$

Given that

$$
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=-1,
$$

evaluate $\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r$.

For $C_2$, use $\mathbf r_2(t)=(-1)\mathbf i+(2 - 2 t)\mathbf j$, with $t$ running from $0$ to $1$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use additivity over the two oriented pieces.

$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r+\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
$$

The contribution from $C_1$ is supplied, so calculate $C_2$ only. Choose $x=-1$ and $y=2 - 2 t$, with $t$ running from $0$ to $1$ in that order. The endpoint substitutions give the start and end of the stated piece.

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_2(t)&=(-1)\mathbf i+(2 - 2 t)\mathbf j, \\ \mathbf r_2'(t)&=(0)\mathbf i+(-2)\mathbf j.\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the field components:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\mathbf r_2(t))&=- 2 t, \\ Q(\mathbf r_2(t))&=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the dot product, keeping both tangent factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F(\mathbf r_2(t))\cdot\mathbf r_2'(t)&=(- 2 t)(0) \\ &\quad+(-2)(-2) \\ &=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate in the specified direction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r&=\int_{0}^{1}(4)\,\mathrm dt \\ &=\left[4 t\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Add the supplied contribution:

$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=(-1)+(4)=3.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves

question.:question/problem:
![](images/b4/b4ce481ac8babb7a3e5707f1ef44417b12e73abe4b4c2143c19b45332642c6d2.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment  from the point $B(0,8)$ to the point $A(-2,8),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a section of the curve $y=-{x}^{3}$ from the point $A(-2,8)$ to the point $O(0,0).$

Traverse $C=C_1\cup C_2$ in the stated order. Let

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=(x y)\mathbf i+(2 y)\mathbf j.
$$

Given that

$$
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=16,
$$

evaluate $\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use additivity over the two oriented pieces.

$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r+\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
$$

The contribution from $C_1$ is supplied, so calculate $C_2$ only. Choose $x=t$ and $y=- t^{3}$, with $t$ running from $-2$ to $0$ in that order. The endpoint substitutions give the start and end of the stated piece.

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_2(t)&=(t)\mathbf i+(- t^{3})\mathbf j, \\ \mathbf r_2'(t)&=(1)\mathbf i+(- 3 t^{2})\mathbf j.\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the field components:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\mathbf r_2(t))&=- t^{4}, \\ Q(\mathbf r_2(t))&=- 2 t^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the dot product, keeping both tangent factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F(\mathbf r_2(t))\cdot\mathbf r_2'(t)&=(- t^{4})(1) \\ &\quad+(- 2 t^{3})(- 3 t^{2}) \\ &=6 t^{5} - t^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate in the specified direction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r&=\int_{-2}^{0}(6 t^{5} - t^{4})\,\mathrm dt \\ &=\left[t^{6} - \frac{t^{5}}{5}\right]_{-2}^{0} \\ &=- \frac{352}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Add the supplied contribution:

$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=(16)+\left(- \frac{352}{5}\right)=- \frac{272}{5}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Which diagram represents

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\left(y+2\right)\,i+\left(x-2\right)\,j
$$

at $A=(1,3)$, $B=(-1,-2)$, $C=(-1,3)$? All diagrams use one unit per grid interval.

Evaluate both components at each point, then place the tail of its vector at that point.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $\mathbf F=P\,i+Q\,j$. Substitute into each component, then combine the results:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(1,3)&=(3)-(-2)=5 \\
Q(1,3)&=(1)+(-2)=-1 \\
\mathbf F(1,3)&=5\,i-j \\
P(-1,-2)&=(-2)-(-2)=0 \\
Q(-1,-2)&=(-1)+(-2)=-3 \\
\mathbf F(-1,-2)&=-3\,j \\
P(-1,3)&=(3)-(-2)=5 \\
Q(-1,3)&=(-1)+(-2)=-3 \\
\mathbf F(-1,3)&=5\,i-3\,j
\end{aligned}
$$

The first component gives the horizontal displacement and the second gives the vertical displacement. Place each tail at its labeled point. A zero component gives no displacement along that axis; a zero vector stays at its tail.

question.:question/problem: Let $C$ be the straight segment from $A=(2,3)$ to $B=(2,2)$. Let $f(x,y)=e^{x+y}$. Which definite integral is equivalent to $\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$? Do not evaluate the integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The endpoint position vectors give

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r(t)&=\mathbf a+t(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\\
&=\langle 2,- t + 3\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=0$ and $t=1$ this gives $A=(2,3)$ and $B=(2,2)$, respectively.

Differentiate, compute the speed, and substitute both coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 0,-1\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(0)^2+(-1)^2}=1,\\
f(\mathbf r(t))&=e^{(2)+(- t + 3)}\\
&=e^{- t + 5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the scalar arc-length formula,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,\\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(e^{- t + 5}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The endpoints are $A=(3,1)$ and $B=(5,-1)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r(1)&=\langle 5,-1\rangle,\\
\mathbf r(3)&=\langle 3,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $1\le u\le 3$ covers the segment from $B$ to $A$. Reversing traversal does not negate a scalar arc-length integral; its speed is positive.

Differentiate, compute the speed, and substitute both coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(u)&=\langle -1,1\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(u)\|&=\sqrt{(-1)^2+(1)^2}=\sqrt{2},\\
f(\mathbf r(u))&=e^{(- u + 6)+(u - 2)}\\
&=e^{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the scalar arc-length formula,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{1}^{3}f(\mathbf r(u))\,\|\mathbf r'(u)\|\,\mathrm{d}u,\\
&=\sqrt{2}\int_{1}^{3}\left(e^{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z},$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,1,-2)$ to $(1,-1,-1)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For scalar arc length, use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Parametrize the segment and check its endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=A+t(B-A) \\  &=\left(t,1 - 2 t,t - 2\right) \\  \mathbf r(0)&=\left(0,1,-2\right) \\  \mathbf r(1)&=\left(1,-1,-1\right)\end{aligned}
$$

For $0\le t\le1$, the velocity and speed are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left(1,-2,1\right) \\  \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{(1)^2+(-2)^2+(1)^2} \\  &=\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute all three coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\sqrt{2(t)+(1 - 2 t)-(t - 2)} \\  &=\sqrt{3 - t}\end{aligned}
$$

The equivalent definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{3 - t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}\sin \left(\frac{πy}{4}\right)ds$ along the line segment from $(0, 4, -3)$ to $(-3, 2, -5)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For scalar arc length, use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Parametrize the segment and check its endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=A+t(B-A) \\  &=\left(- 3 t,4 - 2 t,- 2 t - 3\right) \\  \mathbf r(0)&=\left(0,4,-3\right) \\  \mathbf r(1)&=\left(-3,2,-5\right)\end{aligned}
$$

For $0\le t\le1$, the velocity and speed are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left(-3,-2,-2\right) \\  \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{(-3)^2+(-2)^2+(-2)^2} \\  &=\sqrt{17}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute all three coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}(4 - 2 t)\right) \\  &=\sin{\left(- \frac{\pi t}{2} + \pi \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

The equivalent definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\sqrt{17}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\sin{\left(- \frac{\pi t}{2} + \pi \right)})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Use $u=- \frac{\pi t}{2} + \pi$ and $\mathrm{d}u=\left(- \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t$. The new bounds are $u(0)=\pi$ and $u(1)=\frac{\pi}{2}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}I&=- \frac{2 \sqrt{17}}{\pi}\int_{\pi}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin u\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &=- \frac{2 \sqrt{17}}{\pi}\left[-\cos u\right]_{\pi}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\  &=- \frac{2 \sqrt{17}}{\pi}\left(-\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)+\cos(\pi)\right) \\  &=- \frac{2 \sqrt{17}}{\pi}\left((0)-(1)\right) \\  &=\frac{2 \sqrt{17}}{\pi}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(1,1,1)$ to $(4,3,3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For scalar arc length, use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Parametrize the segment and check its endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=A+t(B-A) \\  &=\left(3 t + 1,2 t + 1,2 t + 1\right) \\  \mathbf r(0)&=\left(1,1,1\right) \\  \mathbf r(1)&=\left(4,3,3\right)\end{aligned}
$$

For $0\le t\le1$, the velocity and speed are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left(3,2,2\right) \\  \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{(3)^2+(2)^2+(2)^2} \\  &=\sqrt{17}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute all three coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=(3 t + 1)(2 t + 1)^2 \\  &=12 t^{3} + 16 t^{2} + 7 t + 1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate the expanded polynomial and subtract the endpoint values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\sqrt{17}{\int }_{0}^{1}(12 t^{3} + 16 t^{2} + 7 t + 1)\,\text{d}t \\  &=\sqrt{17}\left[3 t^{4} + \frac{16 t^{3}}{3} + \frac{7 t^{2}}{2} + t\right]_0^1 \\  &=\sqrt{17}\left(\left(\frac{77}{6}\right)-(0)\right) \\  &=\frac{77 \sqrt{17}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given $f(x,y)=\left(x + 2\right)^{2} + \left(y + 1\right)^{2}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $\nabla f=\mathbf 0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A gradient vanishes exactly when every component vanishes. Differentiate with respect to each variable, holding the others constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}&=2 x + 4 \\ f_{y}&=2 y + 2\end{aligned}
$$

Set all components equal to zero:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2 x + 4&=0 \\ 2 y + 2&=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To write the simultaneous equations compactly, let $u=x + 2,\ v=y + 1$. 

$$
\begin{aligned}u&=0 \\ v&=0\end{aligned}
$$

 Recover the original coordinates using $x=u - 2,\ y=v - 1$.

Therefore, the complete set of points in the domain is $(-2,-1)$. Each satisfies every component equation.

question.:question/problem:

$$

find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $\nabla f=\mathbf 0$.

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A gradient vanishes exactly when every component vanishes. Differentiate with respect to each variable, holding the others constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}&=- 2 y + 2 \left(y + 1\right)^{2} - 2 \\ f_{y}&=- 2 x + 4 \left(x + 2\right) \left(y + 1\right) - 4 \\ f_{z}&=6 \left(z + 3\right)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Set all components equal to zero:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}- 2 y + 2 \left(y + 1\right)^{2} - 2&=0 \\ - 2 x + 4 \left(x + 2\right) \left(y + 1\right) - 4&=0 \\ 6 \left(z + 3\right)^{2}&=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To write the simultaneous equations compactly, let $u=x + 2,\ v=y + 1,\ w=z + 3$. Factor the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}v \left(2 v - 2\right)&=0 \\ v&=0\quad\text{or}\quad v=1\end{aligned}
$$

For $v=0$, the second equation is $- 2 u=0$; for $v=1$, it is $2 u=0$. Both give $u=0$. The third equation gives $w=0$. Recover the original coordinates using $x=u - 2,\ y=v - 1,\ z=w - 3$.

Therefore, the complete set of points in the domain is $(-2,-1,-3)$ and $(-2,0,-3)$. Each satisfies every component equation.

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2 x + 2 \left(y + 1\right)^{2} + 4&=0 \\ 4 z + 4 \left(x + 2\right) \left(y + 1\right) + 12&=0 \\ 4 y - 4 z - 8&=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To write the simultaneous equations compactly, let $u=x + 2,\ v=y + 1,\ w=z + 3$. The first and third equations give $u=- v^{2}$ and $w=v$. Substitute into the second:

question.:question/problem:

$$

find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $\nabla f=\mathbf 0$. The domain is $x>-2,\ y>-1,\ z>-3$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A gradient vanishes exactly when every component vanishes. Differentiate with respect to each variable, holding the others constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}&=\ln{\left(x + 2 \right)} - 1 \\ f_{y}&=\ln{\left(y + 1 \right)} + 1 \\ f_{z}&=\ln{\left(z + 3 \right)} - 1\end{aligned}
$$

Set all components equal to zero:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\ln{\left(x + 2 \right)} - 1&=0 \\ \ln{\left(y + 1 \right)} + 1&=0 \\ \ln{\left(z + 3 \right)} - 1&=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To write the simultaneous equations compactly, let $u=x + 2,\ v=y + 1,\ w=z + 3$. The product rule gives $\frac{d}{du}(u\ln u)=\ln u+1$ (and similarly for the other coordinates). Solve each logarithmic equation by exponentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln u&=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=e \\ \ln v&=-1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v=e^{-1} \\ \ln w&=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad w=e\end{aligned}
$$

All resulting shifted coordinates are positive. Recover the original coordinates using $x=u - 2,\ y=v - 1,\ z=w - 3$.

Therefore, the complete set of points in the domain is $(-2 + e,-1 + e^{-1},-3 + e)$. Each satisfies every component equation.

question.:question/problem:
Given $f(x,y)=x + 2 +  rac{1}{y + 1} -  rac{y + 1}{x + 2}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $
abla f=\mathbf 0$. The domain is $x
e -2,\ y
e -1$.

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A gradient vanishes exactly when every component vanishes. Differentiate with respect to each variable, holding the others constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}&=1 + \frac{y + 1}{\left(x + 2\right)^{2}} \\ f_{y}&=- \frac{1}{\left(y + 1\right)^{2}} - \frac{1}{x + 2}\end{aligned}
$$

Set all components equal to zero:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}1 + \frac{y + 1}{\left(x + 2\right)^{2}}&=0 \\ - \frac{1}{\left(y + 1\right)^{2}} - \frac{1}{x + 2}&=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To write the simultaneous equations compactly, let $u=x + 2,\ v=y + 1$. The first equation gives $v=-u^2/1$. Because $u,v\ne0$, substitution in the second and multiplication by $u^4$ are valid:

$$
\begin{aligned}1+u^{3}&=0 \\ u^3&=-1 \\ u&=-1 \\ v&=-1\end{aligned}
$$

 Recover the original coordinates using $x=u - 2,\ y=v - 1$.

Therefore, the complete set of points in the domain is $(-3,-2)$. Each satisfies every component equation.

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes

question.:question/problem:
Given $f(x,y)=\left(x + 2\right)^{2} + 4 \left(x + 2\right) \cos{\left(y + 1 \right)}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $\nabla f=\mathbf 0$. The domain is $-1\le y<-1 + \pi$.

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A gradient vanishes exactly when every component vanishes. Differentiate with respect to each variable, holding the others constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_{x}&=2 x + 4 \cos{\left(y + 1 \right)} + 4 \\ f_{y}&=- 4 \left(x + 2\right) \sin{\left(y + 1 \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Set all components equal to zero:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2 x + 4 \cos{\left(y + 1 \right)} + 4&=0 \\ - 4 \left(x + 2\right) \sin{\left(y + 1 \right)}&=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To write the simultaneous equations compactly, let $u=x + 2,\ v=y + 1$. The first equation gives $u=- 2 \cos{\left(v \right)}$. After substitution and division by the nonzero constant $8$, the second equation becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\sin{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(v \right)}&=0\end{aligned}
$$

A product is zero if at least one factor is zero. In $0\le v<\pi$, this gives $v=0$ or $v=\frac{\pi}{2}$. The corresponding values of $u$ are $-2$ and $0$, respectively. The upper boundary is excluded. Recover the original coordinates using $x=u - 2,\ y=v - 1$.

Therefore, the complete set of points in the domain is $(-4,-1)$ and $(-2,-1 + \frac{\pi}{2})$. Each satisfies every component equation.

knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Line Integral Along a Segment in the Cartesian Plane

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=2 x + 2 y$ along the line segment from $(3,-3)$ to $(3,0)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{t_a}^{t_b} f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,
$$

where $C$ is the line segment from $(3,-3)$ to $(3,0).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(3)\,i+(-3)\,j$ and $b=(3)\,i+(0)\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(3)\,i+(-3)\,j+t((0)\,i+(3)\,j) \\  & =(3)\,i+(3 \cdot t - 3)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=3$ and $y=3 \cdot t - 3$ along the segment.

Computing $r\prime(t)$ and $\|r\prime(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 \cdot t - 3)j \\  & =(0)\,i+(3)\,j \\ \|r\prime(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^2+(3)^2} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2 \cdot x + 2 \cdot y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(3)+2(3 \cdot t - 3) \\  & =6 \cdot t.\end{aligned}
$$

Write $I=\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_0^1 f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\int_0^1 (6 \cdot t)\cdot 3\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =3\int_0^1 (6 \cdot t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =3[3 \cdot t^{2}]_0^1 \\  & =3((3)+(0))-3(0) \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\left(6 x + 9\right) e^{x y}$ along the line segment from $(-1,3)$ to $(1,6)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{t_a}^{t_b} f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,
$$

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,3)$ to $(1,6).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(-1)\,i+(3)\,j$ and $b=(1)\,i+(6)\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-1)\,i+(3)\,j+t((2)\,i+(3)\,j) \\  & =(2 \cdot t - 1)\,i+(3 \cdot t + 3)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2 \cdot t - 1$ and $y=3 \cdot t + 3$ along the segment.

Computing $r\prime(t)$ and $\|r\prime(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 \cdot t - 1)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 \cdot t + 3)j \\  & =(2)\,i+(3)\,j \\ \|r\prime(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(2)^2+(3)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\left(6 \cdot x + 9\right) \cdot e^{x \cdot y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(6(2 \cdot t - 1)+9)e^{(2 \cdot t - 1)(3 \cdot t + 3)} \\  & =(12 \cdot t + 3)e^{6 \cdot t^{2} + 3 \cdot t - 3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Write $I=\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_0^1 f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\int_0^1 ((12 \cdot t + 3)e^{6 \cdot t^{2} + 3 \cdot t - 3})\cdot \sqrt{13}\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{13}\int_0^1 ((12 \cdot t + 3)e^{6 \cdot t^{2} + 3 \cdot t - 3})\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=6 \cdot t^{2} + 3 \cdot t - 3,$ $\mathrm{d}u=(12 \cdot t + 3)\,\mathrm{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\sqrt{13}\int_{-3}^{6}e^u\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{13}[e^u]_{-3}^{6} \\  & =\sqrt{13}(e^{6}-e^{-3}) \\  & =\sqrt{13} \cdot \left(- \frac{1}{e^{3}} + e^{6}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\sec^{2}{\left(\frac{\pi \left(- x + y\right)}{4} \right)}$ along the line segment from $(1,1)$ to $(-1,0)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{t_a}^{t_b} f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,
$$

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,1)$ to $(-1,0).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(1)\,i+(1)\,j$ and $b=(-1)\,i+(0)\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(1)\,i+(1)\,j+t((-2)\,i+(-1)\,j) \\  & =(1 - 2 \cdot t)\,i+(1 - t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1 - 2 \cdot t$ and $y=1 - t$ along the segment.

Computing $r\prime(t)$ and $\|r\prime(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(1 - 2 \cdot t)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(1 - t)j \\  & =(-2)\,i+(-1)\,j \\ \|r\prime(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^2+(-1)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sec^{2}{\left(\frac{\pi \cdot \left(- x + y\right)}{4} \right)}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sec^2\left(\frac{\pi((1 - t)-(1 - 2 \cdot t))}{4}\right) \\  & =\sec^2\left(\frac{\pi \cdot t}{4}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Write $I=\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_0^1 f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\int_0^1 (\sec^2\left(\frac{\pi \cdot t}{4}\right))\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{5}\int_0^1 (\sec^2\left(\frac{\pi \cdot t}{4}\right))\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\frac{\pi \cdot t}{4},$ $\mathrm{d}u=\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{4 \cdot \sqrt{5}}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\sec^2 u\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\frac{4 \cdot \sqrt{5}}{\pi}[\tan u]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\  & =\frac{4 \cdot \sqrt{5}}{\pi}(\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-\tan(0)) \\  & =\frac{4 \cdot \sqrt{5}}{\pi}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{4 \cdot \sqrt{5}}{\pi}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=e^{- x + y}$ along the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,4)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{t_a}^{t_b} f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,
$$

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,4).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(0)\,i+(0)\,j$ and $b=(1)\,i+(4)\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(0)\,i+(0)\,j+t((1)\,i+(4)\,j) \\  & =(t)\,i+(4 \cdot t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=t$ and $y=4 \cdot t$ along the segment.

Computing $r\prime(t)$ and $\|r\prime(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(4 \cdot t)j \\  & =(1)\,i+(4)\,j \\ \|r\prime(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(1)^2+(4)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{17}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=e^{- x + y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =e^{-1(t)+1(4 \cdot t)} \\  & =e^{3 \cdot t}.\end{aligned}
$$

The exponent has derivative $3$. With $u=3 t$, $\mathrm{d}u=3\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $0$ and $3$. Write $I=\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_0^1 f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\int_0^1 (e^{3 \cdot t})\cdot \sqrt{17}\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{17}\int_0^1 (e^{3 \cdot t})\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{17}[\frac{e^{3 \cdot t}}{3}]_0^1 \\  & =\sqrt{17}\left(\frac{e^{3}}{3}\right)-\sqrt{17}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{17} \cdot \left(- \frac{1}{3} + \frac{e^{3}}{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=2 x y$ along the line segment from $(2,-2)$ to $(4,-1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{t_a}^{t_b} f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,
$$

where $C$ is the line segment from $(2,-2)$ to $(4,-1).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(2)\,i+(-2)\,j$ and $b=(4)\,i+(-1)\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(2)\,i+(-2)\,j+t((2)\,i+(1)\,j) \\  & =(2 \cdot t + 2)\,i+(t - 2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2 \cdot t + 2$ and $y=t - 2$ along the segment.

Computing $r\prime(t)$ and $\|r\prime(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 \cdot t + 2)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t - 2)j \\  & =(2)\,i+(1)\,j \\ \|r\prime(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(2)^2+(1)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2 \cdot x \cdot y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(2 \cdot t + 2)(t - 2) \\  & =4 \cdot t^{2} - 4 \cdot t - 8.\end{aligned}
$$

Write $I=\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_0^1 f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\int_0^1 (4 \cdot t^{2} - 4 \cdot t - 8)\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{5}\int_0^1 (4 \cdot t^{2} - 4 \cdot t - 8)\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{5}[\frac{4 \cdot t^{3}}{3} - 2 \cdot t^{2} - 8 \cdot t]_0^1 \\  & =\sqrt{5}(\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)+(-2)+(-8))-\sqrt{5}(0) \\  & =- \frac{26 \cdot \sqrt{5}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x + \sqrt{2} \sqrt{y}$ along the line segment from $(3,0)$ to $(3,8)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{t_a}^{t_b} f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,
$$

where $C$ is the line segment from $(3,0)$ to $(3,8).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(3)\,i+(0)\,j$ and $b=(3)\,i+(8)\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(3)\,i+(0)\,j+t((0)\,i+(8)\,j) \\  & =(3)\,i+(8 \cdot t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=3$ and $y=8 \cdot t$ along the segment.

Computing $r\prime(t)$ and $\|r\prime(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(8 \cdot t)j \\  & =(0)\,i+(8)\,j \\ \|r\prime(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^2+(8)^2} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x + \sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3+\sqrt{2(8 \cdot t)} \\  & =4 \cdot \sqrt{t} + 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Write $I=\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_0^1 f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\int_0^1 (4 \cdot \sqrt{t} + 3)\cdot 8\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =24\int_0^1 (\frac{4 \cdot \sqrt{t}}{3} + 1)\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =24[\frac{8 \cdot t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9} + t]_0^1 \\  & =24(1+\frac{8}{9})-0 \\  & =\frac{136}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: The Parametric Equations of an Ellipse Centered at the Origin

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186152187/ellipse-f79ff84401d5181e6be2d31c.png)

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$, generate the ellipse shown above?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The intercepts are $(\pm6,0)$ and $(0,\pm2)$, so the horizontal radius is $6$ and the vertical radius is $2$. Each radius is measured from the center, rather than across the whole ellipse.

An ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal radius $a$ and vertical radius $b$ has parametric equations

$$
x=a\cos\theta,\qquad y=b\sin\theta,\qquad \theta\in[0,2\pi).
$$

Here $a=6$ and $b=2$, so

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=2\sin\theta,\qquad \theta\in[0,2\pi).
$$

Both sine and cosine range from $-1$ to $1$, giving the horizontal and vertical extents shown.

knowledge_point.title: The Parametric Equations of an Ellipse Centered at the Origin

question.:question/worked-solution:
The intercepts are $(\pm6,0)$ and $(0,\pm2)$, so the horizontal radius is $6$ and the vertical radius is $2$. Each radius is measured from the center, rather than across the whole ellipse.

An ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal radius $a$ and vertical radius $b$ has parametric equations

$$
x=a\cos\theta,\qquad y=b\sin\theta,\qquad \theta\in[0,2\pi).
$$

Here $a=6$ and $b=2$, so

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=2\sin\theta,\qquad \theta\in[0,2\pi).
$$

At $\theta=0$, cosine is $1$ and sine is $0$, giving $J(6,0)$. For increasing $\theta$, the quarter-turn points are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\theta=0&:\quad (6,0)\\
\theta=\pi/2&:\quad (0,2)\\
\theta=\pi&:\quad (-6,0)\\
\theta=3\pi/2&:\quad (0,-2).
\end{aligned}
$$

This order is counterclockwise. The interval $[0,2\pi)$ covers one full traversal without including the initial point twice.

knowledge_point.title: The Parametric Equations of an Ellipse Centered at a General Point

question.:question/problem:
An ellipse has center $(-6,-3)$, horizontal radius $4$ and vertical radius $3$.

Which set of parametric equations generates this ellipse for $0\leq\theta<2\pi$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
An ellipse with center $(h,k)$, horizontal radius $a$ and vertical radius $b$ has the standard parametrization

$$
x=h+a\cos\theta,\qquad y=k+b\sin\theta,\qquad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$

Here $h=-6$, $k=-3$, $a=4$ and $b=3$. Substituting gives

$$
x=4\cos\theta-6,\,y=3\sin\theta-3,\qquad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$

knowledge_point.title: The Parametric Equations of an Ellipse Centered at a General Point

question.:question/worked-solution:
An ellipse with center $(h,k)$, horizontal radius $a$ and vertical radius $b$ has the standard parametrization

$$
x=h+a\cos\theta,\qquad y=k+b\sin\theta,\qquad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$

Here $h=-6$, $k=3$, $a=4$ and $b=3$. Substituting gives

$$
x=4\cos\theta-6,\,y=3\sin\theta+3,\qquad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$

Check the starting point and direction at successive quarter turns:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\theta=0 &: (-2,3)\\\theta=\frac{\pi}{2} &: (-6,6)\\\theta=\pi &: (-10,3)\\\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2} &: (-6,0)
\end{aligned}
$$

The path goes right, top, left, bottom: counterclockwise. The scaled and translated unit circle makes one full traversal; excluding $2\pi$ avoids repeating the starting point.

$$
\begin{aligned} h&=\frac{-10+(-2)}{2}=-6, &k&=\frac{-6+(0)}{2}=-3,\\
 a&=\frac{-2-(-10)}{2}=4, &b&=\frac{0-(-6)}{2}=3.
\end{aligned}
$$

An ellipse with center $(h,k)$, horizontal radius $a$ and vertical radius $b$ has the standard parametrization

$$
x=h+a\cos\theta,\qquad y=k+b\sin\theta,\qquad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$

Here $h=-6$, $k=-3$, $a=4$ and $b=3$. Substituting gives

$$
x=4\cos\theta-6,\,y=3\sin\theta-3,\qquad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.

knowledge_point.title: The Cartesian Equation of an Ellipse

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse defined by

$$
x=5\cos\theta,\quad y=2\sin\theta,\quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$

The trigonometric terms have been isolated for you:

$$
\frac{x}{5}=\cos\theta,\qquad \frac{y}{2}=\sin\theta.
$$

Square both equations and use $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$. Choose the resulting Cartesian equation.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Square the isolated $x$ equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(\frac{x}{5}\right)^2&=\cos^2\theta\\\frac{x^2}{25}&=\cos^2\theta
\end{aligned}
$$

Square the isolated $y$ equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)^2&=\sin^2\theta\\\frac{y^2}{4}&=\sin^2\theta
\end{aligned}
$$

Add the squared equations and use $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$:

$$
\frac{x^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{4}=\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1.
$$

Thus the Cartesian equation is

$$
\frac{x^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1.
$$

The full parameter interval traces the entire ellipse.

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse defined by

$$
x=5\cos\theta+1,\quad y=7\sin\theta,\quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Isolate the trigonometric term in the $x$ equation, then square.

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=5\cos\theta+1\\x-1&=5\cos\theta\\\frac{x-1}{5}&=\cos\theta\\\left(\frac{x-1}{5}\right)^2&=\cos^2\theta\\\frac{(x-1)^2}{25}&=\cos^2\theta
\end{aligned}
$$

Isolate the trigonometric term in the $y$ equation, then square.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y&=7\sin\theta\\\frac{y}{7}&=\sin\theta\\\left(\frac{y}{7}\right)^2&=\sin^2\theta\\\frac{y^2}{49}&=\sin^2\theta
\end{aligned}
$$

Add the squared equations and use $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$:

$$
\frac{(x-1)^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{49}=\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1.
$$

Thus the Cartesian equation is

$$
\frac{(x-1)^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{49}=1.
$$

The full parameter interval traces the entire ellipse.

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse defined by

$$
x=\frac{4}{5}\cos\theta,\quad y=\frac{4}{3}\sin\theta,\quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Isolate the trigonometric term in the $x$ equation, then square.

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=\frac{4}{5}\cos\theta\\\frac{5}{4}x&=\cos\theta\\\left(\frac{5}{4}x\right)^2&=\cos^2\theta\\\frac{25}{16}x^2&=\cos^2\theta
\end{aligned}
$$

Isolate the trigonometric term in the $y$ equation, then square.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y&=\frac{4}{3}\sin\theta\\\frac{y}{\frac{4}{3}}&=\sin\theta\\\left(\frac{y}{\frac{4}{3}}\right)^2&=\sin^2\theta\\\frac{9}{16}y^2&=\sin^2\theta
\end{aligned}
$$

Add the squared equations and use $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$:

$$
\frac{25}{16}x^2+\frac{9}{16}y^2=\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1.
$$

Thus the Cartesian equation is

$$
\frac{25}{16}x^2+\frac{9}{16}y^2=1.
$$

The full parameter interval traces the entire ellipse.

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179718/curve-85e07c94540df01bb38ccb0d.png)

Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C 6 y\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=2 y - 4$ between $(14,9)$ and $(8,6)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $6\le t\le 9$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle 2 t - 4,t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 2,1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(2)^2+1}=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=6 t=6 t\end{aligned}
$$
Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 y\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{6}^{9}\left(6 t\right)\left(\sqrt{5}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{6}^{9}6 \sqrt{5} t\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use the power rule and subtract the endpoint values:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 y\,\mathrm{d}s&=\left[3 \sqrt{5} t^{2}\right]_{6}^{9} \\ &=\left(243 \sqrt{5}\right)-\left(108 \sqrt{5}\right) \\ &=135 \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C 3 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=e^{\frac{y}{2}}$ between $(\sqrt{2},\ln{\left(2 \right)})$ and $(\sqrt{3},\ln{\left(3 \right)})$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $\ln{\left(2 \right)}\le t\le \ln{\left(3 \right)}$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle e^{\frac{t}{2}},t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle \frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2},1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2}\right)^2+1}=\frac{\sqrt{e^{t} + 4}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=3 \left(e^{\frac{t}{2}}\right)^{6} e^{- 2 t}=3 e^{t}\end{aligned}
$$
Here $(e^{t/2})^6e^{-4t/2}=e^{(6-4)t/2}=e^{2t/2}$ by the exponent laws.

Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 3 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}^{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}\left(3 e^{t}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{e^{t} + 4}}{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}^{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}\frac{3 \sqrt{e^{t} + 4} e^{t}}{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=e^{t} + 4$, so $\mathrm{d}u=e^{t}\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $6$ and $7$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 3 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{6}^{7}\frac{3 \sqrt{u}}{2}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[u^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{6}^{7} \\ &=\left(7 \sqrt{7}\right)-\left(6 \sqrt{6}\right) \\ &=- 6 \sqrt{6} + 7 \sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the line integral

where $C$ is the section of the curve $y^2=6x$ between $(\frac{20}{3},2 \sqrt{10})$ and $(\frac{8}{3},4)$.

First solve the curve equation for $x$: $y^2=6x$, so $x=\frac{y^{2}}{6}$.

Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $4\le t\le 2 \sqrt{10}$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle \frac{t^{2}}{6},t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle \frac{t}{3},1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{t}{3}\right)^2+1}=\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\end{aligned}

Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\frac{6 \left(\frac{t^{2}}{6}\right)}{t}=t\end{aligned}

Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6 x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{4}^{2 \sqrt{10}}\left(t\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{4}^{2 \sqrt{10}}\frac{t \sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6 x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{25}^{49}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{6}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right]_{25}^{49} \\ &=\left(\frac{343}{9}\right)-\left(\frac{125}{9}\right) \\ &=\frac{218}{9}\end{aligned}

\int_C 6 x y\,\mathrm{d}s

where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\sqrt{y}$ between $(2,4)$ and $(1,1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $1\le t\le 4$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle \sqrt{t},t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{t}},1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{t}}\right)^2+1}=\frac{\sqrt{4 t + 1}}{2 \sqrt{t}}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=6 \left(\sqrt{t}\right) t=6 t^{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$
Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 x y\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{1}^{4}\left(6 t^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{4 t + 1}}{2 \sqrt{t}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{4}3 t \sqrt{4 t + 1}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=4 t + 1$, so $\mathrm{d}u=4\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $5$ and $17$.
Also $t=(u-1)/4$, so the transformed integrand has two powers of $u$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 x y\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{5}^{17}\sqrt{u} \left(\frac{3 u}{16} - \frac{3}{16}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[\frac{3 u^{\frac{5}{2}}}{40} - \frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{8}\right]_{5}^{17} \\ &=\left(\frac{391 \sqrt{17}}{20}\right)-\left(\frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{4}\right) \\ &=- \frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{4} + \frac{391 \sqrt{17}}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C \frac{6}{- x + y}\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=2 y - 5$ between $(3,4)$ and $(-1,2)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $2\le t\le 4$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle 2 t - 5,t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 2,1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(2)^2+1}=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\frac{6}{- \left(2 t - 5\right) + t}=- \frac{6}{t - 5}\end{aligned}
$$
Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6}{- x + y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{2}^{4}\left(- \frac{6}{t - 5}\right)\left(\sqrt{5}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{2}^{4}- \frac{6 \sqrt{5}}{t - 5}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=5 - t$, so $\mathrm{d}u=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $3$ and $1$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6}{- x + y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{3}^{1}- \frac{6 \sqrt{5}}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[- 6 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(u \right)}\right]_{3}^{1} \\ &=\left(0\right)-\left(- 6 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(3 \right)}\right) \\ &=6 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(3 \right)}\end{aligned}
$$
Both logarithm arguments are positive. The identity $\ln A-\ln B=\ln(A/B)$ combines the endpoint logarithms.

Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 y^{3} e^{- x}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{1}^{2 \sqrt{6}}\left(6 t^{2}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}{t}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{2 \sqrt{6}}6 t \sqrt{t^{2} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186152190/50fcc4b4b6c933e5b9f0823e-prompt.png)

The solid arc belongs to the ellipse

$$
x=4\cos\theta,\qquad y=3\sin\theta.
$$

Find the **closed interval** of $\theta$ that traces exactly the solid arc once. Use endpoints between $0$ and $2\pi$, including both endpoints of the arc.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The ellipse has center $(0,0)$, horizontal radius $4$ and vertical radius $3$. The standard parametrization travels counterclockwise from the rightmost point. Substituting the cardinal parameter values gives

$$
\begin{array}{c|c}\theta &(x,y)\\\hline 0 & (4,0) \\ \frac{\pi}{2} & (0,3) \\ \pi & (-4,0) \\ \frac{3\pi}{2} & (0,-3) \\ 2\pi & (4,0)\end{array}
$$

The **solid arc** is the upper part relative to the center. It starts at $(4,0)$ when $\theta=0$ and ends at $(-4,0)$ when $\theta=\pi$. The counterclockwise traversal between these endpoints follows exactly the solid part, including both endpoints.

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186152190/50fcc4b4b6c933e5b9f0823e-solution.png)

Here $\theta$ is the angle on the scaled unit circle $((x-h)/a,(y-k)/b)$; it is generally different from the geometric angle on the ellipse. The required restricted parametrization is

$$
x=4\cos\theta,\qquad y=3\sin\theta,\qquad \theta \in [0,\pi].
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the line integral

$$
\int_C x - 4 y\,\mathrm{d}s=\sqrt{2}\int_{1}^{4}\boxed{}\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

where $C$ is the segment of the line $\frac{x}{3}=1 - \frac{y}{3}$ traversed between the points $(2,1)$ and $(-1,4)$. Which of the following is the missing expression under the integral on the right?

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve can be expressed in the form $x=x(y),$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{3}=1 - \frac{y}{3}\,\Longrightarrow\,x=3 - y
$$

Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=3 - t.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=\langle 3 - t,\,t\rangle,\quad 1\le t\le 4
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 4$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}j \\ &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 - t)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)j \\ &=(-1)i+j \\ \|r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{(-1)^2+1^2} \\ &=\sqrt{1+1} \\ &=\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=x - 4 y,$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=1\left(3 - t\right)-4t \\ &=3 - 5 t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C x - 4 y\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{1}^{4}f(r(t))\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{4}(3 - 5 t)\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\sqrt{2}\int_{1}^{4}(3 - 5 t)\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the line integral

$$
\int_C x^{2} y\,\mathrm{d}s=\sqrt{2}\int_{1}^{5}\boxed{}\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

where $C$ is the segment of the line $x=3 - y$ traversed between the points $(2,1)$ and $(-2,5)$. Which of the following is the missing expression under the integral on the right?

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=3 - t.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=\langle 3 - t,\,t\rangle,\quad 1\le t\le 5
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 5$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}j \\ &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 - t)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)j \\ &=(-1)i+j \\ \|r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{(-1)^2+1^2} \\ &=\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x^{2} y,$ then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=1\left(3 - t\right)^{2}t^{1} \\ &=t \left(3 - t\right)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C x^{2} y\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{1}^{5}f(r(t))\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{5}(t \left(3 - t\right)^{2})\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\sqrt{2}\int_{1}^{5}t \left(3 - t\right)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the line integral

$$
\int_C 16 x^{2} y^{3}\,\mathrm{d}s=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\int_{1}^{8}\boxed{}\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

where $C$ is the segment of the line $2x=y$ from $(\frac{1}{2},1)$ to $(4,8)$. Which is the missing expression under the integral on the right?

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Solve for $x$ and set $y=t$:

$$
x=\frac{y}{2},\qquad \mathbf r(t)=\left\langle \frac{t}{2},t\right\rangle,\qquad 1\le t\le 8.
$$

The bounds are the endpoint $y$-coordinates. Differentiate and take the speed:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left\langle \frac{1}{2},1\right\rangle, \\ \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute both coordinates into the scalar density:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=16\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)^2t^{3}, \\ &=4 t^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

The speed is already outside the integral, so the missing expression is $4 t^{5}$. The complete setup is

$$
\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\int_{1}^{8}\left(4 t^{5}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Solve the curve relation for $x$:

$$
x=2 - 2 \left(y + 1\right)^{3}.
$$

Set $y=t$ to cover the whole arc with one parametrization:

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle 2 - 2 \left(t + 1\right)^{3},t\right\rangle,\qquad -3\le t\le 0.
$$

Use the endpoint $y$-coordinates for the parameter bounds. Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left\langle - 6 \left(t + 1\right)^{2},1\right\rangle, \\ \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{1+\left(- 6 \left(t + 1\right)^{2}\right)^2}=\sqrt{36 \left(t + 1\right)^{4} + 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute both coordinates into the density:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=3\left(2 - 2 \left(t + 1\right)^{3}\right)t, \\ &=3 t \left(2 - 2 \left(t + 1\right)^{3}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Assemble the scalar arc-length integral, without evaluating:

$$
\int_C 3 x y\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{-3}^{0}f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Substituting the two factors gives

$$
\int_{-3}^{0}\left(3 t \left(2 - 2 \left(t + 1\right)^{3}\right) \sqrt{36 \left(t + 1\right)^{4} + 1}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

question.:question/problem:

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\int_C 3 y^{2} e^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}s$

where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\ln{\left(y \right)}$ traversed between the points $(0,1)$ and $(2,e^{2})$.

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=\ln{\left(t \right)}.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=\langle \ln{\left(t \right)},\,t\rangle,\quad 1\le t\le e^{2}
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le e^{2}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}j \\ &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\ln{\left(t \right)})i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)j \\ &=\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)i+j \\ \|r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)^2+1^2} \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{1}{t^2}+1} \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{t^{2} + 1}{t^2}} \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}{|t|} \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=3 y^{2} e^{2 x},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=3\left(e^{2\ln t}\right)t^{2} \\ &=3\left(t^{2}\right)t^{2} \\ &=3 t^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 3 y^{2} e^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{1}^{e^{2}}f(r(t))\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{e^{2}}(3 t^{4})\cdot \sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{e^{2}}3 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{2} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider $\mathbf F(x,y)=\bigl(- 6 x\bigr)\mathbf i+\bigl(4 y\bigr)\mathbf j$ and the circle $C$ given by $x^2+y^2=4.$ The outward flux is written as

$$
\oint_C\boxed{\phantom{x^2y}}\,\mathrm{d}s.
$$

What is the missing expression? Do not evaluate the integral.

*Hint: The outward unit normal is $\mathbf n=\frac{x}{2}\mathbf i+\frac{y}{2}\mathbf j.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
The integrand is the dot product with the outward **unit** normal. Multiply corresponding components and add.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n&=\bigl(- 6 x\bigr)\frac{x}{2}+\bigl(4 y\bigr)\frac{y}{2}\\
&=\bigl(- 3 x^{2}\bigr)+\bigl(2 y^{2}\bigr)\\
&=- 3 x^{2} + 2 y^{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The missing expression is $- 3 x^{2} + 2 y^{2}.$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

Consider $\mathbf F(x,y)=\bigl(- 2 y^{2}\bigr)\mathbf i+\bigl(2 x^{2} y + 2 x\bigr)\mathbf j.$ The rectangle $C$ has right, top, left, and bottom sides $C_1,C_2,C_3,C_4,$ respectively. Write its outward flux in the following order.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{C_3}g_1\,\mathrm{d}s+\int_{C_4}g_2\,\mathrm{d}s\\
&\quad+\int_{C_2}g_3\,\mathrm{d}s+\int_{C_1}g_4\,\mathrm{d}s.
\end{aligned}
$$

Which ordered quadruple $(g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4)$ gives the four dot products? Leave expressions in terms of $x$ and $y,$ before substituting side equations. Do not evaluate any integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The outward normals on the right, top, left, and bottom sides are $\mathbf i,\mathbf j,-\mathbf i,-\mathbf j,$ respectively. Use the order in the supplied decomposition.

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_1&=\mathbf F\cdot(-\mathbf i)=2 y^{2}\qquad\text{(left side)},\\
g_2&=\mathbf F\cdot(-\mathbf j)=- 2 x^{2} y - 2 x\qquad\text{(bottom side)},\\
g_3&=\mathbf F\cdot(\mathbf j)=2 x^{2} y + 2 x\qquad\text{(top side)},\\
g_4&=\mathbf F\cdot(\mathbf i)=- 2 y^{2}\qquad\text{(right side)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the ordered quadruple is

$$
\begin{aligned}&\bigl(2 y^{2},\ - 2 x^{2} y - 2 x,\\&\quad 2 x^{2} y + 2 x,\ - 2 y^{2}\bigr)\end{aligned}.
$$

These are integrands on different sides; opposite signs alone do not cancel their integrals.

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: \begin{aligned}&\bigl(- 2 y^{2},\ - 2 x^{2} y - 2 x,\\&\quad 2 x^{2} y + 2 x,\ 2 y^{2}\bigr)\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}&\bigl(2 x^{2} y + 2 x,\ 2 y^{2},\\&\quad - 2 y^{2},\ - 2 x^{2} y - 2 x\bigr)\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}&\bigl(- 2 x^{2} y - 2 x,\ - 2 y^{2},\\&\quad 2 y^{2},\ 2 x^{2} y + 2 x\bigr)\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}&\bigl(2 y^{2},\ 2 x^{2} y + 2 x,\\&\quad - 2 x^{2} y - 2 x,\ - 2 y^{2}\bigr)\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}&\bigl(2 y^{2},\ - 2 x^{2} y - 2 x,\\&\quad 2 x^{2} y + 2 x,\ - 2 y^{2}\bigr)\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the cosine of the included angle to find the signed scalar projection.

We project $\mathbf{v}$, so we use $|\mathbf{v}|=9 \sqrt{3}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{comp}_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{v} &=|\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta \\
&=9 \sqrt{3}\cos\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right) \\
&=9 \sqrt{3}\cdot\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right) \\
&=- \frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{2}.

$$

The scalar projection is negative because the included angle is obtuse.

question.:question/problem:
The nonzero vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ start at $O$, with $|\mathbf{u}|=7 \sqrt{2}$ and $|\mathbf{v}|=11 \sqrt{2}$. The diagram shows their counterclockwise inclinations from the same reference ray $r$. The diagram is not to scale.

![Vectors u and v at inclinations 165 degrees and 45 degrees from r, respectively.](assets/projection-4b626c400ba74efa7fba.png)

Find the scalar projection of $\mathbf{v}$ onto $\mathbf{u}$. Give an exact answer.

$\operatorname{comp}_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{v}=$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Both inclinations are measured counterclockwise from the same ray. Subtract the smaller inclination from the larger to find the included angle.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\theta &=165^\circ-45^\circ=120^\circ.
\end{aligned}
$$

We project $\mathbf{v}$, so we use $|\mathbf{v}|=11 \sqrt{2}$. The magnitude of $\mathbf{u}$ does not enter the formula.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{comp}_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{v} &=|\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta \\
&=11 \sqrt{2}\cos\left(120^\circ\right) \\
&=11 \sqrt{2}\cdot\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right) \\
&=- \frac{11 \sqrt{2}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The scalar projection is negative because the included angle is obtuse.

question.:question/problem:
The nonzero vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ start at $O$, with $|\mathbf{u}|=7 \sqrt{2}$ and $|\mathbf{v}|=11 \sqrt{2}$. The dashed ray points in the direction opposite to $\mathbf{v}$; the marked $60^\circ$ angle is between that ray and $\mathbf{u}$. The diagram is not to scale.

![Vectors u and v; angle 60 degrees between u and the ray opposite v.](assets/projection-e0d959e7d06583739b5c.png)

Find the scalar projection of $\mathbf{v}$ onto $\mathbf{u}$. Give an exact answer.

$\operatorname{comp}_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{v}=$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The dashed ray points opposite to $\mathbf{v}$, so the included angle is supplementary to the marked angle.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\theta &=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ.
\end{aligned}
$$

We project $\mathbf{v}$, so we use $|\mathbf{v}|=11 \sqrt{2}$. The magnitude of $\mathbf{u}$ does not enter the formula.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{comp}_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{v} &=|\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta \\
&=11 \sqrt{2}\cos\left(120^\circ\right) \\
&=11 \sqrt{2}\cdot\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right) \\
&=- \frac{11 \sqrt{2}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The scalar projection is negative because the included angle is obtuse.

question.:question/problem:
![Vector fields and the directed boundary](flux-074b7ecff299cc0383ef72e5.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and boundary $S$ shown above. The blue boundary and gray reference curves are concentric similar ellipses. Boundary crossing directions and tangencies shown by the arrows hold between the sampled points as well.

Let $C$ traverse $S$ once clockwise, and let $-C$ be the reversed traversal. In both cases use the **outward-pointing normal**.

Which statements are true? Select all that apply. Here *nonzero* means positive or negative; *not positive* includes zero, and *not negative* includes zero.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Flux measures net outward flow:

$$
\Phi_C=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds.
$$

Outward normal components contribute positively; inward ones contribute negatively; tangential ones contribute zero.

The field points into the boundary everywhere. Its outward normal component is negative, giving net inflow.

![Field vectors and outward normals](flux-15b47ada5da79a241e0a99e5.png)

Reversing traversal changes neither the outward normal nor arc length. Therefore

$$
\Phi_{-C}=\Phi_C<0.
$$

Evaluate each statement:

- The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is positive. **false**.
- The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is zero. **false**.
- The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is negative. **true**.

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is positive.
The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is zero.
The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is negative.

question.:question/problem:
![Vector fields and the directed boundary](flux-1d254c2d6e221e63cd6ad4b6.png)

The vector field is $\mathbf F=\mathbf U+\mathbf V$. The panels show the two components separately at the same arrow scale, on the same boundary $S$. The field $\mathbf U$ is uniform throughout the plane. The blue boundary and gray reference curves are concentric circles. Boundary crossing directions and tangencies shown by the arrows hold between the sampled points as well.

Let $C$ traverse $S$ once counterclockwise, and let $-C$ be the reversed traversal. In both cases use the **outward-pointing normal**.

Which statements are true? Select all that apply. Here *nonzero* means positive or negative; *not positive* includes zero, and *not negative* includes zero.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Flux measures net outward flow:

$$
\Phi_C=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds.
$$

Outward normal components contribute positively; inward ones contribute negatively; tangential ones contribute zero.

For the uniform field $\mathbf U$, opposite small boundary arcs have equal lengths and opposite outward normals. The same field vector meets both arcs, so their normal contributions cancel in pairs. Thus $\Phi_C(\mathbf U)=0$.

Every boundary vector of $\mathbf V$ is tangent to the boundary, hence perpendicular to the outward normal. Thus $\mathbf V\cdot\mathbf n=0$ at every point, and its flux is zero.

The normal component of a sum is the sum of its normal components. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_C(\mathbf F)&=\Phi_C(\mathbf U)+\Phi_C(\mathbf V)\\
&=0+\Phi_C(\mathbf V).
\end{aligned}
$$

![Field vectors and outward normals](flux-a7bb45526ffb643a645aada9.png)

Reversing traversal changes neither the outward normal nor arc length. Therefore

$$
\Phi_{-C}=\Phi_C=0.
$$

Evaluate each statement:

- The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is zero. **true**.
- The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is not positive. **true**.
- The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is positive. **false**.

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is zero.
The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is not positive.
The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is positive.

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179742/d8544577858d06746ca1-prompt.png)

The gray arrows show the non-constant field $\mathbf F(x,y)=\left(4 y,- 9 x\right)$. The blue path lies on $\frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}=1$. Let $C$ be three-quarters of this ellipse, traversed counterclockwise from $A=(0,-3)$ to $B=(-2,0)$. Let $-C$ denote the same path with the orientation reversed.

Which statements are true? **Select all that apply.**
question.:question/worked-solution:
The line integral measures signed work: assistance contributes positive work, opposition negative work, and perpendicular force zero work.

The field is tangent to the ellipse. Along the indicated orientation, the field points against the motion at every point. Every contribution is therefore negative.

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179742/d8544577858d06746ca1-forward.png)

Thus $\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r<0$. Reversing the path reverses every displacement while keeping the field fixed:

$$
\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=-\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
$$

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179742/d8544577858d06746ca1-reverse.png)

Therefore $\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r>0$.

Statement 1, $\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r<0$, is **false**.

Statement 2, $\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=0$, is **false**.

Statement 3, $\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r<0$, is **true**.

knowledge_point.title: Interpreting the Sign of a Line Integral Over a Non-Constant Vector Field

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179742/c77b9985c70f9254a356-prompt.png)

The gray arrows show the non-constant field $\mathbf F(x,y)=\left(x - y + 3,0\right)$. The blue path lies on $\frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1$. Let $C$ be the half of this ellipse in $x>0$ from $A=(0,-2)$ to $B=(0,2)$. Let $-C$ denote the same path with the orientation reversed.

Which statements are true? **Select all that apply.**
question.:question/worked-solution:
The line integral measures signed work: assistance contributes positive work, opposition negative work, and perpendicular force zero work.

The field points rightward everywhere on this arc. On the first half it does positive work; on the second half it does negative work. The work parallel to the other coordinate axis is zero.

Pair the point on the first half with its reflection on the second half at the same $x=v$, where $v>0$. Their $y$ coordinates are $- u$ and $u$, where $u>0$. Their small $x$ displacements have equal magnitudes and opposite signs. The signed field components at the paired points differ by

$$
\begin{aligned}F_{x,1}-F_{x,2}&=\left(u + v + 3\right)-\left(- u + v + 3\right) \\ &=2 u\end{aligned}
$$

The first displacement in $x$ is positive. Multiplying it by the displayed force difference gives positive work for every pair. The positive contribution dominates, so the total work has that sign. Equal endpoint coordinates alone would not establish cancellation.

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179742/c77b9985c70f9254a356-forward.png)

Thus $\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r>0$. Reversing the path reverses every displacement while keeping the field fixed:

$$
\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=-\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
$$

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179742/c77b9985c70f9254a356-reverse.png)

Therefore $\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r<0$.

Statement 1, $\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=0$, is **false**.

Statement 2, $\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r<0$, is **false**.

Statement 3, $\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r<0$, is **true**.

question.:question/worked-solution:
The line integral measures signed work: assistance contributes positive work, opposition negative work, and perpendicular force zero work.

Separate the field into its normal and tangent components:

$$
\mathbf F=\left(9 x,4 y\right)+\left(- 4 y,9 x\right)
$$

The first component is proportional to the gradient of the displayed ellipse equation. It is perpendicular to the curve and contributes *zero work*. The second component is tangent and points with the indicated motion throughout the arc. Thus the total work is positive.

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179742/0ac127bb1b620f839501-forward.png)

Thus $\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r>0$. Reversing the path reverses every displacement while keeping the field fixed:

$$
\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=-\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
$$

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179742/0ac127bb1b620f839501-reverse.png)

Therefore $\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r<0$.

Statement 1, $\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=0$, is **false**.

Statement 2, $\int_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r<0$, is **false**.

Statement 3, $\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r<0$, is **true**.

question.:question/problem:
Let $f(x,y)=x^{3} y$. Let $C$ follow the curve $y=\ln{\left(x \right)} + 1$ as $x$ goes from $e^{2}$ to $e$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r.
$$

*Hint: Use $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t,\ln{\left(t \right)} + 1\right\rangle$, with $t$ going from $e^{2}$ to $e$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $x=t$ and use the Cartesian equation to obtain the other coordinate. A parametrization in the stated direction is $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t,\ln{\left(t \right)} + 1\right\rangle$, with $t$ going from $e^{2}$ to $e$. The initial point is $A=\left(e^{2},3\right)$ and the terminal point is $B=\left(e,2\right)$. The gradient is continuous on this arc, so the fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(B)&=\left(e\right)^{3} \left(2\right)\\
&=2 e^{3}\\
f(A)&=\left(e^{2}\right)^{3} \left(3\right)\\
&=3 e^{6}
\end{aligned}
$$

Writing $I=\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=f(B)-f(A)\\
&=\left(2 e^{3}\right)\\
&\quad -\left(3 e^{6}\right)\\
&=- 3 e^{6} + 2 e^{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

conversions: evaluate supplied potential at directed endpoints
generation.domain: real; x>0 on logarithmic curves; y>0 on radical curves

question.:question/problem:
Let $f(x,y)=2 x y + 2 y^{2}$. Let $C$ be the part of the curve $y^2=x+1$ lying above the $x$-axis, traversed from its intersection with $x=0$ to its intersection with $x=8$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The specified half-plane selects the positive values of $y$. Solving the curve equation at the two boundary lines gives the directed endpoints below. A parametrization in the stated direction is $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t^{2} - 1,t\right\rangle$, with $t$ going from $1$ to $3$. The initial point is $A=\left(0,1\right)$ and the terminal point is $B=\left(8,3\right)$. The gradient is continuous on this arc, so the fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(B)&=2 \left(8\right) \left(3\right) + 2 \left(3\right)^{2}\\
&=66\\
f(A)&=2 \left(0\right) \left(1\right) + 2 \left(1\right)^{2}\\
&=2
\end{aligned}
$$

Writing $I=\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=f(B)-f(A)\\
&=\left(66\right)\\
&\quad -\left(2\right)\\
&=64.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $f(x,y)=- x + y^{2} + y$. Let $C$ follow the curve $x=\cos{\left(y \right)}$ as $y$ goes from $\frac{\pi}{2}$ to $\pi$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$ and use the Cartesian equation to obtain the other coordinate. A parametrization in the stated direction is $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle \cos{\left(t \right)},t\right\rangle$, with $t$ going from $\frac{\pi}{2}$ to $\pi$. The initial point is $A=\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and the terminal point is $B=\left(-1,\pi\right)$. The gradient is continuous on this arc, so the fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(B)&=- \left(-1\right) + \left(\pi\right)^{2} + \left(\pi\right)\\
&=1 + \pi + \pi^{2}\\
f(A)&=- \left(0\right) + \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\\
&=\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi^{2}}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

Writing $I=\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=f(B)-f(A)\\
&=\left(1 + \pi + \pi^{2}\right)\\
&\quad -\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi^{2}}{4}\right)\\
&=1 + \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{3 \pi^{2}}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the curve $C$, traversed in the direction of increasing $t$, where

$$
r(t)=\langle t + 1,t + 2\rangle,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Evaluate $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ for $F(x,y)=\left(- 2 y\right)\,i+\left(- 2 x\right)\,j.$

*Hint: The field is conservative. Find a potential function, then subtract its value at the starting point from its value at the ending point.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $P=- 2 y$ and $Q=- 2 x.$ A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$
f(x,y)=- 2 x y+g(y)
$$

Match its $y$ derivative to the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}- 2 x+g'(y)&=- 2 x \\ g'(y)&=0 \\ g(y)&=0+K\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=- 2 x y
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(1,2) \\ B&=(2,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the potential at each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=- 2 \left(2\right) \left(3\right) \\ &=-12 \\ f(A)&=- 2 \left(1\right) \left(2\right) \\ &=-4\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(-12\right)-\left(-4\right) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: Field smooth on R^2; path continuous on its given real interval.

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=\left(2 x e^{- y}\right)\,i+\left(- x^{2} e^{- y} + 6 y\right)\,j.
$$

Evaluate $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$, where $C$ is the curve $y=\ln{\left(x - 3 \right)}$ for $x\in [4,5]$, traversed in the direction of decreasing $x$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $P=2 x e^{- y}$ and $Q=- x^{2} e^{- y} + 6 y.$ Both components have continuous partial derivatives on $\mathbb R^2$, and

$$
P_y=Q_x=- 2 x e^{- y}
$$

Since $\mathbb R^2$ is simply connected, the field is conservative. A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$
f(x,y)=x^{2} e^{- y}+g(y)
$$

Match its $y$ derivative to the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}- x^{2} e^{- y}+g'(y)&=- x^{2} e^{- y} + 6 y \\ g'(y)&=6 y \\ g(y)&=3 y^{2}+K\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=x^{2} e^{- y} + 3 y^{2}
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. A parametrization is

$$
r(t)=\langle t,\ln{\left(t - 3 \right)}\rangle,\,t\in [4,5].
$$

For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(5,\ln{\left(2 \right)}) \\ B&=(4,0)\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the potential at each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=\left(4\right)^{2} e^{- \left(0\right)}+3 \left(0\right)^{2} \\ &=16 \\ f(A)&=\left(5\right)^{2} e^{- \left(\ln{\left(2 \right)}\right)}+3 \left(\ln{\left(2 \right)}\right)^{2} \\ &=3 \ln{\left(2 \right)}^{2} + \frac{25}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(16\right)-\left(3 \ln{\left(2 \right)}^{2} + \frac{25}{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{7}{2} - 3 \ln{\left(2 \right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here $e^{-\ln(1)}=1$ and $e^{-\ln(2)}=\frac{1}{2}$.

generation.domain: Field smooth on R^2; path continuous on its given real interval.

question.:question/problem:
Consider the curve $C$, traversed in the direction of decreasing $t$, where

$$
r(t)=\langle \ln{\left(t \right)},t^{2}\rangle,\,t\in [1,3].
$$

Evaluate $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ for $F(x,y)=\left(- x^{2} - 3 y\right)\,i+\left(- 3 x + y^{2}\right)\,j.$

*Hint: You may wish to use the fact that $F$ is conservative.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $P=- x^{2} - 3 y$ and $Q=- 3 x + y^{2}.$ A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$
f(x,y)=- \frac{x^{3}}{3} - 3 x y+g(y)
$$

Match its $y$ derivative to the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}- 3 x+g'(y)&=- 3 x + y^{2} \\ g'(y)&=y^{2} \\ g(y)&=\frac{y^{3}}{3}+K\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=- \frac{x^{3}}{3} - 3 x y + \frac{y^{3}}{3}
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(\ln{\left(3 \right)},9) \\ B&=(0,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the potential at each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=- \frac{\left(0\right)^{3}}{3}+\frac{\left(1\right)^{3}}{3}- 3 \left(0\right) \left(1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{3} \\ f(A)&=- \frac{\left(\ln{\left(3 \right)}\right)^{3}}{3}+\frac{\left(9\right)^{3}}{3}- 3 \left(\ln{\left(3 \right)}\right) \left(9\right) \\ &=- 27 \ln{\left(3 \right)} - \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}^{3}}{3} + 243\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)-\left(- 27 \ln{\left(3 \right)} - \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}^{3}}{3} + 243\right) \\  & =- \frac{728}{3} + \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}^{3}}{3} + 27 \ln{\left(3 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the length of the altitude $RH$ of $\triangle PQR$, where $P(-1,-2,2)$, $Q(-1,-2,4)$, $R(2,-1,1)$. Here $H$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $R$ to the line $PQ$.

The following values have been calculated from the vertices:

$$
PQ=2,\qquad \left|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times \overrightarrow{PR}\right|=2 \sqrt{10}.
$$

Use the area relationship

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle PQR}=\frac12\left|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times \overrightarrow{PR}\right|=\frac12 PQ\cdot RH
$$

to calculate the altitude.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The altitude $RH$ corresponds to the base $PQ$, so

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle PQR}=\frac12 PQ\cdot RH.
$$

The triangle has half the parallelogram area:

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle PQR}=\frac12\left(2 \sqrt{10}\right)=\sqrt{10}.
$$

Substitute the area and matching base, then solve for the altitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10}&=\frac12\left(2\right)RH,\\
2 \sqrt{10}&=\left(2\right)RH,\\
RH&=\frac{2 \sqrt{10}}{2}=\sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

The altitude is $\sqrt{10}$ units.

The altitude $RH$ corresponds to the base $PQ$, so

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle PQR}=\frac12 PQ\cdot RH.
$$

Form the required edge vectors from the vertices:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{PQ}&=\langle -1-(-1),-2-(-2),4-2\rangle,\\
&=\langle 0,0,2\rangle.\\
\overrightarrow{PR}&=\langle 2-(-1),-1-(-2),1-2\rangle,\\
&=\langle 3,1,-1\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the cross product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{PQ}\times \overrightarrow{PR}&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\0&0&2\\3&1&-1\end{vmatrix}\\
w_1&=0\cdot (-1)-2\cdot 1=-2,\\
w_2&=2\cdot 3-0\cdot (-1)=6,\\
w_3&=0\cdot 1-0\cdot 3=0,\\
\overrightarrow{PQ}\times \overrightarrow{PR}&=\langle -2,6,0\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

The magnitude of the cross product gives the parallelogram area:

$$
\left|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times \overrightarrow{PR}\right|=\sqrt{(-2)^2+6^2+0^2}=2 \sqrt{10}.
$$

The matching base length is

$$
PQ=\sqrt{0^2+0^2+2^2}=2.
$$

The triangle has half the parallelogram area:

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle PQR}=\frac12\left(2 \sqrt{10}\right)=\sqrt{10}.
$$

Substitute the area and matching base, then solve for the altitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10}&=\frac12\left(2\right)RH,\\
2 \sqrt{10}&=\left(2\right)RH,\\
RH&=\frac{2 \sqrt{10}}{2}=\sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

The altitude is $\sqrt{10}$ units.

question.:question/problem:

Use two sides starting at $N$:
$$
\mathbf{u}=L-N,\qquad \mathbf{v}=M-N,\qquad T=\frac12\lVert\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\rVert.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Form two sides with the same starting vertex:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{NL}&=\langle -1-(-3),-1-(-1),1-(-1)\rangle \\
&=\langle 2,0,2\rangle \\
\overrightarrow{NM}&=\langle -5-(-3),-3-(-1),-1-(-1)\rangle \\
&=\langle -2,-2,0\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

Compute the cross product:
$$
\overrightarrow{NL}\times \overrightarrow{NM}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\2 & 0 & 2\\-2 & -2 & 0\end{vmatrix}
$$
$$
\begin{aligned}
w_1&=0\cdot 0-2\cdot (-2)=4 \\

w_3&=2\cdot (-2)-0\cdot (-2)=-4 \\

\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
