knowledge_point.title: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following definite integrals is equivalent to

$$
\int_C\left(x^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(2 x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y
$$

where $C$ is the arc of the ellipse $4 x^{2} + 9 y^{2}=36$, traversed clockwise from $\left(0,-2\right)$ to $\left(-3,0\right)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the parametrization $x=3 \cos{\left(t \right)}$, $y=2 \sin{\left(t \right)}$. The endpoints and clockwise traversal give $t$ from $\frac{3 \pi}{2}$ to $\pi$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{d}x &=- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ \mathrm{d}y &=2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the coordinates and their signed differentials. Let $U$ be the contribution from the $\mathrm{d}x$ term and $V$ the contribution from the $\mathrm{d}y$ term:

$$
\begin{aligned}U(t) &=\left(9 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ V(t) &=\left(12 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
I=\int_{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}^{\pi}[U(t)+V(t)]\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

$$
I=\int_{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}^{\pi}\left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

This is the required equivalent definite integral.

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate

$$
\int_C\left(\frac{2 x}{y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}y
$$

where $C$ is the arc of the circle $x^{2} + y^{2}=1$, traversed clockwise from $\left(- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$ to $\left(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},- \frac{1}{2}\right)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the parametrization $x=\cos{\left(t \right)}$, $y=\sin{\left(t \right)}$. The endpoints and clockwise traversal give $t$ from $\frac{5 \pi}{4}$ to $\frac{7 \pi}{6}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{d}x &=- \sin{\left(t \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ \mathrm{d}y &=\cos{\left(t \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the coordinates and their signed differentials. Let $U$ be the contribution from the $\mathrm{d}x$ term and $V$ the contribution from the $\mathrm{d}y$ term:

$$
\begin{aligned}U(t) &=\left(\frac{2 \cos{\left(t \right)}}{\sin{\left(t \right)}}\right)\left(- \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ V(t) &=\left(\frac{\sin{\left(t \right)}}{\cos{\left(t \right)}}\right)\left(\cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
I=\int_{\frac{5 \pi}{4}}^{\frac{7 \pi}{6}}[U(t)+V(t)]\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

The arc stays inside one quadrant, so $x$ and $y$ are nonzero. Cancel the sine and cosine factors to obtain

$$
I=\int_{\frac{5 \pi}{4}}^{\frac{7 \pi}{6}}\left(\sin{\left(t \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

An antiderivative of the displayed integrand is $F(t)=- 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}I &= \left[- 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\right]_{\frac{5 \pi}{4}}^{\frac{7 \pi}{6}} \\ &= \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 1\right)-\left(\frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\ &= - \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 1\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
\int_C\left(x - 2 y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(2 x + 2 y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y
$$

where $C$ is the arc of the ellipse $4 x^{2} + 9 y^{2}=36$, traversed clockwise from $\left(0,-2\right)$ to $\left(-3,0\right)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the parametrization $x=3 \cos{\left(t \right)}$, $y=2 \sin{\left(t \right)}$. The endpoints and clockwise traversal give $t$ from $\frac{3 \pi}{2}$ to $\pi$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{d}x &=- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ \mathrm{d}y &=2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the coordinates and their signed differentials. Let $U$ be the contribution from the $\mathrm{d}x$ term and $V$ the contribution from the $\mathrm{d}y$ term:

$$
\begin{aligned}U(t) &=\left(- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ V(t) &=\left(4 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
I=\int_{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}^{\pi}[U(t)+V(t)]\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Using $\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$, combine the terms to obtain

$$
I=\int_{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}^{\pi}\left(- \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)} + 12\right)\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

An antiderivative of the displayed integrand is $F(t)=12 t - \frac{\sin^{2}{\left(t \right)}}{2}$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}I &= \left[12 t - \frac{\sin^{2}{\left(t \right)}}{2}\right]_{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}^{\pi} \\ &= \left(12 \pi\right)-\left(- \frac{1}{2} + 18 \pi\right) \\ &= \frac{1}{2} - 6 \pi\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ follows $y=x^{2}$ from $A(2,4)$ to $B(1,1)$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(- x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Choose a coordinate parameter that keeps the curve smooth.

$$
x(t)=t,\qquad y(t)=t^{2}.
$$

The stated endpoints give $t=2$ at $A$ and $t=1$ at $B$; retain that order in the integral. Differentiation gives

$$
x'(t)=1,\qquad y'(t)=2 t.
$$

Write the coefficients of $\mathrm{d}x$ and $\mathrm{d}y$ as $P$ and $Q$. Substitute both coordinates and multiply by the corresponding derivative. Denote the two contributions by $A(t)$ and $B(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(t)&=\left(- \left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(1\right) \\ &=- t
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
B(t)&=\left(\left(t^{2}\right)\right)\cdot \left(2 t\right) \\ &=2 t^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

The differential form uses the sum of these contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{2}^{1}\left(A(t)+B(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{2}^{1}\left(2 t^{3} - t\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\left[\frac{t^{4}}{2} - \frac{t^{2}}{2}\right]_{2}^{1} \\ &=\left(0\right)-\left(6\right) \\ &=-6
\end{aligned}
$$

Choose a coordinate parameter that keeps the curve smooth.

$$
x(t)=t,\qquad y(t)=2 \pi t^{2}.
$$

The stated endpoints give $t=1$ at $A$ and $t=2$ at $B$; retain that order in the integral. Differentiation gives

$$
x'(t)=1,\qquad y'(t)=4 \pi t.
$$

Write the coefficients of $\mathrm{d}x$ and $\mathrm{d}y$ as $P$ and $Q$. Substitute both coordinates and multiply by the corresponding derivative. Denote the two contributions by $A(t)$ and $B(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(t)&=\left(\cos{\left(\frac{\left(2 \pi t^{2}\right)}{\left(t\right)^{2}} \right)}\right)\cdot \left(1\right) \\ &=\cos\left(2 \pi\right)\cdot \left(1\right) \\ &=1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
B(t)&=\left(- 4 \left(t\right)^{2}\right)\cdot \left(4 \pi t\right) \\ &=- 16 \pi t^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

The differential form uses the sum of these contributions:

\end{aligned}
$$

Choose a coordinate parameter that keeps the curve smooth.

$$
x(t)=t^{3},\qquad y(t)=t.
$$

The stated endpoints give $t=0$ at $A$ and $t=1$ at $B$; retain that order in the integral. Differentiation gives

$$
x'(t)=3 t^{2},\qquad y'(t)=1.
$$

Write the coefficients of $\mathrm{d}x$ and $\mathrm{d}y$ as $P$ and $Q$. Substitute both coordinates and multiply by the corresponding derivative. Denote the two contributions by $A(t)$ and $B(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(t)&=\left(- 4 \left(t\right) e^{\left(t^{3}\right) \left(t\right)}\right)\cdot \left(3 t^{2}\right) \\ &=\left(- 4 t e^{t^{4}}\right)\cdot \left(3 t^{2}\right) \\ &=- 12 t^{3} e^{t^{4}}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
B(t)&=\left(-2\right)\cdot \left(1\right) \\ &=-2
\end{aligned}
$$

I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(A(t)+B(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\left(- 12 t^{3} e^{t^{4}} - 2\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\left[- 2 t - 3 e^{t^{4}}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=\left(- 3 e - 2\right)-\left(-3\right) \\ &=1 - 3 e
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Use the endpoint parametrization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(t)&=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\
&=\langle 1,-2\rangle+t\langle -1,2\rangle \\
&=\langle 1 - t,2 t - 2\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x(t)=1 - t$, $y(t)=2 t - 2$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -1,2\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=2\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=2 y$ and $Q(x,y)=x$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(2\right)\cdot \left(2 t - 2\right)\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=4 - 4 t, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(1 - t\right)\cdot \left(2\right) \\
&=2 - 2 t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(6 - 6 t\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- 3 t^{2} + 6 t\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=- 3 t^{2} + 6 t, \\
F(1)&=- 3 \left(1\right)^{2} + 6 \left(1\right) \\
&=3, \\
F(0)&=- 3 \left(0\right)^{2} + 6 \left(0\right) \\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\

\end{aligned}

Here $x(t)=- 2 t - 2$, $y(t)=2 t + 2$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -2,2\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-2\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=2\,\mathrm{d}t$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(- 2 t - 2\right)\cdot \left(2 t + 2\right)\cdot \left(-2\right) \\

Write $P(x,y)=x y$ and $Q(x,y)=x$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(2 - t\right)\cdot \left(- 2 t\right)\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=- 2 t^{2} + 4 t, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(2 - t\right)\cdot \left(-2\right) \\
&=2 t - 4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(- 2 t^{2} + 6 t - 4\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- \frac{2 t^{3}}{3} + 3 t^{2} - 4 t\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=- \frac{2 t^{3}}{3} + 3 t^{2} - 4 t, \\
F(1)&=- \frac{2 \left(1\right)^{3}}{3} + 3 \left(1\right)^{2} - 4 \left(1\right) \\
&=- \frac{5}{3}, \\
F(0)&=- \frac{2 \left(0\right)^{3}}{3} + 3 \left(0\right)^{2} - 4 \left(0\right) \\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\
&=\left(- \frac{5}{3}\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=- \frac{5}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(2,0)$ to $B(1,-2)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the endpoint parametrization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(t)&=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\
&=\langle 2,0\rangle+t\langle -1,-2\rangle \\
&=\langle 2 - t,- 2 t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x(t)=2 - t$, $y(t)=- 2 t$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -1,-2\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=-2\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=y$ and $Q(x,y)=x y$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(- 2 t\right)\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=2 t, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(2 - t\right)\cdot \left(- 2 t\right)\cdot \left(-2\right) \\
&=- 4 t^{2} + 8 t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(- 4 t^{2} + 10 t\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- \frac{4 t^{3}}{3} + 5 t^{2}\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=- \frac{4 t^{3}}{3} + 5 t^{2}, \\
F(1)&=- \frac{4 \left(1\right)^{3}}{3} + 5 \left(1\right)^{2} \\
&=\frac{11}{3}, \\
F(0)&=- \frac{4 \left(0\right)^{3}}{3} + 5 \left(0\right)^{2} \\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\
&=\left(\frac{11}{3}\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=\frac{11}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

Which definite integral is equivalent to

$$
\int_C\left(2 x - 2 y + 1\right)\,\mathrm{d}y
$$

where $C$ is three quarters of the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{1}=1$, directed counterclockwise from $A=(0,-1)$ to $B=(-3,0)$, as shown above? Do not evaluate the integral.

*Hint: Use the parametrization $\mathbf r(t)=\langle 3 \cos{t},\,\sin{t}\rangle$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a parametrization following the directed path,

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y=\int_a^b f(x(t),y(t))\,y\prime(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Choose

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 3 \cos{t},\,\sin{t}\rangle,\qquad \frac{3 \pi}{2}\le t\le 3 \pi.
$$

The squared coordinate ratios sum to $\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1$, so this parametrization lies on the curve. It travels counterclockwise. The endpoints occur at $t=\frac{3 \pi}{2}$ and $t=3 \pi$; the interval covers the specified portion once.

The signed differential factor is

$$
y\prime(t)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\sin{t}\right)=\cos{t}.
$$

Substituting both coordinates into the given function gives

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x(t),y(t))&=\left.\left(2 x - 2 y + 1\right)\right|_{x=3 \cos{t},\,y=\sin{t}}\\&=- 2 \sin{t} + 6 \cos{t} + 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, retaining the signed derivative,

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y\\&\quad=\int_{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}^{3 \pi}\left(- 2 \sin{t} + 6 \cos{t} + 1\right)\left(\cos{t}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![Oriented path](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186133891/path-6732a9233b2a88097084e1af.png)

Which definite integral is equivalent to

$$
\int_C x y^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

where $C$ is the line segment traversed from $(1,3)$ to $(-3,5)$, as shown? Do not evaluate the integral.

*Hint: Use $\mathbf r(t)=\langle 1 - 4 t,2 t + 3\rangle$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Interpolate from the initial point to the terminal point. The parameter starts at $0$ and ends at $1$, giving the required endpoints.

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 1 - 4 t,2 t + 3\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le 1
$$

Substitute both coordinates, then differentiate the first coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned} f(\mathbf r(t))&=(1 - 4 t)(2 t + 3)^{2}\\&=- 16 t^{3} - 44 t^{2} - 24 t + 9,\\ x\prime(t)&=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply the two factors, keeping the signed derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))x\prime(t)&=(- 16 t^{3} - 44 t^{2} - 24 t + 9)(-4)\\&=64 t^{3} + 176 t^{2} + 96 t - 36.\end{aligned}
$$

Use this density with the oriented parameter limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C x y^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x&=\int_{0}^{1} f(\mathbf r(t))x\prime(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\&=\int_{0}^{1} 64 t^{3} + 176 t^{2} + 96 t - 36\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The coordinate scales follow from $\frac{x^2}{1}+\frac{y^2}{16}=1$. Choose the parametrization below. Increasing the parameter follows the stated counterclockwise direction. At the initial endpoint, $\cos t=\frac{x}{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\sin t=\frac{y}{4}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Thus the initial parameter in $[0,2\pi)$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. Continue the parameter through $\frac{3 \pi}{2}$ to follow the stated arc. The parameter starts at $\frac{\pi}{3}$ and ends at $\frac{11 \pi}{6}$, giving the required endpoints.

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle \cos{\left(t \right)},4 \sin{\left(t \right)}\rangle,\qquad \frac{\pi}{3}\le t\le \frac{11 \pi}{6}
$$

Substitute both coordinates, then differentiate the first coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned} f(\mathbf r(t))&=(\cos{\left(t \right)})(4 \sin{\left(t \right)})^{2}\\&=16 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)},\\ x\prime(t)&=- \sin{\left(t \right)}.\end{aligned}

Multiply the two factors, keeping the signed derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))x\prime(t)&=(16 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)})(- \sin{\left(t \right)})\\&=- 16 \sin^{3}{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Use this density with the oriented parameter limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C x y^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x&=\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{11 \pi}{6}} f(\mathbf r(t))x\prime(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\&=\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{11 \pi}{6}} - 16 \sin^{3}{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=x^{2} y + 2 x y^{2} + 3 x y$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through $P=(2,1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold the other coordinate constant when taking each partial derivative. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=2 x y + 2 y^{2} + 3 y \\ f_y(x,y)&=x^{2} + 4 x y + 3 x \\ \nabla f(2,1)&=\langle 9,18\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero, so it is **normal** to the tangent line. Its dot product with the displacement along the line is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(2,1)\cdot\langle x - 2,y - 1\rangle&=0 \\ 9 x + 18 y - 36&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying or dividing the whole equation by a nonzero constant preserves the line. Thus the tangent equation is

$$
\langle 1,2\rangle\cdot\langle x - 2,y - 1\rangle=0
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent line at $P=(1,0)$ to the curve $2 x e^{x y} - 2 y^{2}=- x^{2} - 3 y + 3$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Move all terms to the left to define a level function:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y)&=x^{2} + 2 x e^{x y} - 2 y^{2} + 3 y - 3 \\ F(1,0)&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Apply the chain rule to the exponential and the product rule to its coordinate multiplier. 

$$
\begin{aligned}F_x(x,y)&=2 x + \left(2 x y + 2\right) e^{x y} \\ F_y(x,y)&=2 x^{2} e^{x y} - 4 y + 3 \\ \nabla F(1,0)&=\langle 4,5\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero, so it is **normal** to the tangent line. Its dot product with the displacement along the line is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla F(1,0)\cdot\langle x - 1,y\rangle&=0 \\ 4 x + 5 y - 4&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying or dividing the whole equation by a nonzero constant preserves the line. Thus the tangent equation is

$$
4 x + 5 y - 4=0

question.:question/problem:
At which point on the curve $- 2 x^{2} - 4 x + y - 2=3$ is a tangent vector perpendicular to $\mathbf v=\langle -8,1\rangle$?

Use $F(x,y)=- 2 x^{2} - 4 x + y - 2$ and $\mathbf t=\langle F_y,-F_x\rangle$. Perpendicular vectors have dot product zero.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $F(x,y)=- 2 x^{2} - 4 x + y - 2$, so the curve is $F(x,y)=3$. A tangent vector is $\mathbf t=\langle F_y,-F_x\rangle$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_x&=- 4 x - 4\\
F_y&=1\\
\mathbf t(x,y)&=\langle 1,4 x + 4\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

Perpendicularity requires

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf t\cdot \langle -8,1\rangle&=0\\
4 x - 4&=0\\
4 (x - 1)&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

The condition gives $x=1$. Substitution into the original curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
y - 8&=3
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $y=11$. Recovering the other coordinate gives $(1,11)$.

Thus the qualifying point is $(1,11)$. All listed points lie on the curve. The following nonzero tangent vectors check every choice:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf t(-3,11)&=\langle 1,-8\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle -8,1\rangle=-16\\
\mathbf t(-2,5)&=\langle 1,-4\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle -8,1\rangle=-12\\
\mathbf t(-1,3)&=\langle 1,0\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle -8,1\rangle=-8\\
\mathbf t(0,5)&=\langle 1,4\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle -8,1\rangle=-4\\
\mathbf t(1,11)&=\langle 1,8\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle -8,1\rangle=0
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
At which points on the curve $- 2 x^{3} - 9 x^{2} y - 13 x y^{2} - 6 y^{3}=2$ is a tangent vector perpendicular to $\mathbf v=\langle -2,-3\rangle$?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $F(x,y)=- 2 x^{3} - 9 x^{2} y - 13 x y^{2} - 6 y^{3}$, so the curve is $F(x,y)=2$. A tangent vector is $\mathbf t=\langle F_y,-F_x\rangle$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_x&=- 6 x^{2} - 18 x y - 13 y^{2}\\
F_y&=- 9 x^{2} - 26 x y - 18 y^{2}\\
\mathbf t(x,y)&=\langle - 9 x^{2} - 26 x y - 18 y^{2},6 x^{2} + 18 x y + 13 y^{2}\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

Perpendicularity requires

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf t\cdot \langle -2,-3\rangle&=0\\
- 2 x y - 3 y^{2}&=0\\
- y (2 x + 3 y)&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

The condition gives $y=0$. Substitution into the original curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
- 2 x^{3}&=2\\
- 2 x^{3}&=2\\
x^{3}&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $x=-1$. Recovering the other coordinate gives $(-1,0)$.

The condition gives $y=- \frac{2 x}{3}$. Substitution into the original curve gives $$
\begin{aligned}
0&=2
\end{aligned}
$$
This is impossible, so this branch supplies no points.

Thus the qualifying point is $(-1,0)$. All listed points lie on the curve. The following nonzero tangent vectors check every choice:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf t(-4,3)&=\langle 6,-3\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle -2,-3\rangle=-3\\
\mathbf t(5,-3)&=\langle 3,-3\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle -2,-3\rangle=3\\
\mathbf t(-1,0)&=\langle -9,6\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle -2,-3\rangle=0
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
At which points on the curve $x^{2} + 2 x + y^{2} + 1=25$ is a tangent vector perpendicular to $\mathbf v=\langle 4,-3\rangle$?

question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $F(x,y)=x^{2} + 2 x + y^{2} + 1$, so the curve is $F(x,y)=25$. A tangent vector is $\mathbf t=\langle F_y,-F_x\rangle$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_x&=2 x + 2\\
F_y&=2 y\\
\mathbf t(x,y)&=\langle 2 y,- 2 x - 2\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

Perpendicularity requires

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf t\cdot \langle 4,-3\rangle&=0\\
6 x + 8 y + 6&=0\\
2 (3 x + 4 y + 3)&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

The condition gives $y=- \frac{3 x}{4} - \frac{3}{4}$. Substitution into the original curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{25 x^{2}}{16} + \frac{25 x}{8} + \frac{25}{16}&=25\\
\frac{25 (x - 3) (x + 5)}{16}&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $x=-5$ or $x=3$. Recovering the other coordinate gives $(-5,3)$ and $(3,-3)$.

Thus the qualifying points are $(3,-3)$ and $(-5,3)$. All listed points lie on the curve. The following nonzero tangent vectors check every choice:

$$

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating Flux Through a Surface

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the signed flux

$$
\Phi=\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S
$$

for the vector field

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=\langle 1 - 2 x,y,- 2 z\rangle.
$$

The parametric surface is

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle u + v + 1,u,v\rangle.
$$

Use the parameter rectangle

$$
0\le u\le 2,\qquad 1\le v\le 3.
$$

Use the orientation induced by $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$. Enter an exact value.

*Hint:* The oriented area vector is

$$
\mathbf N=\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\langle 1,-1,-1\rangle.
$$

You may use

$$
\Phi=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv.
$$

$\Phi=$ {{flux}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the parametric flux formula with the specified orientation:

$$
\Phi=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv.
$$

Use the supplied oriented area vector $\mathbf N=\langle 1,-1,-1\rangle$.

Substitute the surface coordinates into the field:

$$
x=u + v + 1,\quad y=u,\quad z=v.
$$

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\langle - 2 u - 2 v - 1,u,- 2 v\rangle.
$$

Form the three signed dot-product contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1}&=(- 2 u - 2 v - 1)(1) \\ &=- 2 u- 2 v \\ &\quad {}-1 \\ T_{2}&=(u)(-1) \\ &=- u \\ T_{3}&=(- 2 v)(-1) \\ &=2 v\end{aligned}
$$

Collect the polynomial terms, writing $g(u,v)=T_1+T_2+T_3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(u,v)&=- 3 u-1\end{aligned}
$$

A primitive with respect to $v$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(u,v)&=- 3 u v- v\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate both inner endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}H(u)&=\int_{1}^{3}g(u,v)\,\mathrm dv \\ &=\left[P(u,v)\right]_{v=1}^{v=3}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}H(u)&=- 6 u-2\end{aligned}
$$

A primitive of $H(u)$ with respect to $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(u)&=- 3 u^{2}- 2 u\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate both outer endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\Phi&=\int_{0}^{2}H(u)\,\mathrm du \\ &=\left[Q(u)\right]_{u=0}^{u=2} \\ &=-16.\end{aligned}
$$

The cross product includes the surface area scale; there is no extra normalization factor.

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating Flux Through a Surface

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the signed flux

$$
\Phi=\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S
$$

for the vector field

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=\langle 6 y z,- x,3\rangle.
$$

The parametric surface is

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle 1 - 2 u,u v^{2},-1\rangle.
$$

Use the parameter rectangle

$$
2\le u\le 4,\qquad 1\le v\le 3.
$$

Use the orientation induced by $\mathbf r_v\times\mathbf r_u$. Enter an exact value.

$\Phi=$ {{flux}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the parametric flux formula with the specified orientation:

$$
\Phi=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv.
$$

Differentiate the parametrization:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle -2,v^{2},0\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v&=\langle 0,2 u v,0\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Compute the cross product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k \\ -2&v^{2}&0 \\ 0&2 u v&0\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\langle 0,0,- 4 u v\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Reverse its sign for the specified order:

$$
\mathbf N=-\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\langle 0,0,4 u v\rangle.
$$

Substitute the surface coordinates into the field:

$$
x=1 - 2 u,\quad y=u v^{2},\quad z=-1.
$$

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\langle - 6 u v^{2},2 u - 1,3\rangle.
$$

Form the three signed dot-product contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1}&=(- 6 u v^{2})(0) \\ &=0 \\ T_{2}&=(2 u - 1)(0) \\ &=0 \\ T_{3}&=(3)(4 u v) \\ &=12 u v\end{aligned}
$$

Collect the polynomial terms, writing $g(u,v)=T_1+T_2+T_3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(u,v)&=12 u v\end{aligned}
$$

A primitive with respect to $v$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(u,v)&=6 u v^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate both inner endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}H(u)&=\int_{1}^{3}g(u,v)\,\mathrm dv \\ &=\left[P(u,v)\right]_{v=1}^{v=3}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}H(u)&=48 u\end{aligned}
$$

A primitive of $H(u)$ with respect to $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(u)&=24 u^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate both outer endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\Phi&=\int_{2}^{4}H(u)\,\mathrm du \\ &=\left[Q(u)\right]_{u=2}^{u=4} \\ &=288.\end{aligned}
$$

The cross product includes the surface area scale; there is no extra normalization factor.

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the signed flux

$$
\Phi=\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S
$$

for the vector field

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=\langle -3,3 y,2 z^{2}\rangle.
$$

The parametric surface is

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle - v,3 u v,u\rangle.
$$

Use the parameter rectangle

$$
0\le u\le 2,\qquad 1\le v\le 3.
$$

Use the orientation induced by $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$. Enter an exact value.

*Hint:* The oriented area vector is

$$
\mathbf N=\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\langle - 3 u,-1,3 v\rangle.
$$

$\Phi=$ {{flux}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the parametric flux formula with the specified orientation:

$$
\Phi=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv.
$$

Use the supplied oriented area vector $\mathbf N=\langle - 3 u,-1,3 v\rangle$.

Substitute the surface coordinates into the field:

$$
x=- v,\quad y=3 u v,\quad z=u.
$$

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\langle -3,9 u v,2 u^{2}\rangle.
$$

Form the three signed dot-product contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{1}&=(-3)(- 3 u) \\ &=9 u \\ T_{2}&=(9 u v)(-1) \\ &=- 9 u v \\ T_{3}&=(2 u^{2})(3 v) \\ &=6 u^{2} v\end{aligned}
$$

Collect the polynomial terms, writing $g(u,v)=T_1+T_2+T_3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(u,v)&=6 u^{2} v- 9 u v \\ &\quad {}+9 u\end{aligned}
$$

A primitive with respect to $v$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(u,v)&=3 u^{2} v^{2}- \frac{9 u v^{2}}{2} \\ &\quad {}+9 u v\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate both inner endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}H(u)&=\int_{1}^{3}g(u,v)\,\mathrm dv \\ &=\left[P(u,v)\right]_{v=1}^{v=3}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}H(u)&=24 u^{2}- 18 u\end{aligned}
$$

A primitive of $H(u)$ with respect to $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(u)&=8 u^{3}- 9 u^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate both outer endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\Phi&=\int_{0}^{2}H(u)\,\mathrm du \\ &=\left[Q(u)\right]_{u=0}^{u=2} \\ &=28.\end{aligned}
$$

The cross product includes the surface area scale; there is no extra normalization factor.

knowledge_point.title: Expressing Flux Through a Surface as a Double Integral

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ parametrized by $\mathbf r(u,v)$ for $D=(0,1)\times(0,1)$, where

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=\left\langle - 2 x z,\,- y,\,- 3 x z\right\rangle.
$$

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\left\langle u,\,u v,\,v\right\rangle.
$$

Orient $S$ in the direction of $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.

If

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D ?\,\mathrm dA,
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You may use $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\left\langle v,\,-1,\,u\right\rangle$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
The vector area element must agree with the specified orientation. Use the supplied cross product:

$$
\mathbf N=\left\langle v,\,-1,\,u\right\rangle.
$$

For this orientation,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N(u,v)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Substitute $x=u$, $y=u v$, $z=v$ into the field:

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\left\langle - 2 u v,\,- u v,\,- 3 u v\right\rangle.
$$

Compute the three component contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{x} & =\left(- 2 u v\right)\left(v\right) \\  & =- 2 u v^{2} \\ T_{y} & =\left(- u v\right)\left(-1\right) \\  & =u v \\ T_{z} & =\left(- 3 u v\right)\left(u\right) \\  & =- 3 u^{2} v\end{aligned}
$$

Take the dot product component by component:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot\mathbf N & =T_x+T_y+T_z \\  & =- 3 u^{2} v - 2 u v^{2} + u v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\left(- 3 u^{2} v - 2 u v^{2} + u v\right)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ parametrized by $\mathbf r(u,v)$ for $D=(0,1)\times(0,2\pi)$, where

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=\left\langle - 2 x,\,- 2 y,\,- 3 z\right\rangle.
$$

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\left\langle u \cos{\left(v \right)},\,u \sin{\left(v \right)},\,u^{2}\right\rangle.
$$

Orient $S$ in the direction of $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.

If

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D ?\,\mathrm dA,
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You may use $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\left\langle - 2 u^{2} \cos{\left(v \right)},\,- 2 u^{2} \sin{\left(v \right)},\,u\right\rangle$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
The vector area element must agree with the specified orientation. Use the supplied cross product:

$$
\mathbf N=\left\langle - 2 u^{2} \cos{\left(v \right)},\,- 2 u^{2} \sin{\left(v \right)},\,u\right\rangle.
$$

For this orientation,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N(u,v)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Substitute $x=u \cos{\left(v \right)}$, $y=u \sin{\left(v \right)}$, $z=u^{2}$ into the field:

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\left\langle - 2 u \cos{\left(v \right)},\,- 2 u \sin{\left(v \right)},\,- 3 u^{2}\right\rangle.
$$

Compute the three component contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{x} & =\left(- 2 u \cos{\left(v \right)}\right)\left(- 2 u^{2} \cos{\left(v \right)}\right) \\  & =4 u^{3} \cos^{2}{\left(v \right)} \\ T_{y} & =\left(- 2 u \sin{\left(v \right)}\right)\left(- 2 u^{2} \sin{\left(v \right)}\right) \\  & =4 u^{3} \sin^{2}{\left(v \right)} \\ T_{z} & =\left(- 3 u^{2}\right)\left(u\right) \\  & =- 3 u^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Take the dot product and use $\cos^2 v+\sin^2 v=1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot\mathbf N & =T_x+T_y+T_z \\  & =4 u^{3}(\cos^2 v+\sin^2 v)+- 3 u^{3} \\  & =u^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\left(u^{3}\right)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ parametrized by $\mathbf r(u,v)$ for $D=(0,1)\times(0,1)$, where

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=\left\langle - 2 x - y,\,- 3 z,\,2 y - 3 z\right\rangle.
$$

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\left\langle - u^{2},\,2 u^{2} - v^{2},\,v^{2}\right\rangle.
$$

Orient $S$ in the direction of $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.

If

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D ?\,\mathrm dA,
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You may use $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\left\langle 8 u v,\,4 u v,\,4 u v\right\rangle$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
The vector area element must agree with the specified orientation. Use the supplied cross product:

$$
\mathbf N=\left\langle 8 u v,\,4 u v,\,4 u v\right\rangle.
$$

For this orientation,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N(u,v)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Substitute $x=- u^{2}$, $y=2 u^{2} - v^{2}$, $z=v^{2}$ into the field:

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\left\langle v^{2},\,- 3 v^{2},\,4 u^{2} - 5 v^{2}\right\rangle.
$$

Compute the three component contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{x} & =\left(v^{2}\right)\left(8 u v\right) \\  & =8 u v^{3} \\ T_{y} & =\left(- 3 v^{2}\right)\left(4 u v\right) \\  & =- 12 u v^{3} \\ T_{z} & =\left(4 u^{2} - 5 v^{2}\right)\left(4 u v\right) \\  & =16 u^{3} v - 20 u v^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Take the dot product component by component:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot\mathbf N & =T_x+T_y+T_z \\  & =16 u^{3} v - 24 u v^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\left(16 u^{3} v - 24 u v^{3}\right)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=\left\langle - 3 x,\,2 y,\,z\right\rangle.
$$

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\left\langle u^{2},\,- u v,\,v^{2}\right\rangle.
$$

Orient $S$ in the direction of $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.

If

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D ?\,\mathrm dA,
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You may use $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\left\langle - 2 v^{2},\,- 4 u v,\,- 2 u^{2}\right\rangle$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
The vector area element must agree with the specified orientation. Use the supplied cross product:

$$
\mathbf N=\left\langle - 2 v^{2},\,- 4 u v,\,- 2 u^{2}\right\rangle.
$$

For this orientation,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N(u,v)\,\mathrm dA.

Substitute $x=u^{2}$, $y=- u v$, $z=v^{2}$ into the field:

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\left\langle - 3 u^{2},\,- 2 u v,\,v^{2}\right\rangle.
$$

Compute the three component contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{x} & =\left(- 3 u^{2}\right)\left(- 2 v^{2}\right) \\  & =6 u^{2} v^{2} \\ T_{y} & =\left(- 2 u v\right)\left(- 4 u v\right) \\  & =8 u^{2} v^{2} \\ T_{z} & =\left(v^{2}\right)\left(- 2 u^{2}\right) \\  & =- 2 u^{2} v^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Take the dot product component by component:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot\mathbf N & =T_x+T_y+T_z \\  & =12 u^{2} v^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\left(12 u^{2} v^{2}\right)\,\mathrm dA.

$$

$$

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\left\langle u^{2},\,v,\,u\right\rangle.
$$

Orient $S$ in the direction of $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.

If

$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You may use $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\left\langle -1,\,0,\,2 u\right\rangle$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
The vector area element must agree with the specified orientation. Use the supplied cross product:

$$
\mathbf N=\left\langle -1,\,0,\,2 u\right\rangle.
$$

For this orientation,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N(u,v)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Substitute $x=u^{2}$, $y=v$, $z=u$ into the field:

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\left\langle - 2 u^{2},\,- v^{2},\,- 3 u^{2}\right\rangle.
$$

Compute the three component contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{x} & =\left(- 2 u^{2}\right)\left(-1\right) \\  & =2 u^{2} \\ T_{y} & =\left(- v^{2}\right)\left(0\right) \\  & =0 \\ T_{z} & =\left(- 3 u^{2}\right)\left(2 u\right) \\  & =- 6 u^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Take the dot product component by component:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot\mathbf N & =T_x+T_y+T_z \\  & =- 6 u^{3} + 2 u^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\left(- 6 u^{3} + 2 u^{2}\right)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

$$

$$

Orient $S$ in the direction of $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.

If

$$

*Hint: You may use $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\left\langle - 3 v^{3},\,- 3 u^{3},\,9 u^{2} v^{2}\right\rangle$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:

knowledge_point.title: Expressing Flux Through a Surface as a Double Integral

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ parametrized by $\mathbf r(u,v)$ for $D=(0,1)\times(0,1)$, where

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=\left\langle - 3 x y,\,- 2 x,\,- z\right\rangle.
$$

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\left\langle u,\,v,\,u v^{2}\right\rangle.
$$

Orient $S$ so that its unit normal has a **positive $z$-component**.

If

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D ?\,\mathrm dA,
$$

what is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The vector area element must agree with the specified orientation. First compute the tangent vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u & =\left\langle 1,\,0,\,v^{2}\right\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v & =\left\langle 0,\,1,\,2 u v\right\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Their ordered cross product is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1&0&v^{2}\\0&1&2 u v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle - v^{2},\,- 2 u v,\,1\right\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Its $z$-component is positive. Keep this direction to satisfy the stated orientation:

$$
\mathbf N=(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)=\left\langle - v^{2},\,- 2 u v,\,1\right\rangle.
$$

For this orientation,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N(u,v)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Substitute $x=u$, $y=v$, $z=u v^{2}$ into the field:

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\left\langle - 3 u v,\,- 2 u,\,- u v^{2}\right\rangle.
$$

Compute the three component contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{x} & =\left(- 3 u v\right)\left(- v^{2}\right) \\  & =3 u v^{3} \\ T_{y} & =\left(- 2 u\right)\left(- 2 u v\right) \\  & =4 u^{2} v \\ T_{z} & =\left(- u v^{2}\right)\left(1\right) \\  & =- u v^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Take the dot product component by component:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot\mathbf N & =T_x+T_y+T_z \\  & =4 u^{2} v + 3 u v^{3} - u v^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\left(4 u^{2} v + 3 u v^{3} - u v^{2}\right)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Expressing Flux Through a Surface as a Double Integral

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ parametrized by $\mathbf r(u,v)$ for $D=(0,1)\times(0,1)$, where

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=\left\langle -2,\,0,\,-1\right\rangle.
$$

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\left\langle u + v,\,u^{2} + v,\,u^{3} + 3 v\right\rangle.
$$

Orient $S$ in the direction of $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.

If

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D (a u^{2} + b u + c)\,\mathrm dA,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The vector area element must agree with the specified orientation. First compute the tangent vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u & =\left\langle 1,\,2 u,\,3 u^{2}\right\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v & =\left\langle 1,\,1,\,3\right\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Their ordered cross product is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1&2 u&3 u^{2}\\1&1&3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle - 3 u^{2} + 6 u,\,3 u^{2} - 3,\,1 - 2 u\right\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Use $\mathbf N=\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.

For this orientation,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N(u,v)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Substitute $x=u + v$, $y=u^{2} + v$, $z=u^{3} + 3 v$ into the field:

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\left\langle -2,\,0,\,-1\right\rangle.
$$

Compute the three component contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{x} & =\left(-2\right)\left(- 3 u^{2} + 6 u\right) \\  & =6 u^{2} - 12 u \\ T_{y} & =\left(0\right)\left(3 u^{2} - 3\right) \\  & =0 \\ T_{z} & =\left(-1\right)\left(1 - 2 u\right) \\  & =2 u - 1\end{aligned}
$$

Take the dot product component by component:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot\mathbf N & =T_x+T_y+T_z \\  & =6 u^{2} - 10 u - 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\left(6 u^{2} - 10 u - 1\right)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Matching coefficients gives $a=6$, $b=-10$, $c=-1$. Hence

$$
a+b+c=(6)+(-10)+(-1)=-5.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ parametrized by $\mathbf r(u,v)$ for $D=(0,1)\times(0,1)$, where

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=\left\langle x + \frac{3}{z},\,y + \frac{2}{z},\,z\right\rangle.
$$

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\left\langle u e^{v},\,u e^{- v},\,u\right\rangle.
$$

Orient $S$ in the direction of $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.

If

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D (a e^{v} + b e^{- v})\,\mathrm dA,
$$

what is the value of $a+b$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The vector area element must agree with the specified orientation. First compute the tangent vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u & =\left\langle e^{v},\,e^{- v},\,1\right\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v & =\left\langle u e^{v},\,- u e^{- v},\,0\right\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Their ordered cross product is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\e^{v}&e^{- v}&1\\u e^{v}&- u e^{- v}&0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle u e^{- v},\,u e^{v},\,- 2 u\right\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Use $\mathbf N=\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.

For this orientation,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N(u,v)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Substitute $x=u e^{v}$, $y=u e^{- v}$, $z=u$ into the field:

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\left\langle u e^{v} + \frac{3}{u},\,u e^{- v} + \frac{2}{u},\,u\right\rangle.
$$

Compute the three component contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{x} & =\left(u e^{v} + \frac{3}{u}\right)\left(u e^{- v}\right) \\  & =u^{2} + 3 e^{- v} \\ T_{y} & =\left(u e^{- v} + \frac{2}{u}\right)\left(u e^{v}\right) \\  & =u^{2} + 2 e^{v} \\ T_{z} & =\left(u\right)\left(- 2 u\right) \\  & =- 2 u^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Take the dot product component by component:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot\mathbf N & =T_x+T_y+T_z \\  & =2 e^{v} + 3 e^{- v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\left(2 e^{v} + 3 e^{- v}\right)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Matching coefficients gives $a=2$, $b=3$. Hence

$$
a+b=(2)+(3)=5.
$$

The vector area element must agree with the specified orientation. First compute the tangent vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u & =\left\langle v,\,1,\,0\right\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v & =\left\langle u,\,1,\,-1\right\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Their ordered cross product is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\v&1&0\\u&1&-1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle -1,\,v,\,- u + v\right\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Use $\mathbf N=\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$.

For this orientation,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\mathbf N(u,v)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Substitute $x=u v$, $y=u + v$, $z=1 - v$ into the field:

$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=\left\langle 3 u v^{2} - 3 u v,\,2 u + 2 v,\,1\right\rangle.
$$

Compute the three component contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}T_{x} & =\left(3 u v^{2} - 3 u v\right)\left(-1\right) \\  & =- 3 u v^{2} + 3 u v \\ T_{y} & =\left(2 u + 2 v\right)\left(v\right) \\  & =2 u v + 2 v^{2} \\ T_{z} & =\left(1\right)\left(- u + v\right) \\  & =- u + v\end{aligned}
$$

Take the dot product component by component:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot\mathbf N & =T_x+T_y+T_z \\  & =- 3 u v^{2} + 5 u v - u + 2 v^{2} + v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf S=\iint_D\left(- 3 u v^{2} + 5 u v - u + 2 v^{2} + v\right)\,\mathrm dA.
$$

Matching coefficients gives $a=-3$, $b=2$, $c=5$. Hence

$$
a+b+c=(-3)+(2)+(5)=4.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the following lines.

$$
\begin{aligned}2 x - y&=-3,\qquad 2 x - y=2, \\ x - 2 y&=-3,\qquad x - 2 y=1.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
**Step 1: Choose coordinates.** Rewrite each boundary using its shared expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}2 x - y&=-3,\qquad 2 x - y=2, \\ x - 2 y&=-3,\qquad x - 2 y=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $u=2 x - y$ and $v=x - 2 y$.

**Step 2: Map the boundaries.** The four boundaries become $u=-3$, $u=2$, $v=-3$, and $v=1$. Therefore

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):-3\leq u\leq 2,\ -3\leq v\leq 1\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186129262/rectangle-4c1e7a294f06da50.png)

**Step 3: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}2&-1 \\ 1&-2\end{vmatrix} \\ &=-3\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4: Take the reciprocal and its magnitude.** The inverse is

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=\frac{2 u}{3} - \frac{v}{3}, \\ y&=\frac{u}{3} - \frac{2 v}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant is nonzero, so this linear inverse is defined everywhere. Area uses the absolute value of the reciprocal determinant:

$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\left|\frac{1}{-3}\right|=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

**Step 5: Integrate over the rectangle.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\iint_{\Delta}\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\int_{-3}^{1}\int_{-3}^{2}1\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\left(2-(-3)\right)\cdot\left(1-(-3)\right) \\ &=\frac{20}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the following curves and lines.

$$
\begin{aligned}y&=\frac{5}{x},\qquad y=\frac{7}{x}, \\ x&=3 y^{2},\qquad x=4 y^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
**Step 1: Choose coordinates.** Rewrite each boundary using its shared expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}x y&=5,\qquad x y=7, \\ \frac{x}{y^{2}}&=3,\qquad \frac{x}{y^{2}}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $u=x y$ and $v=\frac{x}{y^{2}}$.

**Step 2: Map the boundaries.** The four boundaries become $u=5$, $u=7$, $v=3$, and $v=4$. Therefore

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):5\leq u\leq 7,\ 3\leq v\leq 4\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186129262/rectangle-eeb362a486097e36.png)

**Step 3: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}y&x \\ \frac{1}{y^{2}}&- \frac{2 x}{y^{3}}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=- \frac{3 x}{y^{2}} \\ &=- 3 v.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4: Take the reciprocal and its magnitude.** The inverse is

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=u^{\frac{2}{3}} \sqrt[3]{v}, \\ y&=\frac{\sqrt[3]{u}}{\sqrt[3]{v}}.\end{aligned}
$$

These formulas give the unique positive inverse on the whole rectangle. Area uses the absolute value of the reciprocal determinant:

$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\left|\frac{1}{- 3 v}\right|=\frac{1}{3 v}.
$$

**Step 5: Integrate over the rectangle.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\iint_{\Delta}\frac{1}{3 v}\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv \\ &=\int_{3}^{4}\int_{5}^{7}\frac{1}{3 v}\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\left(\ln(4)-\ln(3)\right) \\ &=\frac{2}{3}\ln\left(\frac{4}{3}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

The last step uses the logarithm quotient rule: $\ln(4)-\ln(3)=\ln\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)$.

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the following lines.

$$
\begin{aligned}2 y&=3 x - 3,\qquad 2 y=3 x - 8, \\ 2 x&=3 y + 2,\qquad 2 x=3 y + 6.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
**Step 1: Choose coordinates.** Rewrite each boundary using its shared expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}3 x - 2 y&=3,\qquad 3 x - 2 y=8, \\ 2 x - 3 y&=2,\qquad 2 x - 3 y=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $u=3 x - 2 y$ and $v=2 x - 3 y$.

**Step 2: Map the boundaries.** The four boundaries become $u=3$, $u=8$, $v=2$, and $v=6$. Therefore

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):3\leq u\leq 8,\ 2\leq v\leq 6\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186129262/rectangle-b48a1d910cbfd221.png)

**Step 3: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}3&-2 \\ 2&-3\end{vmatrix} \\ &=-5\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4: Take the reciprocal and its magnitude.** The inverse is

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=\frac{3 u}{5} - \frac{2 v}{5}, \\ y&=\frac{2 u}{5} - \frac{3 v}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant is nonzero, so this linear inverse is defined everywhere. Area uses the absolute value of the reciprocal determinant:

$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\left|\frac{1}{-5}\right|=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

**Step 5: Integrate over the rectangle.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\iint_{\Delta}\frac{1}{5}\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv \\ &=\frac{1}{5}\int_{2}^{6}\int_{3}^{8}1\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv \\ &=\frac{1}{5}\cdot\left(8-(3)\right)\cdot\left(6-(2)\right) \\ &=4.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\int 7 xe^{6 x}\,\text{d}x=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 7 xe^{6 x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =7 x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=7 \\ {v}^{′} & =e^{6 x}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{e^{6 x}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 7 x\cdot e^{6 x}\,\text{d}x & =7 x\cdot \frac{e^{6 x}}{6}-\int \frac{e^{6 x}}{6}\cdot 7\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 7 xe^{6 x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot 7 xe^{6 x}-\frac{7}{6}\cdot \int e^{6 x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot 7 xe^{6 x}-\frac{7}{36}\cdot e^{6 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting the linear terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 7 xe^{6 x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\frac{7 x e^{6 x}}{6} - \frac{7 e^{6 x}}{36}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate 

$$
\int (6 x + 7)e^{- 7 x}\,\text{d}x.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int (6 x + 7)e^{- 7 x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =6 x + 7\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=6 \\ {v}^{′} & =e^{- 7 x}\, & ⟹\,v=- \frac{e^{- 7 x}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (6 x + 7)\cdot e^{- 7 x}\,\text{d}x & =(6 x + 7)\cdot \left(- \frac{e^{- 7 x}}{7}\right)-\int \left(- \frac{e^{- 7 x}}{7}\right)\cdot 6\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (6 x + 7)e^{- 7 x}\,\text{d}x & =- \frac{1}{7}\cdot (6 x + 7)e^{- 7 x}+\frac{6}{7}\cdot \int e^{- 7 x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =- \frac{1}{7}\cdot (6 x + 7)e^{- 7 x}-\frac{6}{49}\cdot e^{- 7 x}+C \\  & =-\frac{(6 x + \frac{55}{7})e^{- 7 x}}{7}+C \\  & =\left(- \frac{42 x + 55}{49}\right)e^{- 7 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting the linear terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (6 x + 7)e^{- 7 x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\left(- \frac{6 x}{7} - \frac{55}{49}\right)e^{- 7 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

We need to express $\int x5^{x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 6 xe^{7 x + 7}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =6 x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=6 \\ {v}^{′} & =e^{7 x + 7}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{e^{7 x + 7}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 6 x\cdot e^{7 x + 7}\,\text{d}x & =6 x\cdot \frac{e^{7 x + 7}}{7}-\int \frac{e^{7 x + 7}}{7}\cdot 6\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6 xe^{7 x + 7}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot 6 xe^{7 x + 7}-\frac{6}{7}\cdot \int e^{7 x + 7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot 6 xe^{7 x + 7}-\frac{6}{49}\cdot e^{7 x + 7}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting the linear terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6 xe^{7 x + 7}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\frac{6 x e^{7 x + 7}}{7} - \frac{6 e^{7 x + 7}}{49}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- 2 x^{2} - x y - 3 y=-10$. Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point $(-2,2)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $f(x,y)=- 2 x^{2} - x y - 3 y$. The curve is the level curve $f(x,y)=-10$, and $f(-2,2)=-10$ confirms that the point lies on it.

A tangent vector is perpendicular to the nonzero gradient. Use $\mathbf t=f_y\mathbf i-f_x\mathbf j$. Differentiate while holding the other variable constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=- 4 x - y\\ f_y(x,y)&=- x - 3\end{aligned}
$$

At the supplied point,

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(-2,2)&=- 4 \left(-2\right) - \left(2\right)\\ &=6\\ f_y(-2,2)&=- \left(-2\right) - 3\\ &=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus one tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf t(-2,2)=-\mathbf i-6\,\mathbf j.
$$

The gradient is nonzero. The dot product is

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(-2,2)\cdot\mathbf t(-2,2)&=\left(6\right)\left(-1\right)\\ &\quad-\left(-1\right)\left(6\right)\\ &=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Any nonzero scalar multiple has the same tangent direction; none of the other listed vectors is perpendicular to this gradient.

$$

$$

The gradient is nonzero. The dot product is

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- 2 e^{x y}=x + 3 y - 4 - \frac{2}{e^{4}}$. Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point $(-2,2)$.

Bring the variable terms to one side and set $f(x,y)=- x - 3 y - 2 e^{x y}$. The curve is the level curve $f(x,y)=-4 - \frac{2}{e^{4}}$, and $f(-2,2)=-4 - \frac{2}{e^{4}}$ confirms that the point lies on it.

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=- 2 y e^{x y} - 1\\ f_y(x,y)&=- 2 x e^{x y} - 3\end{aligned}
$$

At the supplied point,

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(-2,2)&=- 2 \left(2\right) e^{\left(-2\right) \left(2\right)} - 1\\ &=-1 - \frac{4}{e^{4}}\\ f_y(-2,2)&=- 2 \left(-2\right) e^{\left(-2\right) \left(2\right)} - 3\\ &=-3 + \frac{4}{e^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

The gradient is nonzero. The dot product is

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(-2,2)\cdot\mathbf t(-2,2)&=\left(-1 - \frac{4}{e^{4}}\right)\left(-3 + \frac{4}{e^{4}}\right)\\ &\quad-\left(-3 + \frac{4}{e^{4}}\right)\left(-1 - \frac{4}{e^{4}}\right)\\ &=0.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(1,e)\cdot\mathbf t(1,e)&=\left(- e\right)\left(-1 - \frac{2}{e}\right)\\ &\quad-\left(-1 - \frac{2}{e}\right)\left(- e\right)\\ &=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Any nonzero scalar multiple has the same tangent direction; none of the other listed vectors is perpendicular to this gradient.

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=2 x + y,\qquad v=- x + y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the lines

$$
\begin{aligned}y &=2 - 2 x,\qquad y=x - 4, \\ y &=5 - 2 x,\qquad y=x + 1.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The supplied map sends $(x,y)$ to $(u,v)$. The area formula uses the absolute determinant of its *inverse*.

$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_\Delta\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v.
$$

**Step 1: Map the boundaries.**

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2 - 2 x&\Longrightarrow u=2. \\ y=5 - 2 x&\Longrightarrow u=5. \\ y=x - 4&\Longrightarrow v=-4. \\ y=x + 1&\Longrightarrow v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):2\leq u\leq 5,\quad -4\leq v\leq 1\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle; the two axes may use different scales.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186129261/rectangle-04e471c48b11f713da341833d9d3977857fbd9c29dd6fa587958752d7d9085b5.png)

**Step 2: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: Express the inverse area factor in the new coordinates.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=\frac{1}{3} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

The affine determinant is nonzero, so the map is one-to-one.

**Step 4: Integrate over the rectangle.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{2}^{5}\int_{-4}^{1}\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left[u\right]_{2}^{5}\left[v\right]_{-4}^{1} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left(5-(2)\right)\left(1-(-4)\right) \\ &=5.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=x y^{2},\qquad v=x^{2} y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{27}{y^{2}},\qquad x=\frac{64}{y^{2}}, \\ y &=\frac{27}{x^{2}},\qquad y=\frac{1}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The supplied map sends $(x,y)$ to $(u,v)$. The area formula uses the absolute determinant of its *inverse*.

$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_\Delta\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v.
$$

**Step 1: Map the boundaries.**

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{27}{y^{2}}&\Longrightarrow u=27. \\ x=\frac{64}{y^{2}}&\Longrightarrow u=64. \\ y=\frac{1}{x^{2}}&\Longrightarrow v=1. \\ y=\frac{27}{x^{2}}&\Longrightarrow v=27.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):27\leq u\leq 64,\quad 1\leq v\leq 27\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle; the two axes may use different scales.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186129261/rectangle-f39c6a9c0cc4e61da3eb716664acc5262adb9685fd30b0510c2bd22d049162ed.png)

**Step 2: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}y^{2} & 2 x y \\ 2 x y & x^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=- 3 x^{2} y^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: Express the inverse area factor in the new coordinates.**

Both coordinates are positive. Multiplying the supplied expressions gives

$$
uv=x^3y^3=(xy)^3,\qquad x^2y^2=(uv)^{2/3}.
$$



$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=- \frac{1}{3 x^{2} y^{2}} \\ &=- \frac{1}{3 u^{\frac{2}{3}} v^{\frac{2}{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac{1}{3 u^{\frac{2}{3}} v^{\frac{2}{3}}}.
$$

The positive inverse is unique:

$$
x=\frac{v^{\frac{2}{3}}}{\sqrt[3]{u}},\qquad y=\frac{u^{\frac{2}{3}}}{\sqrt[3]{v}}.
$$

These expressions are defined throughout the positive rectangle, and the determinant never vanishes.

**Step 4: Integrate over the rectangle.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{27}^{64}\int_{1}^{27}\frac{1}{3 u^{\frac{2}{3}} v^{\frac{2}{3}}}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left[3 \sqrt[3]{u}\right]_{27}^{64}\left[3 \sqrt[3]{v}\right]_{1}^{27} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left(12-(9)\right)\left(9-(3)\right) \\ &=6.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=x y,\qquad v=\frac{y^{2}}{x},
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{y^{2}}{5},\qquad y=\frac{4}{x}, \\ x &=\frac{y^{2}}{3},\qquad y=\frac{2}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The supplied map sends $(x,y)$ to $(u,v)$. The area formula uses the absolute determinant of its *inverse*.

$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_\Delta\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v.
$$

**Step 1: Map the boundaries.**

$$
\begin{aligned}y=\frac{2}{x}&\Longrightarrow u=2. \\ y=\frac{4}{x}&\Longrightarrow u=4. \\ x=\frac{y^{2}}{3}&\Longrightarrow v=3. \\ x=\frac{y^{2}}{5}&\Longrightarrow v=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):2\leq u\leq 4,\quad 3\leq v\leq 5\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle; the two axes may use different scales.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186129261/rectangle-13c7db0fad8cf26467f308d6c18699f0e977154c04b37a77e7594c927f706756.png)

**Step 2: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}y & x \\ - \frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}} & \frac{2 y}{x}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\frac{3 y^{2}}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: Express the inverse area factor in the new coordinates.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=\frac{x}{3 y^{2}} \\ &=\frac{1}{3 v}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac{1}{3 v}.
$$

The positive inverse is unique:

$$
x=\frac{u^{\frac{2}{3}}}{\sqrt[3]{v}},\qquad y=\sqrt[3]{u} \sqrt[3]{v}.
$$

These expressions are defined throughout the positive rectangle, and the determinant never vanishes.

**Step 4: Integrate over the rectangle.**

For the logarithmic endpoint difference, use $\ln A-\ln B=\ln(A/B)$ and $\ln(a^m)=m\ln a$ for positive arguments.

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln 5-\ln 3&=\ln\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)=- \ln{\left(3 \right)} + \ln{\left(5 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{2}^{4}\int_{3}^{5}\frac{1}{3 v}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left[u\right]_{2}^{4}\left[\ln{\left(v \right)}\right]_{3}^{5} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left(4-(2)\right)\left(\ln{\left(5 \right)}-(\ln{\left(3 \right)})\right) \\ &=- \frac{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{3} + \frac{2 \ln{\left(5 \right)}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{2}^{4}\int_{3}^{5}\frac{1}{3 v}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left[u\right]_{2}^{4}\left[\ln{\left(v \right)}\right]_{3}^{5} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left(4-(2)\right)\left(\ln{\left(5 \right)}-(\ln{\left(3 \right)})\right) \\ &=- \frac{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{3} + \frac{2 \ln{\left(5 \right)}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=x^{2} y,\qquad v=\frac{1}{x y},
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
\begin{aligned}y &=\frac{1}{5 x},\qquad y=\frac{4}{x^{2}}, \\ y &=\frac{1}{3 x},\qquad y=\frac{2}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The supplied map sends $(x,y)$ to $(u,v)$. The area formula uses the absolute determinant of its *inverse*.

$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_\Delta\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v.
$$

**Step 1: Map the boundaries.**

$$
\begin{aligned}y=\frac{2}{x^{2}}&\Longrightarrow u=2. \\ y=\frac{4}{x^{2}}&\Longrightarrow u=4. \\ y=\frac{1}{3 x}&\Longrightarrow v=3. \\ y=\frac{1}{5 x}&\Longrightarrow v=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):2\leq u\leq 4,\quad 3\leq v\leq 5\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle; the two axes may use different scales.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186129261/rectangle-13c7db0fad8cf26467f308d6c18699f0e977154c04b37a77e7594c927f706756.png)

**Step 2: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}2 x y & x^{2} \\ - \frac{1}{x^{2} y} & - \frac{1}{x y^{2}}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=- \frac{1}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: Express the inverse area factor in the new coordinates.**

The reciprocal simplifies using the supplied products:

$$
y=\frac{(xy)^2}{x^2y}=\frac{1}{v^2u}.
$$



$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=- y \\ &=- \frac{1}{u v^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac{1}{u v^{2}}.
$$

The positive inverse is unique:

$$
x=u v,\qquad y=\frac{1}{u v^{2}}.
$$

These expressions are defined throughout the positive rectangle, and the determinant never vanishes.

**Step 4: Integrate over the rectangle.**

For the logarithmic endpoint difference, use $\ln A-\ln B=\ln(A/B)$ and $\ln(a^m)=m\ln a$ for positive arguments.

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln 4-\ln 2&=\ln\left(\frac{4}{2}\right)=\ln{\left(2 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{2}^{4}\int_{3}^{5}\frac{1}{u v^{2}}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=1\left[\ln{\left(u \right)}\right]_{2}^{4}\left[- \frac{1}{v}\right]_{3}^{5} \\ &=1\left(2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}-(\ln{\left(2 \right)})\right)\left(- \frac{1}{5}-\left(- \frac{1}{3}\right)\right) \\ &=\frac{2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

These expressions are defined throughout the positive rectangle, and the determinant never vanishes.

\begin{aligned}\ln 5-\ln 3&=\ln\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)=- \ln{\left(3 \right)} + \ln{\left(5 \right)}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{2}^{4}\int_{3}^{5}\frac{1}{3 v}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left[u\right]_{2}^{4}\left[\ln{\left(v \right)}\right]_{3}^{5} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left(4-(2)\right)\left(\ln{\left(5 \right)}-(\ln{\left(3 \right)})\right) \\ &=- \frac{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{3} + \frac{2 \ln{\left(5 \right)}}{3}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y^{2}}{x},\qquad v=\frac{y}{x^{2}},
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
\begin{aligned}y &=5 x^{2},\qquad x=\frac{y^{2}}{4}, \\ y &=3 x^{2},\qquad x=\frac{y^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The supplied map sends $(x,y)$ to $(u,v)$. The area formula uses the absolute determinant of its *inverse*.

$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_\Delta\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v.
$$

**Step 1: Map the boundaries.**

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{y^{2}}{2}&\Longrightarrow u=2. \\ x=\frac{y^{2}}{4}&\Longrightarrow u=4. \\ y=3 x^{2}&\Longrightarrow v=3. \\ y=5 x^{2}&\Longrightarrow v=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):2\leq u\leq 4,\quad 3\leq v\leq 5\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle; the two axes may use different scales.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186129261/rectangle-13c7db0fad8cf26467f308d6c18699f0e977154c04b37a77e7594c927f706756.png)

**Step 2: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}- \frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}} & \frac{2 y}{x} \\ - \frac{2 y}{x^{3}} & \frac{1}{x^{2}}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\frac{3 y^{2}}{x^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: Express the inverse area factor in the new coordinates.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=\frac{x^{4}}{3 y^{2}} \\ &=\frac{1}{3 v^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac{1}{3 v^{2}}.
$$

The positive inverse is unique:

$$
x=\frac{\sqrt[3]{u}}{v^{\frac{2}{3}}},\qquad y=\frac{u^{\frac{2}{3}}}{\sqrt[3]{v}}.
$$

These expressions are defined throughout the positive rectangle, and the determinant never vanishes.

**Step 4: Integrate over the rectangle.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{2}^{4}\int_{3}^{5}\frac{1}{3 v^{2}}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left[u\right]_{2}^{4}\left[- \frac{1}{v}\right]_{3}^{5} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left(4-(2)\right)\left(- \frac{1}{5}-\left(- \frac{1}{3}\right)\right) \\ &=\frac{4}{45}.\end{aligned}
$$

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?

question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=9$ and the vertical radius has length $b=7.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{9}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{7}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{81}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{49} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
